News.title: Woke council chiefs ban staff from calling people ‘old’ over fears it will upset OAPs
News.content:
ONE of the most elderly parts of the UK has told staff not to use the word “old” – for fear of offending OAP residents.

Woke chiefs at New Forest District Council, where the average age of a resident is 52, have told workers they should not use terms that could be viewed as ageist.



Barred words include “the elderly”, “old”, “young” and “millennials” – the generational term for people born between 1981 and 1996.

In a language guide obtained by The Sun, diversity bosses wrote: “It’s usually unnecessary to refer to people using age-related descriptors.



“Think about it first.”

Instead, bosses reckon more suitable terms are “older people” and “younger people”.

Elsewhere, the baffling guide, issued to staff who work on the council’s website, warns that non-inclusive language could “alienate the people you’re creating content for”.

Other common language now thought to be too offensive includes “mentally ill”, “sick person”, “fireman/woman” and “ladies”.

It is the latest example of council staff being told to use person-first language.

The guide goes on: “Avoid medical labels. They say little about people as individuals and tend to reinforce stereotypes of disabled people as ‘patients’ or unwell.



“Use neutral, non-gendered terms for professions. Avoid patronising language.”

Gender should also not be a compulsory field on forms to avoid potentially upsetting non-binary residents.

Lord Young, of the Free Speech Union, said: “As usual, a local authority thinks it’s protecting the vulnerable by banning hurty words.

“If the New Forest district councillors really want to help local pensioners they should lay on more buses.

“But, of course, that’s expensive, while banning the word ‘old’ costs nothing.”



The New Forest was created by William the Conqueror in 1079 as a royal hunting ground for deer and wild boar.

Nearly 1,000 years later much of the ancient woodland remains untouched.

Famous residents include Dire Straits rock legend Mark Knopfler, 76, and F1 commentator Murray Walker, who lived there until his death aged 97 in 2021.

New Forest District Council was invited to comment.

News.title: Boy, 5, rushed to hospital as eight swimmers poisoned by chlorine fumes at pool in Rome
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SWIM SHOCK Boy, 5, rushed to hospital as eight swimmers poisoned by chlorine fumes at pool in Rome

A FIVE-YEAR-OLD boy is fighting for his life after eight swimmers were poisoned by chlorine fumes at a pool in Rome.

Four other children, aged between 10 and 15, were also treated after the incident in the Italian capital.



Around 20 people were in the water when they began to feel terrifying symptoms.

They included seven children under the age of 10.



They suffered intense burning in the eyes and throat, coughing, and shortness of breath.

The poisoning took place at a sports club in Mentana, on the outskirts of Rome.



Firefighters rushed to the scene around 3.30pm.

All fifty people were evacuated from the busy pool as poisonous fumes seeped out.

The boy was taken to Rome’s Sant’Andrea Hospital and the club was temporarily closed.

Police also attended the scene.



Investigators believe a leak caused the toxic chemical to poison swimmers.

It comes after five children drowned in Italian pools in just three months as experts warn of “death trap” drains.

An 11-year-old died last week after getting her hair got caught in a swimming pool drain.

The young girl, named Alice, was on a family holiday in the beach town of Sestri Levante, Italy, when tragedy struck.

She had travelled south from Milan for a sunny getaway with her mum.



The duo were at the same beach resort on the tourist town’s Descalzo promenade that they had stayed at several years in a row.

The horror incident happened in the indoor pool, where the water is cooler than the sea.

Despite the shallow water, her hair got stuck in the pool’s drain.

The force dragged Alice under water and was trapped.

Onlookers desperately tried to pull her out but struggled to disentangle her hair from the drain.



An ambulance rushed to the scene and paramedics attempted CPR.

She was taken by helicopter to hospital in nearby Genoa and put in intensive care in critical condition.

Tragically, she was pronounced dead in hospital.

Police are investigating the death and attended the scene.

Investigators are considering if swimming caps should be mandatory to swim in the shallow pool.

News.title: Labour MPs better hope that Burnham has got a better plan than he’s shared so far – our readers need much more from him
News.content:
No plan-dy

TODAY, barely two years after winning a huge General Election majority, Sir Keir Starmer will be ejected from No10.

There’s nothing to be gained from dwelling on what went wrong — basically, it was everything.



Indeed, it says much about the state of the Labour Party he led that, despite having 400 MPs, they replaced him by parachuting in a man who didn’t even stand in 2024. So enter, Andy Burnham — Labour’s messiah without a mandate.

Labour bristles at the idea the ex-mayor of Greater Manchester lacks legitimacy, pointing out the Tories repeatedly changed PMs between elections.



Yet Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak had all at least stood on the party’s manifesto, and been prominent Westminster figures.

Nobody casting a vote for Labour two years ago could have had any expectation Burnham would soon be foisted upon them. The only public endorsement he has is from 25,000 people in Makerfield, near Wigan — akin to about 0.1 per cent of the electorate.

Why does this matter? Because Burnham is threatening to impose the “most significant change” for 40 years.

The PM whose settlement he is most determined to destroy — Margaret Thatcher — had massive public consent. Burnham has next to none.

If — when — his Premiership goes wrong, he should expect the backlash to be ferocious.

So what should we expect from our new PM? To date, he’s shared mostly vibes, his Spotify playlist and his admiration for Neil Kinnock — a socialist relic twice decisively rejected by voters.



All indications are that he wants to drag the country to the Left — or, more specifically, back to the 1970s. This means re-nationalisation, a huge programme of council house building and vicious taxes on anybody who grows wealthy.

He’ll set up an outpost of No10 in Manchester — the Prime Ministerial equivalent of WFH. On mass immigration, the flat-lining economy, the ballooning welfare bill and our threadbare defences, he has said next to nothing.

His team has hinted he may allow some drilling in the North Sea. Don’t let him fool you into thinking this alone brings an end to the Net Zero madness — it emphatically does not.

We wish our new PM well — Britain can’t continue lurching from crisis to political crisis, leaving would-be investors in despair. But our readers need to hear much more from Burnham about how he is going to improve their lives.

How is he going to reward strivers over skivers, and end the scandal of one million young people not in jobs, education or training? How will he fix our broken borders, ensure the deportation of foreign rapists and killers and get a grip on shoplifting and violent crime?



These are the issues that REALLY matter — and which Labour promised to sort out at the last election, before failing catastrophically to do so.

Nobody — save for a few hundred Labour MPs desperate to save their own skin — has put Burnham in No10.

Those MPs better hope and pray that he’s got a better plan than he’s shared so far.

News.title: Brit troops war-game ‘punishing’ jet-powered drone strikes on Vladimir Putin’s home city of St Petersburg
News.content:
THE Army has war-gamed strikes on Vladimir Putin’s home city of St Petersburg with new jet-powered drones.

The Sun met Royal Artillery gunners armed with Nyan one-way attack aircraft at their base on Nato’s eastern frontier in Estonia.



The drones have a range of more than 150 miles and are designed to destroy targets such as oil depots, ammunition dumps and military command posts.

The base at Tapa is almost exactly 150 miles as the crow flies from the centre of St Petersburg — and the strategic Kronstadt naval base and Levashovo military airfield.



One gunner said: “On an exercise we tested whether it can reach St Petersburg from here. It all depends on enemy air defences and electronic warfare, which affects how much we would have to dog-leg around.”

The Nyan drones are replacing a squadron of Challenger 2 tanks that was in Estonia ten years.

A top Army source told The Sun: “A tank can deny Russia ground, a drone can punish them.”

The historic shift follows warnings from allies that Russia is plotting a provocation to test Nato’s resolve.

Defence Secretary Dan Jarvis, who visited Estonia last week, said he was “acutely aware of the threats”.

He told The Sun: “We have looked very carefully at the right mix of capabilities. We are determined to provide the most credible deterrent with the most lethal and effective kit available.”



Sgt James Henry, from 26 Artillery Regiment, said of the £80,000 Nyans: “Air defence missiles cost £100,000 to £200,000. So it costs them more than us.

“And if an enemy shoots it down, they reveal air defences we’d then target.”

News.title: Human remains found in hunt for nurse, 33, killed by husband six years ago after he finally confessed & led cops to body
News.content:
FINALLY FOUND Human remains found in hunt for nurse, 33, killed by husband six years ago after he finally confessed & led cops to body

THE remains of a nurse who was murdered six years ago have been found after her killer husband confessed to the crime.

After years of denial, Cedric Jubillar, 38, finally admitted to killing his wife Delphine, 33, and told cops that he had hidden her body on a farm in the French countryside.



In a case that rocked France during the COVID pandemic, Cedric was charged and found guilty of murder – despite there being no corpse and no DNA evidence to link him to the crime.

The Frenchman was sentenced to 30 years behind bars but has always maintained his innocence – until now.



Earlier this month, the depraved Frenchman told cops that he had killed his wife and stashed the cadaver in a field near their home in southern France.

Investigators raced to Mailhoc and, after two days of searching, discovered human remains about 10km from the couple’s former home.

DNA analysis confirmed that the body – which had been scattered across the field during farming work – was that of murdered mum-of-two Delphine.

At the time of her death, the couple shared two young children, aged six and 18 months.

Their son Louis, then six, said his parents had a violent quarrel on the night of his mum’s disappearance in December 2020, the court heard.

A neighbour also reported hearing a commotion at the home.



Delphine reportedly wanted to divorce Cedric and start a new life with another man.

The pair allegedly had a turbulent marriage – with Cedric reportedly smoking cannabis every day and barely holding down a job.

The convicted killer had been due to appeal his 30-year prison sentence when he suddenly confessed to the murder.



His lawyer Pierre Debuisson said: “A few weeks ago he said to me, ‘I need to tell you the truth. It was me.’”

Jubillar told how he killed his wife “after yet another marital row”, and used his car to move the body, Debuisson said.

It is still unclear how he murdered the nurse on the night of December 15 and 16 in 2020.

Commentators believe this latest confession may be an attempt to get a lighter sentence by portraying the killing as a domestic dispute which accidentally spiralled out of control.

Malika Chmani, the lawyer representing the two children, said: “We are relieved for the children”, saying that the confession may help them find closure.



She added that Louis had always been certain his dad was guilty.

And Cedric’s lawyer Debuisson said that his client “clearly regrets” his actions, adding “it was the worst thing he did in his life”.

His legal team said they hoped the bombshell revelation will allow the couple’s two young children to “grieve and give Delphine a proper burial”.

The appeal trial will now likely take place in September after the killer has been re-interrogated and the search for the body completed.

In the original trial over Delphine’s murder, jurors were told that though there was “no body and no blood”, there was “no plausible alternative either”.



Prosecuting lawyer Pierre Aurignac said in October: “No matter how you look at this case, you come to the same conclusion – guilt.”

But the husband’s lawyer Emmanuelle Franck said: “We have created a criminal to explain a crime.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“This is a castle of sand. When you cannot prove, you imagine. When you cannot find, you invent.”

Their case previously rested on the fact that the body of Delphine had not been found – and so there was no evidence for the crime.

News.title: Burnham is far too young to remember what Britain was REALLY like in the 70s – we don’t need a ride in his time machine
News.content:
GREAT Scott! In just a few hours, Andy Burnham will become Prime Minister and we’re yet to learn which direction he’ll take us in.

All we know for sure is that he has one destination in mind — and that’s straight back to the 1970s.



Perhaps he’s yearning for a return to his idyllic childhood in a leafy Cheshire village, a golden age of pop music or the halcyon days when his beloved Everton were winning trophies.

But the misty-eyed nostalgia we’ve heard from him over the past month is no basis for running the country.



Nor is taking the nation for a ride in a time machine.

Burnham, 56, is far too young to remember what Britain was really like before Margaret Thatcher walked into Downing Street.



Back then, we were paralysed by militant trade unions, blighted by failing nationalised industries and punished by income tax rates that reached an eye-watering 98 per cent.

Rubbish piled high in the streets, there were regular power cuts and we became known around the world as “the sick man of Europe”.

Crippling inflation hit 27 per cent and Harold Wilson — the last born-and-bred Northerner to become PM — had to go cap in hand for a bailout from the International Monetary Fund.

If he were a time-traveller like Marty McFly, Burnham would soon leap back into his DeLorean and yell: “We’ve got to get back to the future.”



Today’s challenges bear little resemblance to 1979, as Britain wrestles with a flatlining economy, mass immigration, £3trillion national debt, threadbare military forces and a million-strong army of jobless youngsters.

Yet Crash and Burnham seems determined to turn the political clock back.

His answer to almost every modern problem seems to be: “Blame Thatcher”.

Harping on about the past won’t fix the problems we face today any more than dwelling on “60 years of hurt” will win England the World Cup.

Burnham’s first duty when entering No 10 today will be to ditch the vague, vacuous vibes of the past month and deliver a real, forward-looking plan.



Barely a month after being elected MP, he was anointed as leader without a manifesto or a mandate in the swiftest rise to power since the office of PM was created in 1721.

The only scrutiny he’s undergone so far was a soft-soap interview with Gary Lineker — a Labour luvvie and one of his Everton heroes.

Even then, we were left with a clearer sense of the former footballer’s politics than of our next PM’s. In fact, we know more about what joke by- election candidate Count Binface would do in power.



We will soon learn whether there’s more to the Manchester messiah than his passion for sport, dad dancing and eating chips and gravy.

Yes, his cheerful and charismatic nature is a breath of fresh air after the dull, technocratic style of his predecessor.

But it will quickly dawn on our people-pleasing PM that running the country is much tougher than being mayor.

It will hit him the second he gets an ultra-secret national security briefing and is tasked with writing “letters of last resort” for the crews of our Trident nuclear submarines.

Big decisions will come in thick and fast after that.



The first major test will be naming his top team.

Many of the 379 Labour MPs who nominated him as leader will be hoping for a front bench role.

He seems to be getting cold feet about installing eco-zealot Ed Miliband as Chancellor.

Talk of promoting Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood instead has calmed the markets.

But it would simply be a sop to Labour’s Left, who would be glad to stop the tough cookie’s asylum crackdown in its tracks.



The rudest awakening for our seventh PM in ten years will come when he grapples with the two biggest headaches — spearheading economic growth and reacting to global events in an increasingly unstable world.

Our time traveller must learn to deal with Donald Trump.

And he must spell out his economic game plan, and fast.



His plan for a “No 10 North” will please the Manchester “mafia’” of Labour activists.

But hopping between offices 200 miles apart and giving more power to regional mayors and assemblies won’t help cut illegal migration, deport foreign rapists, slash the £334billion welfare bill or rebuild Britain’s threadbare defence capability.

All the same, Burnham will be swept into Downing Street by a wave of enthusiasm from Labour MPs and staff.

But his big ambitions bring with them high expectations.

And without a flux capacitor, time is not on his side.



Once he’s outlined his masterplan, he must decide how he will fund it — by squeezing over-taxed workers and businesses or taking the axe to the bloated welfare bill.

Only then can he move on to renationalising water companies, building council houses, cutting energy bills, rebuilding confidence in the police, and tackling our crumbling roads.

“Roads?” as Doc Brown might ask. “Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.”

Which is just as well, as most of them are littered with potholes.

ON Friday, King of the North Andy Burnham vowed to be a leader for “the North, the South, the East and the West”.



His soundbite was remarkably similar to W.H. Auden’s poem Funeral Blues, brought to a new generation in the film Four Weddings And A Funeral.

It says: “He was my North, my South, my East, my West.”

Let’s hope our new PM hasn’t written his own eulogy before entering Number 10.

BACK in September, this column revealed a joke doing the rounds in the bars of Westminster about Andy Burnham.

Since then it has been quoted widely by political pundits, rival columnists and on BBC Radio 4’s flagship Today programme.



Even the newly crowned Labour leader referred to the joke in his acceptance speech on Friday.

For those who missed it, the gag goes: “A Blairite, a Brownite and a Corbynista walk into a pub. The landlord says: ‘Good evening, Mr Burnham’.”

But it’s not just the political shape-shifting of our new PM that has been the source of humour, but his changing identity as a Northerner.

Liverpool-born Mr Burnham has a bee – the symbol of Manchester – tattooed on his right arm, and recently told the people of Makerfield that he was proud to have been brought up in the area.

So here’s a new variation currently circulating “oop” North.



“A Scouser, a Manc and a Wiganer walk into a pub . . . ”

I think you can all work out what the punchline is.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

First with the news – and the jokes.

You heard ’em here first!

News.title: Fury as asylum seekers staying at UK’s biggest migrant camp given ‘Strictly’ dancing lessons partly funded by YOU
News.content:
MIGRANT ON THE DANCEFLOOR Fury as asylum seekers staying at UK’s biggest migrant camp given ‘Strictly’ dancing lessons partly funded by YOU

ASYLUM seekers at Britain’s biggest migrant camp are receiving dance therapy and cricket coaching funded by the taxpayer and charities.

Photography, art and rambling sessions are also laid on for hundreds of male migrants.

It comes amid protests over the expansion of the Wethersfield Asylum Centre, Essex, from about 800 residents to around 1,245.



Tensions have increased recently after an asylum seeker at the Home Office site, on a former RAF airfield, appeared in court charged with assaulting a woman in a Braintree charity shop.



We found Ben & Jerry’s UK Fund paid for photography, art and rambling sessions, while The Salvation Army allowed refugee charity Care4Calais to use its church in Braintree to hand out freebies.

Dance classes called Echoes of Home are being provided until 2028 by Art Refuge in conjunction with performing arts company Atelier Armonico.

Some funding is from the National Lottery and Essex Community Foundation, which hands out grants to charities and voluntary groups.

More comes from the Asylum Large Sites and Vessels Grant — a Home Office fund for local authorities to ease pressure on services.

Braintree Council got £50,000 for local groups to provide activities for migrants.

This included £14,125 for Art Refuge, £17,490 for the Catholic Church’s St Vincent de Paul Society to put on English, art and gardening sessions, £7,650 for cricket coaching and £10,750 for sports sessions.

Since 2023, the council has also received more than £3.7million to provide 1,078 beds for asylum seekers.



Alp Mehmet, of Migration Watch UK, said: “The money, would be far better spent making life more tolerable for the thousands of elderly and vulnerable people in Braintree genuinely in need.”

A council spokesman said “there is no intention to provide any further funding” on top of the Home Office grant.

News.title: New PM Andy Burnham’s reign in chaos on first day after North Sea oil and gas drilling row erupts after Trump praise
News.content:
ANDY Burnham enters No10 today with chaos already engulfing the crucial issue of oil and gas drilling.

US President Donald Trump praised the incoming Prime Minister for “opening up, all the way” North Sea oil reserves.



But Labour Deputy Leader Lucy Powell said Mr Burnham would be sticking to the party’s election manifesto — which ruled out any new drilling licences.

Burnham is set to make a speech in Downing Street, promising that Britain can once again be a grown-up on the world stage.



However he will also get an instant dose of reality, after US President Donald Trump hailed his plans for North Sea drilling — only for his deputy Lucy Powell to rule it out.

Mr Burnham’s allies had signalled a break from Energy Secretary Ed Miliband’s Net Zero crusade, with more drilling, rather than relying on foreign oil and gas imports.



It led Mr Trump to yesterday declare that Scots were “dancing in the streets” of oil industry hub Aberdeen, where he has a golf resort.

He said the move would transform Britain from a “poverty-stricken disaster” to “one of the richest countries anywhere in the world”.

Opening up the North Sea and removing the “horrible windmills” will be a “very big day” for the UK, he added.

Labour MP Al Carns also chipped in, saying harvesting our own resources “is absolutely the right call” to protect jobs and raise taxes.



But Ms Powell went on TV and insisted the new PM will stick to the manifesto — which ruled out new drilling licences.

She said: “We’ve been really clear that the way to achieve in the long-term energy security and lower bills is by ensuring that we do have our own home-grown, clean, much cheaper energy.”

Mr Burnham could approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields — which have licences but have yet to be green-lit by Mr Miliband.

But failing to fully overturn the ban on new oil and gas exploration licences could bring him into an early clash with Mr Trump.



Tory leader Kemi Badenoch last night urged the new PM to get Britain drilling, offering to work together to reduce energy bills.

She said: “You should overturn the destructive ban on new oil and gas licences which amounts to unilateral energy disarmament.

“Getting Britain drilling will be good for our energy security, good for our national security and good for our financial security.”

Reform UK MP Richard Tice said he backed the new PM “parting ways with Labour’s irresponsible ban”.



He told The Sun: “Taking advantage of the energy treasure under our feet is the best way to secure our energy independence and lower bills for households and industry.”

After seeing the King at Buckingham Palace today, Mr Burnham will enter No10 after fail­ing to spell out many policies.

The former Greater Manchester Mayor will make a purposefully detail-light speech, promising to restore confidence in Labour which has been ripped apart by infighting.

He will also be clear Westminster must help hard-up Brits.

Last night there were signs of the “Burnham Bounce”, as Labour’s polling crept up, tying with Reform in some, with Nigel Farage’s party at its lowest level in two years.



Pressure on Israel trip vow By Tom Scotson ANDY Burnham is under pressure to stick to a promise he would make Israel his “first foreign visit” if he ever became leader of the Labour party. A video from the leadership race in 2015 — which he lost to Jeremy Corbyn — shows the PM-in-waiting vowing to go there to build bridges with the Jewish community. Tory MP Greg Smith said he should stick to his guns if he had a “single thread of credibility”. Meanwhile, Labour MP Luke Akehurst said Mr Burnham may be able to reset relations with the country if Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu is ousted in the elections there later this year in October. He said: “That is the moment when there ought to be a positive reset.” Mr Burnham was approached for comment.

Mr Burnham will look to announce a policy blitz in his first 100 days and avoid the torrid first few months Sir Keir Starmer faced in office.

He has signalled he wants to devolve more power, take back control of Thames Water and end Labour’s costly digital ID scheme.

But Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “This is a man with no mandate flailing from issue to issue in a desperate attempt to pretend he has a plan.”

Mr Burnham returned to Parliament as MP for Makerfield a month ago after nine years away from Westminster.



It led to Sir Keir’s resignation before Mr Burnham’s unopposed “coronation”, with 379 MPs nominating him for leader.

Meanwhile, it emerged yesterday that households with heat pumps face winter rationing as the Net Zero drive increases fears of blackouts.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

By the end of next year, electricity suppliers will be able to remotely turn down their heating.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said “load control” will help “balance the grid” in peak demand, making blackouts less likely.

News.title: Police 'urgently' searching for missing girl, 10, last seen 'riding her bike'
News.content:
Police 'urgently' searching for missing girl, 10, last seen 'riding her bike'

Police are desperately trying to track down Rosie May Osborne, who was last seen on Sunday morning in her home suburb of Bootle in Liverpool, when she was riding her bike

View 2 Images Rosie May Osborne, last seen at 8am on July 20, 2026 (Image: Merseyside Police)

Police are ‘urgently’ searching for a 10-year-old Liverpool girl who was last seen riding her bike.

‌



Rosie May Osborne, from Bootle in north Liverpool, was last seen on Sunday morning (July 19). She was spotted at 8am on Stanley Road in the North Park area of Bootle , Merseyside Police says.

‌



Cops have now launched an appeal to find Rosie, who was ‘last seen riding a pink bike’. Officers have released an image of the bike Rosie was riding at the time. She is known to visit Bootle often, they added.

‌



Rosie is 5ft tall, of slim build, and had wavy blonde hair. She wears glasses.

View 2 Images The bike Rose May Osborne was riding when she was last seen (Image: Merseyside Police)

‌



A police statement, released in the early hours of Monday (July 20), said: “We are urgently appealing for help in finding a 10-year-old girl who is missing from home in Bootle.

“Rosie May Osborne was last seen in North Park on Stanley Road at around 8am yesterday morning, Sunday 19 July and enquiries are ongoing to find her.

“She is described as 5ft tall, slim build, with blonde wavy hair and wears glasses. When last seen she was riding a pink bike which is pictured below.

Article continues below

“She often visits parks in the Bootle area.

“If you see Rosie, please call 999 so we can make sure she is safe. You can also pass on any sightings via our form: https://www.merseyside.police.uk/ro/report/mp/v2/add-something-reported-missing/ or any other information to @MerPolCC or 101.”

News.title: Arthur's Seat fire live: Emergency services battle huge blaze at iconic UK city site
News.content:
A picture of the fire on Arthur's Seat taken from outside the Scottish Parliament

A picture of the fire taken from the Scottish Parliament shows a large plume of thick smoke billowing from the area

A large blaze has broken out on Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh as fire crews have been battling a number of wildfires around Scotland.

The fire, located next to the Palace of Holyrood House, started around 6.30pm today. Four fire engines from the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service are in attendance.

An image taken from the Scottish Parliament, located nearby, shows a large plume of smoke billowing from the hill. Tonight's blaze comes as Scotland battles a dry spell, with massive wildfires in the Cairngorms ongoing.

An area of Arthur's Seat was also scorched in August last year.

News.title: Donald Trump sends message to Andy Burnham as he brands UK 'poverty-stricken disaster'
News.content:
Donald Trump sends message to Andy Burnham as he brands UK 'poverty-stricken disaster'

US President Donald Trump claimed that further drilling in the North Sea will take the UK "from a Poverty Stricken Disaster" to one of the world's richest countries

View 3 Images US President Donald Trump (Image: Saul Loeb/Pool AFP via AP)

US President Donald Trump has called the UK a "poverty-stricken disaster" after reports that a new oil and gas drilling plan in the North Sea could be approved.

‌



Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Sunday, July 20 that the UK's new Labour leader - an possibly the incoming prime minister - Andy Burnham would "be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!".

‌



Trump's post reads: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!

‌



"It is one of the Greatest Sources of quality Oil on Earth, has hundreds of years of Capacity left, with much not even found yet, and will make the United Kingdom, from a Poverty Stricken Disaster, to one of the Richest Countries anywhere in the World!"

View 3 Images Thousands of jobs depend on Scotland's North Sea oil and gas industry (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

Trump is an avid supporter of fossil fuels.

‌



Burnham has not confirmed the reports and Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell said on Sunday that Burnham would stick to the party's manifesto commitments on North Sea drilling but would "pursue a more pragmatic approach".

The Mirror reported just days earlier that Andy Burnham approving new drilling licences in the North Sea would damage UK's security and hurt families struggling with the cost of living, charities have warned.

In a major intervention, 19 different groups including Oxfam and Greenpeace wrote to the incoming-PM expressing "alarm" at reports he might water down the UK's focus on renewables.

‌



In a speech in Downing Street on Monday, Burnham expected to set out plans to provide "breathing space" on the cost of living and bring economic growth to every part of the UK.

In 2024, Labour said the it would not issue new North Sea licences. The party said doing so would "not take a penny off bills" or improve energy security while accelerating climate change. But Burnham is said to be "open-minded" about the policy.

View 3 Images Andy Burnham (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

It is understood Burnham believes he would not breach the manifesto by backing further drilling in the Scottish Rosebank and Jackdaw fields because licences had already been granted there.

Powell did not say whether Burnham would support more drilling but said she expected a "change of emphasis" rather than a "change of policy".

The US war in Iran has rocked oil markets and Conservatives and Reform UK parties have put pressure on the Labour government to approve new licences.

News.title: Average fatcat's annual pay hits record £5million - 130 times what a typical UK workers earns
News.content:
Average fatcat's annual pay hits record £5million - 130 times what a typical UK workers earns

Research has revealed executives running the UK's top listed companies have seen their pay rise more than twice as fast as other workers, earning 130 times more than the average worker

View 3 Images Pascal Soriot, head of pharmaceuticals giant AstraZeneca, has been paid £150million since 2016 (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

The average fatcat boss running Britain’s biggest companies now earns 130 times what a typical worker does, latest research has revealed.

‌



The gap has widened from 124 times last year and stands at an eight-year high, according to think tank the High Pay Centre. It came as its analysis showed the median average pay and perks for a chief executive running a FTSE 100 had reached a new record high of just over £5million a year, up 8.6% from £4.66m in 2024/25.

‌



Andrew Speke, interim director at the High Pay Centre, said: “The substantial growth in the gap between executive and worker pay in the past year should be a wake-up call to those who’ve turned a blind eye to rising executive pay.

‌



View 3 Images Wael Sawan, boss of oil giant Shell, netted £13.7m last year

“As our findings show, this is the fourth year in a row that FTSE 100 executive pay has risen, and this growth is starting to substantially outstrip growth in worker pay.”

In a message to new PM Andy Burnham, he said: “We hope that a change in Prime Minister and a renewed focus on economic fairness will lead to economic inequality and corporate excess returning up the political agenda. A failure to tackle such disproportionate and inefficient levels of inequality will only further reduce faith in our current economic model and help to accelerate the rise of right-wing populism.”

‌



View 3 Images Tesco CEO Ken Murphy's pay package jumped from £9.7m to £10.8m last year (Image: No credit)

The research by the think tank - which has long shone a spotlight on the issue of excessive boardroom pay - comes as it being forced to close due to a decline in funding.

According to the data, a total of 66 FTSE 100 firms increased their chief executive’s pay package from the previous year, up from 61% of firms who did so last year. The average 8.6% jump in the pay and perks of top bosses far outstrips the 3.6% for a typical UK employee in the year to April, with a typical full-time work on just under £40,000 a year. In total, £856.6million was spent on FTSE 100 executives, including £550.4 million on CEOs.

‌



Pay-setting committees at many big firms argue they need to reward top executives with bumper salaries and perks to both attract the best and to compete with companies in other countries - including the US - and those owned by private equity firms.

The High Pay Centre argues the case for a "fat cat tax", whereby firms would pay a corporation tax surcharge on their yearly profits if the total a boss gets exceeds a specified multiple of the median UK worker’s salary. It says it could start with a small tax on those pay packages that exceed 10 times, before increasing in size at thresholds of 50 times. 100 times, 200 times and 500 times.. "Not only would this incentivise firms to scale back the levels of corporate wealth flowing to a small handful of individuals but also could be used to raise funds to be invested in education and early years provision, helping to tackle inequality at source," it says.

It also calls for wider reforms to boost employee involvement at the top of companies, including having workers on the board. It also believes all companies should be made to provide more detailed information in their annual reports around pay, including the number of workers paid less than a living wage.

‌

(Nb: The High Pay Centre included Karim Bitar of Convatec, although he passed away in late 2025. He was replaced by chief financial officer Jonny Mason)

News.title: Desperate rescue operation after ferry carrying 133 sinks off coast of Guyana
News.content:
Desperate rescue operation after ferry carrying 133 sinks off coast of Guyana

A rescue operation continues after 15 children were among 67 people that have been recovered after a ferry sunk off the coast of Guyana, with dozens remaining missing

View Image Sixty-seven people have so far been rescued after a ferry carrying 116 passengers and 17 crew sunk (Image: Facebook)

Sixty-seven people have been rescued and dozens are missing after a ferry carrying 116 passengers and 17 crew sunk.

‌



Fifteen children are among those recovered after the MV Barima capsized off the coast of Guyana, according to local officials.

‌



The boat was travelling from the capital Georgetown on Saturday when a distress call was received at 11.03pm local time.

‌



This triggered a search operation involving government teams and privately-owned boats, Public Works Minister Juan Edghill said.

He said that emergency teams continued their search on Sunday afternoon. "We're hopeful we'll be able to account for all that were on board."

‌



Prime Minister Mark Phillips said that those rescued also included 41 men and 11 women, with the boat's captain among that number.

The captain has now returned to the area to assist the "significantly increased" rescue operation, with crews more than doubling their search area on Sunday.

Phillips confirmed that the boat was within its weight capacity at the time of the incident, with it licensed to hold more than 300 passengers.

Article continues below

Once medical checks and rescue operations are complete the names of those onboard will be released.

News.title: Young man dead as police swarm caravan park near Royal Welsh show site - recap
News.content:
Police have swarmed a caravan park near the Royal Welsh Show following the death of a 25-year-old man.

Police have swarmed a caravan park near the Royal Welsh Show site following the death of a 25-year-old man.

News.title: Teacher hops on £27 flight to France for lunch — because it's 'cheaper than a UK day out'
News.content:
Teacher hops on £27 flight to France for lunch — because it's 'cheaper than a UK day out'

Claire Howard, 48, flew from Birmingham to Beauvais, northern France, for a day of food, sightseeing and sunshine — she was back in the UK by midnight and said the whole trip cost just £70

View 10 Images Claire Howard jetted off to France for lunch (Image: Jam Press)

A teacher hopped on a plane to France for lunch and claims it was more affordable than a standard day out in the UK.

‌



Claire Howard jetted off to Beauvais, France, for a leisurely day of dining, exploring and sunshine and was back home before midnight. The 48-year-old woman found return Ryanair flights for merely £27 and secured them a month beforehand.

‌



The early morning flight departed Birmingham at approximately 7.30am, with the homebound journey leaving at 11pm. Her husband gave her a lift to the airport, and she caught a £1.80 bus to Beauvais that took 15 minutes. Claire, who is a mum, believes the entire trip, including flights, buses, food, and drink, came to roughly £70.

‌



Woman travels from UK to Spain without flying and total price floors people READ MORE :

10 View 10 Images Claire enjoyed her day in Beauvais (Image: Jam Press) 10 View 10 Images She said the trip was cheaper than a day out in the UK (Image: Jam Press)

Claire, from Birmingham, said: "I've been to Paris a few times and didn't want to travel in from Beauvais as Paris is really pricey and busy.

"I just wanted to see what was actually in Beauvais itself for a relaxing day of wandering, eating, and drinking. I just saw on Skyscanner that return flights were only £27, so I went for it.

‌



"It's exciting to go to a different country just for lunch or to explore for a day. The bus from the airport to the centre is very cheap. It's just a different feeling abroad.

"It makes it feel much more like an adventure than just going somewhere at home. I don't want to pay £50 to go to the cinema and lunch here in a shopping centre when I can go and experience so much more abroad for a very reasonable price."

10 View 10 Images She also visited the city's Saturday market (Image: Jam Press) 10 View 10 Images The teacher relaxed while having a French picnic (Image: Jam Press)

‌



The English teacher spent her morning exploring the city's weekly Saturday market, treating herself to a coffee and a pain au chocolat for just £4. She then unwound with a drink in the town square, soaking up live music before hopping in a £10 Uber to Plan d'Eau du Canada, a beloved lakeside destination.

For lunch, she put together an £8 French-style picnic featuring a supermarket baguette, cheese, and a small bottle of wine, which she enjoyed while reading and sunbathing beside the water. Her packed itinerary also took in Beauvais Cathedral and the neighbouring Musée de l'Oise, both of which were completely free to enter.

View 10 Images Claire was back home by midnight (Image: Jam Press)

‌



The day wrapped up with a Pad Thai supper at a nearby Thai restaurant for roughly £10, before she made her way back to the airport for her evening flight home. She also picked up an £8 bracelet as a memento of her trip.

Claire said: "I'd say it could probably be done even cheaper. I do stay over in some places depending on flight times but it wasn't necessary for this trip as the flight times fit and I could still have an evening meal and a full day.

10 View 10 Images Beauvais is located in northern France (Image: Jam Press) 10 View 10 Images She loves jetting off to a new destination almost every month (Image: Jam Press)

‌



"There's no point in staying over to get a flight home the next morning as it's a waste of accommodation money." Claire admits she's become completely addicted to budget day trips overseas after stumbling across bargain flights from Birmingham Airport, jetting off to a new destination almost every month.

Just this year alone, she's already ticked off Bergamo in Italy, Malaga in Spain, Valetta in Malta, Poznan in Poland, and Porto in Portugal. She's already snapped up return flights to Poland and Berlin in August for just £70.

10 View 10 Images She also visited Beauvais Cathedral (Image: Jam Press) 10 View 10 Images She said she has become completely addicted to budget day trips overseas (Image: Jam Press)

Article continues below

Claire said: "I'm just led by what is possible and affordable. I can't take time off at all in term time but I have Tuesdays off so I do like to make use of them.

"I just love the way you can do and see so much in the same time that you might waste a day at home just watching Netflix and doomscrolling. I usually find the best prices four to six weeks in advance. My husband doesn't like short trips so he's not jealous."

News.title: US military find unidentified remains in search for missing soldier after Iranian attacks
News.content:
US military find unidentified remains in search for missing soldier after Iranian attacks

Two other service members were confirmed to have died in Jordan on July 17, while another one died in Iraq during a controlled explosion on July 18

View Image (Image: ANNA SZILAGYI/EPA/Shutterstock)

Unidentified remains have been found in the search for a missing US soldier following Iranian attacks in Jordan, the US military announced on Sunday.

‌



The ballistic missile and drone attacks took place on July 17, with two other service members already confirmed to have died. One soldier was declared missing but US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced this evening (July 19) that unidentified remains have been located.

‌



A statement from CENTCOM reads: "Yesterday, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the passing of two U.S. service members and the missing status of one in Jordan following an Iranian attack on July 17.

‌



"After a thorough search, U.S. military personnel found unidentified remains at the location earlier today. An examination process to verify the remains is ongoing."

CENTCOM added that a US service member has also been killed in northern Iraq in action on July 18. This occurred during "a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian one-way attack drone".

Article continues below

A second service member was wounded in the process and continues to receive medical treatment for a minor injury. CENTCOM said: "CENTCOM is withholding additional information, including the identities of the missing and fallen warriors, out of respect for the families during the notification process."

Yesterday, CENTCOM also announced that four other American service members were medically evacuated to hospitals in Jordan. The two deaths announced this evening bring the total of US personnel killed since the start of the war with Iran to at least 18.

News.title: Burnham to promise 'more breathing room' for people in first speech as PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham will promise to give people "more breathing room" when he gives his first speech as prime minister outside No 10 on Monday.

He is expected to say he is "acutely conscious" of the UK's high turnover of prime ministers - and that politics needs to be more stable and responsible.

And he is expected to characterise the moment as one of "reflection and resolution", arguing Britain must be honest about the challenges it faces.

Burnham will officially replace Sir Keir Starmer and become the UK's 59th prime minister - and seventh in 10 years - on Monday, following a meeting with King Charles III.

In a letter published on Sunday evening, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wished Burnham "every success" as prime minister, but warned he was entering office without "any clear plan".

"You have refused calls to come to Parliament for questions from MPs, and you have not submitted yourself to serious media scrutiny," Badenoch wrote.

"This is not a promising start."

It also included a promise of Conservative support to cut the benefits bill, and urged the incoming prime minister to rule out any new tax rises.

The letter followed earlier remarks from Badenoch that Burnham was a "people pleaser" at a time when the country needed someone who could "take tough decisions, who can face down Labour MPs".

Burnham was officially declared Labour Party leader on Friday following a short contest in which he was the only candidate, having secured the backing of 379 MPs.

Some opposition parties have urged Burnham to call a general election in order to ensure he has a mandate for his premiership.

However, earlier Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell insisted Burnham would stick to the promises made in Labour's manifesto in the 2024 general election but will be more ambitious.

"He really understands the bigger, bolder measures that are needed to live up to the manifesto promises," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme.

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham is fifth PM in four years - now he'll try to buck the trend
News.content:
By lunchtime today, the UK will have its fifth prime minister in four years.

No other sentence can so pithily summarise the nature of British politics right now than that one.

In the summer of 2022 Boris Johnson was on his way out, but still in office. Since then there has been Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.

Little wonder Andy Burnham will say later, we are told, that he is "acutely conscious" of this churn at the top. His critics, within the Labour Party and beyond it, may allow themselves a wry smile at that, given they would argue he has been agitating for this moment for ages.

In the post-pandemic, post-Brexit 2020s, when for so long so many have felt like life is getting harder, the national mood is impatient and political support is fragmenting.

The consequence of that in recent years has meant those in government have been unpopular.

That is the backdrop to Burnham's arrival in Downing Street, just as it was for Sir Keir Starmer 746 days ago - on another sunny July day, just two years back.

That trend of unpopular governments is the thing Burnham is now trying to buck.

He is determined to hit the ground running and, where possible, to maintain the style of leadership he adopted as the mayor of Greater Manchester.

The rules of the House of Commons and meetings with the King, among others, will probably mean he wears a suit more often than he has in recent years.

But other conventions may be very intentionally ditched. I hear, for instance, that he may not bother with a lectern for his first speech as prime minister, outside 10 Downing Street, on Monday.

I also hear he is keen on question and answer sessions with voters around the country - "People's Question Time" as one ally put it.

Before Burnham's big moment will come Sir Keir's departure.

News.title: My fitness tracker knew I was pregnant before I did
News.content:
Dr Stuart Lavery, consultant of reproductive medicine at University College Hospital in London, said: "People are understandably using this technology to try to get a greater understanding, and to try and pick up things as early as possible because it has such a profound impact on your life if you're planning a pregnancy."

However, "we might be running before we can walk," he cautioned.

"We probably need a lot more data on the reliability, we need a lot more researchâ¦ otherwise what happens is your levels of anxiety will just skyrocket," he said.

"I have no doubt that more people will be using technology, an app-based approach or a wearable-based approach, to try and pick up these things. But I think it should come with quite a big health warning about how much we can rely on them for accuracy."

When asked about the anxiety women reported feeling early in their pregnancy as a result of checking their ring data, Dr Chris Curry, Oura's clinical director of women's health, told BBC News: "With or without biometric tracking, pregnancy can be an uncertain time where many women, particularly those pregnant for the first time, are in the dark about the range of what's normal."

She added that if women feel overwhelmed, the company "encourages members to take a break from the app experience, whilst Oura Ring continues to collect data and gather insights", adding: "The ring is a support tool, not a replacement for your care team."

Ravika sadly did miscarry. She's hoping to start trying to conceive again soon - and when she does, her experience has made her rethink wearing her tracker again.

"I didn't really see myself as being an anxious person, butâ¦ I think going forward if it came to a point where I had an inkling that I was pregnant and my stats were low, as soon as that positive pregnancy test was there, I do think it would be the best thing for me to take the ring off."

News.title: ‘Everyone's afraid to die’: Struggle to recruit soldiers in Ukraine turns violent
News.content:
Vasyl Krupych knows what it is to fight for Ukraine.

He describes terrifying scenes from battles in the eastern Donbas region where, sometimes praying, sometimes crying, the machine gunner somehow survived the onslaught by Russian troops.

But last December, by then serving in the rear, Krupych was attacked by his own countrymen whilst out searching for draft dodgers.

He says two men ignored demands to show their documents and fled. When his patrol gave chase, Krupych was badly beaten with a crowbar. He spent six weeks in hospital.

"He broke my rib, I was lying there and couldn't breathe," the veteran recalled in a recent interview.

"What did we fight for, if soldiers can now get beaten?"

News.title: Thames Water lenders preparing legal challenge in event of Burnham nationalisation
News.content:
The lenders to Thames Water are preparing a legal challenge in case a Burnham-led government attempts to nationalise the UK's biggest water company.

Burnham - who takes over as PM on Monday - has previously said he wants to see "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors and has called for Thames Water to be nationalised.

Thames Water is about Â£20bn in debt.

Its lenders had proposed a deal to write off nearly half of that and inject new cash in return for some leniency from future pollution fines, but this deal has previously been rejected by the government as being "weak" and bad for consumers and the environment.

Sources close to the creditors have told the BBC that in the event of full nationalisation, they would pursue payment in full of the outstanding debts as has happened in previous cases, which could leave the government with a multi-billion-pound bill.

Fears first emerged three years ago that Thames Water could collapse and on Thursday, the firm warned it has enough cash to last until the end of this year.

Creditors insisted on Sunday that they were still working with officials and regulators to reach an agreement to rescue the company.

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the government was "prepared for any eventuality".

"Thames Water customers have been let down for far too long, with 15 years of under-performance, increasing serious pollution, and customers left to pick up the bill," the spokesperson said.

"The secretary of state has written to Ofwat to outline her early views that she is not convinced Londonâ¯andâ¯Valleyâ¯Water's proposal is good enough for consumers or the environment."

The lenders have offered to write off Â£9.4bn of Thames Water's near Â£20bn debt pile and put Â£3.35bn of cash into the company, but in return they want leniency from future pollution fines in order to turn the firm's fortunes around.

Objecting to the proposal, Emma Reynolds said in June that she did not want a scenario where Thames Water customers had to "pick up the bill for the company's failures".

At the time, she told reporters that the government "stands ready for all eventualities", including temporary nationalisation.

When asked in a Sky News interview on Sunday whether a Burnham government would nationalise Thames Water, Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell said: "Let's see".

"This has been an ongoing issue and concern in government," she said.

"The government has powers to to bring a distressed water company under special measures, and let's see if the government needs to, wants to use those powers."

Powell added that "the privatisation of water hasn't worked".

"It's not created competition. What you've seen is bills going up and up and up over years and years and years. Investment not being being made ... and then now these companies are in are in real distress," she said.

There is a halfway house, in which Thames would be placed into a so called "special administration regime", or SAR, which is usually a temporary situation until another private sector buyer can be found.

The existing lenders have made it clear that they would be prepared to join the bidders for Thames in that scenario.

However, comments from the incoming prime minister Andy Burnham that key utilities should be under increased "public control" make it hard to imagine that the government will have much political appetite to find a new set of private sector owners for a company that serves 16 million people which means that a temporary nationalisation might become permanent.

But under either a SAR or full nationalisation, Thames ongoing problems could then leave taxpayers footing the bill for Thames cash shortfalls - a figure that Thames Water management puts at Â£2bn by the end of next year.

Whatever happens, its customers' taps and loos will still function, but the future of Thames Water is a key policy test for the new administration.

News.title: How Fox kept cool at baked Birkdale to win The Open
News.content:
The Open Championship, final leaderboard

-10 R Fox (NZ); -9 C Young (US); -8 S Burns (US)

Selected: -7 S Scheffler (US), T Fleetwood (Eng); -6 L Herbert (Aus); -5 L Aberg (Swe); -4 B DeChambeau (US); -3 M Penge (Eng), J Smith (Eng), D Brown (Eng); -2 R MacIntyre (Sco), S Lowry (Ire); -1 R McIlroy (NI), M Wallace (Eng)

Full leaderboard

As chaos unfolded on Sunday afternoon at the 154th Open Championship, Ryan Fox was the man who kept cool in the baking conditions at Royal Birkdale.

The 39-year-old New Zealander, who is the son of All Black rugby legend Grant, shot a two-under 68 to finish one ahead of American Cameron Young and lift the Claret Jug.

After a final round full of spills and thrills, Fox knew a birdie on the 18th would be enough to secure his first major title.

Easier said than done. The long par-four had yielded only four birdies all day, but the courageous Fox did not take a step back as he chased down long-time clubhouse leader Young.

Fox grabbed the driver out of the bag and launched a crackerjack of a 330-yard tee-shot into the middle of the fairway.

With 175 yards left, he hit one of the approach shots of his career into the heart of the green.

Then he calmly stepped up and converted the biggest putt of his life from 11 feet.

"I didn't feel anything for the putt - everything was shaking that much," said Fox, who was a 100-1 outsider at the start of the tournament and finished with four birdies in his final six holes to earn the title of 'Champion Golfer of the Year'.

"It's not a very comfortable feeling. It's certainly very enjoyable when you see it go in."

Fox's career has often been overshadowed by his father Grant's achievements, given he helped the All Blacks win the 1987 World Cup and was once their record points scorer.

The family's strong sporting stock also includes Ryan's grandfather Merv Wallace, who captained and coached the New Zealand cricket team.

"We've got a great history in our family," said Fox. "The other great thing is I had no pressure on me to follow in any of their footsteps.

"I don't know if this tops their achievements, but it's certainly right up there. I guess there's no pressure on my kids going forward now."

News.title: New EU border system tripling time at passport control, airport boss says
News.content:
The EU's new border system has nearly tripled the time it's taking for Brits to get through passport control even after improvements have been made, a boss at Rome's main airport has said.

It comes as Ryanair has warned passengers travelling to Europe this summer to prepare for extended waits.

Border police at Portugal's Faro airport also told the BBC the Entry Exit System technology suffered from bugs, but insisted any queues there would go down quickly.

The European Commission (EC) has said in most EU airports disruption is limited, and added that it will continue to support member states in the system's implementation.

It added: "This support will continue to the fullest extent possible."

The digital Entry Exit System (EES) requires non-EU citizens entering the Schengen area - made up of 29 European countries - to register fingerprints and a photo when they arrive. The information is checked as they leave.

It's often done using standalone, automated machines known as "kiosks" and sometimes with border officers - for example, for children under 12. The new process and machines have been phased in since October.

Some European airports have seen hours-long queues at passport control. Passengers have even reported missing flights home.

This week, Ryanair said "the failed EES rollout" was causing unnecessary delays and long queues.

The airline said UK passengers should "allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for extended waits at passport control."

In Rome, a perennially popular destination for tourists from the UK and around the globe, everyone we spoke to in the Piazza di Spagna had an EES story.

News.title: Chinese firm seeks compensation over British Steel nationalisation
News.content:
The former owner of British Steel has said it will pursue the British government for compensation after the loss-making firm was nationalised.

The UK took control of the Scunthorpe steelworks a year ago after China's Jingye Group said it planned to close the site because it was not financially viable, and fully nationalised the plant on Thursday.

In a statement on Sunday, Jingye said it will seek "full compensation through legal means to the very end" over the UK's move.

A government spokesperson said draft compensation regulations due to be released in the autumn will set out a compensation process through which an independent assessor "would determine what, if any, is payable".

Jingye bought the Lincolnshire steel plant in 2020, but in March last year the firm launched a consultation on its closure saying the plant was losing Â£700,000 a day.

The government took control of British Steel operations in April 2025, but until this week it remained under Jingye's ownership which limited the government's ability to shape the firm's future.

On Thursday the UK government said it was taking the firm into public hands in order to safeguard a "vital national capability", giving the government the power to decide the plant's future.

The decision to nationalise British Steel has threatened to strain the relationship between London and Beijing just as Andy Burnham prepares to enter Downing Street as prime minister on Monday.

News.title: Man injured in dockside crane 'collapse'
News.content:
A man has been taken to hospital after a crane appears to have collapsed on a ship at a dock on the south bank of the River Tyne.

Northumbria Police said it was called to South Shields Port of Tyne at 13:00 BST after "it was reported that, for reasons yet to be established, a ship had collided with a crane".

Images show the crane on its side and leaning on to part of a container vessel.

North East Ambulance service (NEAS) said the man was transported to Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. Police said the man's condition was not thought to be life threatening.

A Northumbria Police spokesperson said: "Just after 13:00 today, we received a report of concern for the safety of a person at the Port of Tyne in South Shields.

"It was reported that, for reasons yet to be established, a ship had collided with a crane.

"Emergency services attended and a man was found to have sustained injuries not believed to be life-threatening."

The man remains in hospital and inquiries are ongoing, the force added.

News.title: Bruno Mars has an unexpected opening before Wembley party starts
News.content:

His last UK performance came in July 2018, shortly after England had been knocked out of the men's World Cup semi-finals. Eight years later, history had repeated itself.

But wearing an England football scarf, Union Jack bucket hat and clutching a Paddington Bear, the showman energised a 75,000-strong, multi-generational crowd.

After nearly a decade away from UK audiences, Mars proved why fans had snapped up tickets in record numbers, external.

News.title: Britain 'set for bumper year' for butterflies
News.content:
A butterfly charity says the UK could be set for a "bumper" year of the insects as it launches its annual appeal for the public to count them.

Butterfly Conservation, based at East Lulworth, in Dorset, said the hot and dry spring meant it was already seeing an increase in several species.

On Friday, it launched its Big Butterfly Count, a yearly event asking members of the public to report the butterflies they see.

Dr Dan Hoare, director of nature recovery at Butterfly Conservation, said it was an opportunity for them to "colonise and reach out to new places".

"I have seen three or four species in the south of England... wandering away from their normal places," he said.

News.title: Digital ID plan to be scrapped in Burnham's first major policy pledge
News.content:
"This reprioritisation of public resource shows a change in direction towards improving everyday life and strengthening local economies over expensive national government schemes."

Plans for a digital ID scheme had initially been introduced by Sir Keir ahead of Labour's conference last year.

At the time, he argued that mandatory digital ID for workers would make it easier to clamp down on immigrants working illegally and modernise the state.

As well as tackling illegal immigration, Sir Keir said a digital ID system would enable citizens to prove identity to access key services quickly instead of having to hunt for utility bills.

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimated last November that the programme would cost Â£1.8bn over three years, but Downing Street rejected this figure.

In January, after nearly three million people signed a parliamentary petition opposing the introduction of digital IDs, the government changed its approach.

Instead, ministers ditched the compulsory part of the scheme and relaunched it as voluntary, saying digital IDs could eventually allow people to do everything from managing their childcare to filling in tax returns on a "one stop" app.

Soon after, Home Affairs Committee Chair Dame Karen Bradley said the government was right to introduce digital ID but had botched the launch.

In a report setting out the committee's investigation into the launch and subsequent changes to the policy, Dame Karen called attempts to set out the plans "nothing short of a fiasco" which "raised fears of government over-reach into people's lives".

Burnham will become prime minister after meeting with King Charles III on Monday, and his office said "one of the first things this government will do is put its focus where people need it right now".

Scrapping digital ID, the spokesperson said, will mean "redirecting the resources earmarked for the scheme towards people's everyday priorities".

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, deputy Labour leader and Burnham ally Lucy Powell said the money saved by scrapping the scheme was "not an insignificant amount" and would be "reprioritised and redistributed in different ways".

"But it's not just about the money - it's actually about the attention and the focus, so that the whole of government machinery can work in service of the agenda and the vision that the Labour government is setting out under Andy Burnham," she said.

News.title: Is Burnham promising a new dawn for North Sea oil and gas?
News.content:
The final weekend before Andy Burnham enters Downing Street is being dominated by suggestions he'll announce plans for new drilling in the North Sea.

On Saturday, the BBC reported the in-coming prime minister would stick to the party's 2024 manifesto pledge to issue no new oil and gas licences but would honour existing ones.

That line has been confirmed as the hours count down to the Burnham premiership.

Speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell said Burnham would stick to the party's manifesto commitments, but there would be a "change of emphasis" on North Sea oil and gas.

"We've been really clear that the way to achieve in the long term energy security and lower bills is by ensuring that we do have our own homegrown, clean, much cheaper energy," she said.

"But we've been absolutely clear that North Sea gas and oil is an important part of that transition.

"It's an important part of the mix, and I think what Andy's talking about is taking a more pragmatic approach and working with the industry to make sure that it can contribute to that [energy] transition and to the mix that is needed over the long term."

News.title: Parts of UK to get break in heatwave but dry spell to continue
News.content:
Cooler temperatures are on the way for some parts of the UK after a first half of summer dominated by warm, sunny and largely dry weather.

Parts of England have experienced more than two weeks of heatwave conditions, and some central areas have had the longest dry spell since 1997.

But the third heatwave of 2026 is now easing as northerly winds introduce some fresher air - although most places still won't have any significant rainfall.

The slightly cooler spell may be very brief for some parts of southern England and south Wales, where we could see heatwave criteria being reached again later this week.

Argentina’s World Cup ended with punches thrown and the former champions left in disgrace following a 1-0 defeat to Spain in the final.

There were chaotic scenes after the full-time whistle in New Jersey as the Spain substitutes ran onto the pitch to celebrate victory.

Nahuel Molina, the Argentina defender, appeared to swing a punch into the stomach of Spain captain Rodri as he ran past him onto the field.

Then, there was a violent clash involving midfielder Leandro Paredes, who was pictured shoving Spain’s Eric Garcia by the throat.

open image in gallery Leandro Paredes wrestles Spain’s Gavi to the ground after full-time ( Reuters )

Paredes wrestled Spain’s Gavi to the ground and pushed into his face while holding him by his substitute bib.

Spain’s Mikel Oyarzabal and Rodri sprinted past Molina after the final whistle was blown and La Roja were crowned champions.

Molina appeared to swing at Rodri, leading to the Spain captain stopping in his tracks and approaching the Argentina defender while shouting.

Molina then squared up to Rodri and bumped him in the chest, which was the flashpoint that triggered Spain’s Eric Garcia to step in.

Paredes, who was booked during the final and was fortunate to not receive a second yellow card, then flew towards Garcia. He jabbed him in the throat just as Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni approached, wagging his finger and trying to break up the scuffles.

With Scaloni separating Garcia and other Argentina coaching staff members getting involved, Paredes then turned his attention to Spain’s 21-year-old midfielder Gavi - who by that point was already wrestling with Argentina’s Thiago Almada.

Paredes, 32, spun Gavi to the ground and appeared to push into his face while holding him by the bib. Several of Gavi’s Spanish team-mates then stepped in to shield him, with Spain’s Borja Iglesias crashing into Paredes.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

It was a sorry way for Argentina’s tournament to end after they had taken an emotional path to the final. They were attempting to a second World Cup in a row for captain Lionel Messi, who was playing on the World Cup stage for the final time.

But the antics of the rest of the Argentina team were quickly condemned as the scenes after the final whistle soured Spain’s deserved victory, with former England goalkeeper Joe Hart labelling Argentina’s behaviour “disgusting”.

"It's a disgrace,” Gary Neville said on ITV. “I love the competitiveness of the Argentines, fighting and scrapping for their lives, Messi has propped them up, but it’s been a disgrace the last few games.”

“Paredes threw two or three haymakers into someone's face. He went for them,” Alan Shearer said on BBC. “There is no place or space for that.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

“We know how much it means to them and we know how much it hurts to lose, but there is a way to lose. Too many times we have seen that from Argentina. The reaction after the final whistle is terrible.”

BBC pundit Hart said: “There was one man on the pitch who did have class and that was Lionel Messi, who shook hands with every one of those Spanish players.“The game’s done. They could have absolutely no complaints about what happened today. Disgusting behaviour.”

Hart added: “Spain fully deserve it. They have been absolutely superb all tournament.“They have dominated all game against a rigid, rugged Argentina. The best team has won this World Cup.”

Argentina were previously criticised for their aggressive behaviour during their 2-1 semi-final win over England, after which players unveiled a banner claiming sovereignty of the Falklands Islands.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

Fellow pundit Wayne Rooney said of Argentina’s behaviour: “Does it surprise you? It doesn’t surprise me.“We’ve seen this with Argentina before. It’s just not the reaction you want. We’ve seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round.“That’s just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It’s really poor from them.”

ITV’s co-commentators were in agreement that Spain were deserved winners, with Lee Dixon accusing Argentina of “anti-football” and questioning how Paredes had remained on the pitch, while Ally McCoist said Spain were “the only team trying to win this game”.

Meanwhile, the tears rolled down Lionel Messi’s face as he watched the Argentina fans following defeat to Spain.

Messi, 39, is yet to confirm his future plans but the expectation is that one of the greatest to grace the game has played his final World Cup before retirement.

The Argentina captain was left frustrated as Spain dominated the final, with the European champions winning 1-0 thanks to Ferran Torres’ goal after extra time.

open image in gallery Argentina's Lionel Messi shakes hands with US President Donald Trump ( Reuters )

Messi had inspired a series of brilliant comebacks in the knockout stages to help Argentina to a second successive final but Spain were deserved winners.

Messi scored eight goals in an incredible tournament and the Argentina fans chanted his name as Spain’s Rodri collected the player of tournament award.

Messi then led his team-mates to collect their runners-up medals. He then stood and cried while he watched the Argentina fans serenade him.

The record eight-time Ballon d’Or winner will be 43 at the next men’s World Cup, which takes place in Spain, Portugal and Morocco - but will kick off in Argentina.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

Messi waited until Spain lifted the World Cup, but then quickly left the pitch in what was perhaps a bitter end to his World Cup journey.

By playing in the final, Messi became just the third player to appear in three men’s World Cup finals - after Brazil’s Cafu.

Elsewhere, Argentina centre-back Cristian Romero snubbed Donald Trump’s handshake during the presentation of the runners-up medals.

Romero started the match at the heart of the Argentine defence, alongside Lisandro Martinez, but was subbed off at the 70-minute mark.

However, the 28-year-old Tottenham defender still made his mark after that as he snubbed a handshake from Trump when the US president was conducting the medal presentation.

Trump was handing out medals to both teams, as well the individual tournament awards, and Romero shook the hand of both Fifa president Gianni Infantino and Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum, who were either side of Trump, but did not engage with the US president.

When Ryan Fox rolled in a 12-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole at Royal Birkdale to win The Open Championship by one shot in Southport, England, it was just past 5.30 a.m. in his homeland and the sun hadn't yet risen.

Most New Zealanders woke Monday to a wintry morning and the news their small nation had its fourth major golf champion.

Those who followed Fox on television throughout the night were able to watch him lift the Claret Jug before heading bleary-eyed but happily to work.

Sir Bob Charles, who was New Zealand's first major winner and the first left-handed golfer to win a major when he won the British Open in 1963, is now 90 and watched Fox's found round in replay at a more congenial hour.

“I’m watching this in color. In my day, it was all black and white,” Charles told the New Zealand Herald newspaper of the TV coverage. “I’m watching every hole that he’s playing. In my day, they only had about the last three or four holes.”

Charles praised Fox for the pace at which he plays the game which goes against a modern tendency toward slow play. Fox hesitated for barely 30 seconds over the final putt that allowed him to join Charles, Michael Campbell and Lydia Ko as a major-winner from New Zealand.

“Ryan is a refreshing player,” Charles told the Herald. “He plays the way the game should be played, the way it used to be played and should be played. And that is: you get on with it, and you don’t spend half an hour lining up every putt.

“Let’s hope that Ryan can be a great example of how the game should be played now, even when you’re playing for, you know, $100 million!”

New Zealand's Parliament is in recess. Had it been in session politicians likely would have taken the opportunity to lavish praise on Fox, seeking some of his reflected glory.

Instead, New Zealanders rushed to social media to praise the 39-year-old Fox, a third-generation sporting champion within his family. His father, Grant Fox, was an All Blacks rugby star and winner of the 1987 Rugby World Cup. His grandfather, Merv Wallace, was a captain of the New Zealand cricket team.

Fox touched on the family history after his win.

“We’ve got a great history in our family,” he said. “The other great thing is I had no pressure on me to follow in any of their footsteps. I don’t know if this tops their achievements, but it’s certainly right up there. I guess there’s no pressure on my kids going forward now!”

As if in tribute, the New Zealand cricket team completed a match and series win over the West Indies in the Caribbean just hours after Fox's triumph.

At Fox's home course, the Royal Auckland and Grange Golf Club, club captain Ian Blair said “you couldn’t find a nicer guy and more worthy champion golfer.”

“Our club has been privileged to watch Ryan develop from a fine young man with potential to a champion player and member,” Blair said.

Club chief executive Ian Chapman told the Stuff news website members will be queuing up to buy Fox a beer.

Michael Campbell, the 2005 U.S. Open champion, described Fox's effort as “an incredible feat ... to beat the world's best players in a difficult situation.”

“I got to experience that 21 years ago. It's mind-blowing. It really changes your world and he's up there with the best players in the world now,” Campbell said on the New Zealand Herald's Ryan Bridge today podcast.
