Sports.title: Spain win World Cup after Ferran Torres breaks 10-man Argentina’s resistance
Sports.content:
It was the triumph of an idea, an identity. Of an unshakable and patient faith. And when it was over, Spain’s new generation having emulated the one from the 2010 World Cup, all of those legendary names, there was simply delirium for them.

Spain were the only team that turned up to play this World Cup final, from the first whistle to the last in extra time. Argentina were damned by their lack of ambition even before they had Enzo Fernández sent off towards the end of the regulation time. It was extraordinary to report that they did not have an attempt on goal until the 115th minute.

Spain did not let them play. Just as they have barely let any of their opponents do so during the course of this tournament. Their miserly defence has been the cornerstone of everything. They have been breached just once in their eight matches.

The question that came to pound concerned their ability to find a way through the sky blue and white ranks. It was the only question. Spain stayed true to their style; to who they are. The possession. The cohesive movements. The control. When they found the answer, it was the moment when they knew that a second World Cup triumph was about to become gloriously real.

The goal came in the 106th minute and it was nothing less than they deserved. Pedro Porro crossed deep and it was a wonderful header back by the substitute Nico Williams. It teed up another replacement, Ferran Torres, for the opportunity of his lifetime. The finish was high and true.

The Argentina manager, Lionel Scaloni, looked ready to cry. It was a white knuckle ride that carried his team to this stage, defined by late goals and a never-say-die spirit. At no point in any of their knock-out games were they ahead in the 90th minute.

Argentina flickered in the very closing stages. The substitute Guiliano Simeone lashed a half chance high. But there would be no successful defence of the title they won in 2022; no fairytale sign-off for Lionel Messi. He could not suppress the tears as he gazed at the Argentina support afterwards.

Messi and his team had won their previous three tournaments – two Copa Américas either side of the last World Cup. They had not lost a knockout tie since the 2019 Copa América. They got what they deserved here. There was an ugly flashpoint after full time when Leandro Paredes, who had come on as a substitute, was given a red card for grabbing the Spain replacement Eric García by the throat.

Argentina’s reaction in defeat was shameful. They turned their backs on the Spain players as the trophy was presented, preferring to keep their eyes on the fans behind one of the goals. Donald Trump, who did not want to leave the stage as the Spain captain, Rodri, got his hands on those six kilograms of solid gold bliss, was not the only person to make a spectacle of himself.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres smashes the ball into the roof of the net to score Spain’s extra-time winner. Photograph: Michael Zemanek/Shutterstock

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres celebrates scoring the only goal of the World Cup final. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

It was quite the show overall in the land of the spectacular show. It started with a ceremony, one to officially close the most bloated tournament there has been, which took in all manner of performances. Jennifer Hudson’s rendition of the US anthem before kick-off was certainly something; ditto Tom Cruise’s speech about the beautiful game. We kicked off six minutes late. There was plenty more at half-time. The action on the field did not keep pace.

Argentina had one flicker in the early running when the Spain goalkeeper, Unai Simon, left his line to deal with a Julián Álvarez throughball for Messi. The clearance was straight to Álvarez but his first touch was poor. That was pretty much it from them in forward-thinking terms.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Enzo Fernández sends Pau Cubarsí flying to receive a second yellow at the end of normal time. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

The game was all about Spain’s dominance of the ball. Nobody cherishes it quite like them. Rodri set the tempo at the back of the midfield while Lamine Yamal had a few eye-catching moments. He went close at the outset. Spain finessed their patterns. They tried to wear Argentina down.

Did anybody enjoy the half-time show? It was a strange detail that Madonna, one of the headline acts, did not actually appear on the pitch. Instead, there was big-screen video of her singing in the back of a car which was driven by Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Spain pressed high. They forced turnovers. They probed. Argentina could not free themselves from the choke hold. The chances started to come for Spain after the hydration break in the second half of normal time and Argentina were indebted to their goalkeeper, Emi Martínez. He finished with 11 saves, some of them excellent. Were Argentina trying to win the World Cup without taking a shot? Scaloni could scarcely have built a lower block, although he doubled down still further in the 101st minute when he introduced Marcos Senesi for Álvarez and went to 5-3-1.

Lionel Scaloni restructured in midfield, introducing Paredes in the holding role for the left-winger Nico González. The Argentina manager wanted his players to get closer to their opponents. It was not long before Paredes barged Rodri off the ball and was booked.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi’s final World Cup game, probably, ends in defeat. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

Fernández was guilty of losing his composure. Booked in the 83rd minute for dissent, he was asking for trouble when he left something in on Pau Cubarsí to send the Spain defender spinning. Argentina just about reached extra time when Martínez dived to repel a Lamine Yamal free-kick. His best saves before that had denied Cubarsí, Aymeric Laporte and Williams.

Spain turned the screw in extra time. Martínez continued to resist, saving once again from Williams. Spain were denied when Mikel Merino, on as a substitute, was adjudged to have fouled another replacement, Nicolás Otamendi, moments before Williams swept home. It was a generous decision for Otamendi, who appeared to throw himself to the ground. Merino glanced wide from a Williams cross when gloriously placed.

Spain’s pressure reached the point when the breakthrough felt inevitable. Torres provided the release, the joy. He would also run through in the 113th minute to beat Martínez again, only to be pulled back for offside. The goal he did score was all that mattered. Luis de la Fuente’s unstarry team have a second one on their shirts.

Sports.title: Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino booed before US president attempts to crash Spain celebrations
Sports.content:
Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino were booed as they took to the field for the presentation ceremony before the US president attempted to gatecrash Spain’s victory party.

Trump arrived at the stadium on Marine One, with the president’s helicopter first flying over the stadium about 45 minutes before kick-off. He sat in a glassed-in section of luxury seats for the match, along with Infantino. Other dignitaries and former players sat nearby, including Spain’s king, Felipe VI, Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum.

Trump was briefly shown on the video screens at the stadium after the US national anthem was played. There were scattered boos from some in the crowd but nothing like the hostile reception he has received at other sporting events during his presidency. However, when the US president and Infantino came on to the field for the presentation after Spain clinched victory, boos rang out around the stadium. The White House pool report said that ambient crowd noise, which had been sitting at approximately 78 decibels before their introduction, rose to 84 decibels when Trump entered the field.

Then, after Trump presented Spain with the World Cup trophy, he attempted to stand with the team at the side of the podium as they celebrated before Infantino quietly ushered him away.

It was a repeat of last summer’s Club World Cup at the same stadium after Trump presented the trophy to champions Chelsea and tried to crash the celebrations to the bemusement of the players.

Trump has made several appearances at sporting events since his re-election. Last year, he attended the Super Bowl, tennis’s US Open, the Daytona 500 and golf’s Ryder Cup. This year, he has attended several golf events, college football’s national championship game and Game 3 of the NBA finals, where he was met with boos from the New York Knicks home crowd.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi receives his runner-up medal from Donald Trump. Photograph: Alex Pantling/FIFA/Getty Images

Trump’s appearance was the first time he has attended a match at this summer’s World Cup, which the have US co-hosted along with Canada and Mexico.

At the 2022 World Cup final, the emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, joined Infantino to award the trophy to Lionel Messi and his Argentina teammates. Vladimir Putin awarded it to Kylian Mbappé and France after their win at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

View image in fullscreen Rodri lifts the World Cup Trophy alongside Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images

Trump is the first sitting US president to attend a World Cup final on home soil. When the US hosted the tournament in 1994, Trump’s predecessor Bill Clinton did not attend the game. The trophy was instead presented by Clinton’s vice-president, Al Gore.

Trump has a close relationship with Infantino, and called the Fifa president to lobby for a review of USA star Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before their last-16 match. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team, who exited a promising World Cup with defeat to Belgium.

Sports.title: Hits, misses and Muppets: the star-studded World Cup half-time show nobody asked for
Sports.content:
Like hydration breaks and Donald Trump’s ability to get refereeing decisions overturned by simply phoning up the president of Fifa and complaining, the final half-time show is an innovation of the 2026 World Cup that comes with a degree of controversy attached. For one thing, its existence automatically means the World Cup final breaks the International Football Association’s 15-minute half-time mandate.

For another, its obvious antecedent lies in the NFL’s Super Bowl, where the half-time entertainment has mushroomed over the decades from a few marching bands to one of the big pop events of the year. To its detractors, it smacks of America not so much embracing the World Cup as imposing itself upon it.

View image in fullscreen Shakira performs during the World Cup final. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

But before you even got to the main event, there was more musical entertainment at the final to wade through, most notably the pre-match closing ceremony, a damp squib that neither the BBC nor ITV elected to broadcast live.

Anyone who hastened to iPlayer was rewarded not merely with Post Malone debuting what’s presumably the first single from his forthcoming album the Eternal Buzz, Chrome Heartbreaker (a pivot back to hip-hop-influenced pop after his recent diversion into country, should you be eagerly tracking the artistic vacillations of Post Malone’s career) and duetting with Swae Lee on their US chart-topper Sunflowers, but also an online influencer-cum-professional wrestler called IShowSpeed performing Champions, a track that gained so much traction online that Fifa felt obliged to include it on the official Fifa World Cup album.

A frightful cocktail of thunderous drums and autotuned vocals, it featured lyrics that make your average football song sound as erudite and profound as the oeuvre of Leonard Cohen: “I take a breath and wait for the ref / This is the World Cup, put your hands in the air.” Alas, news of its social media virality clearly hadn’t reached the audience in the New York New Jersey Stadium. The deathly silence at its conclusion made you wonder if perhaps the TV broadcast couldn’t pick up the sound of the crowd, but no: some fireworks subsequently went off and they went audibly mental.

View image in fullscreen Three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem performed the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

There was, it turned out, more to come. Jennifer Hudson sang the Star-Spangled Banner. Dutifully flogging a dead horse with all the professionalism he could muster, Robbie Williams performed the Fifa anthem, Desire, in the company of Laura Pausini and Nicole Scherzinger. The ballad debuted at the draw ceremony in December and – like all the musical entertainment at said event – it was overshadowed by the news that Fifa had apparently started making up awards in order to give them to Donald Trump. It vanished into obscurity thereafter, failing to chart anywhere in the world. Listening to it exhumed for another airing, you were forced to concede that the world had a point.

After all that, the actual half-time show felt like a comparative triumph. You could argue that the bar had been set pretty low without much dissent, but nonetheless, it zipped along, cramming a lot into its 11 minutes by the simple expedient of paring songs down to their bare essentials and swiftly cutting between artists. Madonna performed a version of her 2000 hit Music – reworked over a backing track immediately recognisable as derived from the Trammps’ Disco Inferno – on a vaguely Mad Max-ish vehicle piloted by Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Then the strains of the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army rang out, ostensibly performed by three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem. There was no sign of their leader, Dr Teeth, but perhaps he was indisposed, being treated backstage after being exposed to Champions by IShowSpeed. BTS rattled through Dynamite, Shakira and Burna Boy played a truncated version of Dai Dai – the solitary World Cup song in recent memory to actually impact on the British charts – and Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir: the latter looks horrendous on paper, but was far less sugary in reality, undercut by the farty blast of a crowd of vuvuzela players.

View image in fullscreen Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir that was far less sugary than it could have been. Photograph: Tullio Puglia/FIFA/Getty Images

The solitary misstep might have involved allowing Justin Bieber to perform a downcast acoustic ballad, Everything Hallelujah – viral hit following his performance at Coachella or not, this perhaps wasn’t the moment for introspection – but no matter: if the half-time show wasn’t sufficiently head-spinning to convince the viewer it should be a regular occurrence at every World Cup final, it worked well enough to justify its existence at least this time. Although clearly not everyone felt the same way: “I thought it was crap,” offered Wayne Rooney, when pressed for his opinions by BBC presenter Gabby Logan.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s World Cup fairytale ends with pitiful Argentina as final villains | Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Sports.content:
Playing on the grandest stage in sport for the last time, Lionel Messi seemed almost certain to provide one last memorable moment in this World Cup final.

Yet as the sun ducked behind the west stand of New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday, it became clearer and clearer that Argentina had lost the magic they had carried through this tournament. And as Spain gradually wrested control, one was left to confront reality: Messi, and Argentina, had finally run out of time, having long since given in to their worst instincts in a 1-0 defeat.

This final presented a stark contrast to the Argentina – and Messi – we observed in every other match of the tournament. Almost without exception, La Albiceleste have been the tournament’s most entertaining team, not so much for how they’ve scored their goals but for when they’ve scored them, offering a masterclass in dramatic timing. Twice they were nearly eliminated by badly outmatched opponents, results that only galvanized them.

Finals are frequently forgettable matches that fail to entertain but even by that lowly standard the pacing of things felt dreadful. Spain were suffocating defensively and – after a forgettable first half – finally worked their way into things in the second 45, eventually breaking through in extra time, quite expectedly. Argentina? They became the first team in the near century-long history of the tournament to fail to record a shot in regular time of a World Cup final. Even when handed an additional half an hour, they never threatened.

And Messi? Until this final, he had presented observers with one of the rarest opportunities in professional sport: a chance to witness greatness free of stakes, entirely devoid of any real pressure to perform. At 39, Messi has done his time and nobody could criticize his collection of hardware – as an individual or as part of a club or country. This defeat does nothing to sully a spotless legacy; a win would have only strengthened his claim as the greatest player in the history of the sport. To some Argentinians, the victory against England in their semi-final likely carries nearly as much weight as a victory in the final would have.

Yet it has to be said: Messi was rarely involved in this match, a far cry from the player who has sometimes carried his team this summer. Much of this, of course, is down to a Spain masterclass in defending. That alone is not always enough to contain the diminutive Argentina captain. But give Spain their due: they badly outclassed Argentina in every way, neutralizing even Messi. By the end Argentina had become what so many observers pegged them to be in the first place, sometimes unfairly: underhanded, dirty and desperate.

Time has almost always been irrelevant to Messi on the field, because he so frequently bends it to his liking to elude those who defend him. The manner in which he performs at age 39 has a similar effect, tearing open a rift in time itself and transporting observers back to his glory days at Barcelona and elsewhere. Time itself has not passed him by as much as he’s marched alongside it, occasionally trailing behind a step or two but always eventually pulling even with it again.

View image in fullscreen Spain kept close tabs on Lionel Messi, who had little impact on the final. Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty Images

Yet now we are left to face the unmistakable reality that Messi is done, with the World Cup at least – this is, it’s worth noting, what was said after he led Argentina to their first World Cup in nearly four decades in 2022 and what was assumed in 2016, when Messi briefly retired from the national team after Argentina’s defeat in the Copa América final. Back then, the dialogue surrounding this player was that he would never play for Argentina the way he did for Barcelona, or even rumblings that Messi himself wasn’t sufficiently Argentinian, having spent so much of his life in Spain. Both arguments feel laughable 10 years later.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It remains to be seen how Argentina’s performance will be perceived back home, where expectations were understandably high. The head coach, Lionel Scaloni, and even Messi had spoken at length before the final about how much they had already achieved. This final result, they implied, would do little to sully that sense of accomplishment.

This was, of course, before they took the field and more or less destroyed the game. Scaloni’s legacy, like Messi’s, was secure before this final, the coach having brought Argentina a third World Cup and a pair of Copa América titles, but this was a lost opportunity to solidify it. Two things can coexist: Scaloni is almost without question Argentina’s greatest coach, and this was one of his worst results and performances.

What feels much more real, though, is a sense of loss and disappointment after this pitiful final performance, which provided Argentina – and Messi – with a perfect opportunity to put the finishing touches on their fairytale. Instead, they turned from hero to villain – and needlessly so.

Sports.title: At the World Cup of superstars, a team take home the trophy | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
Release the pressure, let it out. All of it and all of them. Again and again they had come, again and again they had been halted but they would not be denied. A dozen different players had taken aim at Emi Martínez’s goal but somehow he was still standing and time was slipping away, yet Spain refused to do so, so they came some more.

And then, suddenly, only this wasn’t really sudden, the result instead of the purest logic, the clearest justice, Pedro Porro’s deep cross found Nico Williams at the far post and he headed back. The ball dropped deep inside the Argentina penalty area, bounced on the turf and just kind of sat there: waiting, willing someone take this moment.

So at 5.42pm eastern daylight time, 37 seconds into the second period of extra time, Ferran Torres did. And with Spain’s 20th shot of this final, with all his might and all his soul, he won the World Cup. The ball travelled at 102km/h, tearing into the net, and Torres turned and tore in the other direction, sprinting to the corner where he leapt into the air and volleyed that too. Not quite so hard as he had hit the shot, but hard. From the bench and the pitch his teammates raced towards him, liberated at last, the joy flooding out. Oh, the release.

Andrés Iniesta once said that the moment the ball sat up for him in the 116th minute of the final in South Africa in 2010, he heard the silence. Maybe Torres heard it too; maybe he heard history call. More often he has heard noise. Here there was an explosion, everyone at that end of New York New Jersey Stadium going absolutely mad. Torres stood there, doing a familiar gesture: jibber-jabber hands, ears “listening” wondering where the critics were now. Then he got the biggest hug Lamine Yamal has ever given.

Late in Spain’s victory over Saudi Arabia on the day that Luis de la Fuente celebrated his 65th birthday, Torres had come on as a substitute and scored the final goal – or thought he had – only for the video assistant referee to take it from him. As they reviewed the footage, Ferran had stood with his hands in front of his mouth in a praying position, muttering to himself: por favor, be a goal; por favor, be a goal. This seemed like a portrait of the pressure, of what players put up with sometimes, a picture perhaps of desperation too. Spain were four goals up already, but here he was pleading for it to count.

In the previous game against Cape Verde, he had hit the bar. In the next game, against Uruguay, he did it again. There was something that his critics took as confirmation, something cruel in how close it was. Too often he had felt that fate somehow was conspiring against him. Turned out, it was saving something for him: the greatest goal, the greatest moment in any player’s career. Justice had been done, not just in the game, which Spain had dominated Spain’s way – at that point Argentina had not had a shot – but to this team. This family, as De la Fuente calls them, all in it together.

It felt right almost that it should be Torres, a symbol of all of them – like this was another moment shared, the collective expressed in one man who hasn’t always felt it but will now be for ever beloved. Torres became the seventh different Spain player to score in the US. At the World Cup of the stars, a team took the trophy. The European champions were the best team here, lifting that trophy having conceded just one goal, and this was a victory for a system, an ideal, a commitment to an identity. In that, it can feel almost inevitable but it is not. This was also a victory for vindication, for the belief their manager has in them and they have in each other, even if others do not. “People have been very unfair with him but he has a spectacular mentality, he keeps going, keeps working, and today life has paid him back,” Pedro Porro said of Torres. “This is for all 26 of us.”

Coming into the tournament, Rodri, the captain, had not completed his rehabilitation yet. Lamine Yamal, the star, was returning from injury too, everyone waiting for him until they realised that maybe they didn’t have to. Williams, who had provided the assist, thought he wouldn’t get there: injured for much of the season, he fought back then feared Uruguay had kicked him out of the World Cup.

Fabián Ruiz had missed most the season injured. Aymeric Laporte, imperious again, suffered with Athletic. Behind him, the debate around Unai Simón wouldn’t relent. Eric García and Martín Zubimendi came on here to win it: neither had had a minute yet, meaning Spain finished the competition with only two outfielders who have not played. Who had Pedro Porro and Marc Cucurella down as the world’s best full-backs before the tournament? Plenty do now. Mikel Merino, the superest of super subs, had played only 28 minutes since March, but appeared to rescue them. Not once, but twice.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And then, at the biggest moment of all, there was Torres.

De la Fuente said that Spain had been “stung” by the doubts in those early games, the lack of recognition. “They are the best players in the world,” he kept saying, and it turned out he was right. Spain’s coach is a man of faith; faith in his footballers, his “family”. Every day over the last month he has exchanged messages with a friend Antonio, who is like a son to him, expressing the conviction they both felt. “It is written,” the messages say, and now it is.

Sports.title: Kane says Tuchel will ‘learn a lot’ from England pressures after exit to Argentina
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has backed Thomas Tuchel to learn from England’s World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina and believes they must use the forthcoming Nations League campaign to gain experience of playing against the top teams.

Kane was an unused substitute as England sealed third place with an entertaining 6-4 victory against France on Saturday – their best finish at a World Cup on foreign soil. Tuchel, who signed a contract extension before the tournament, has been criticised heavily for his tactics against Argentina when he opted to switch to a back five to try to defend a 1-0 lead.

Kane admitted England had fallen short against Lionel Scaloni’s side but described the environment Tuchel has created since succeeding Gareth Southgate in 2025 as “the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness”.

The captain said: “I know there are a lot of questions after the other night. We have to process it as players. I’m sure the manager will. It’s his first major tournament. He’ll learn a lot from the players, the situations, the pressures, the travel.

“There are also a lot of things as players we can learn from the other night. For now it’s just trying to process everything. We had a lot of good things, a lot of tough situations we overcame. The group is incredible, the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness. The boss was a big part of creating that as well.

“Fans are going to be angry and we understand it. It’s a major tournament and that’s why you dream so big. When it doesn’t go your way you have to take the criticism. We’re all willing to do that, to dare to reach the biggest goal of all. We know over the next two years until we’re facing that situation again there is always going to be a question mark. It’s something we have to take and use as motivation.”

England missed out on facing regular top-class opposition in the buildup to the World Cup after being relegated from the top Nations League group in 2022 under Southgate. They were promoted in 2024 and will face Spain, Croatia and Czechia, starting with a rematch of the Euro 2024 final against Luis de la Fuente’s side on 26 September at Wembley. After beating France – albeit in a largely meaningless game – Kane thinks England must take the competition seriously if they are to thrive in tournaments.

View image in fullscreen Defeat to an established opponent was a familiar feeling for England. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

“The last 30 minutes of Argentina is not the team we want to be,” he said. “We spent a lot of time over the last two years talking about that situation, to attack those moments. The bottom line is we lost anyway. It’s easy to go away and talk about it. We need to get better at actually being in those situations. We can train, play the qualifiers … I think the Nations League will be big for us, against Spain and Croatia, big teams.

“Getting used to those big environments and finding our best form against those teams, like we did against France, albeit not in the most competitive match. We have to learn, improve. The coach will have improved from these learnings. I can talk as much as I want but ultimately it’s about showing it next time we’re in that situation.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Kane has been on the losing side in two World Cup semi-finals and two European Championship finals and he believes Tuchel is the man to help England to make the final step.

“The enthusiasm he has, the emotion he brings, the tactical experience he has … it doesn’t mean you’re going to get it right every time. We want to get it right on the biggest occasions and he expects that from himself as well. He’s a fantastic coach. He not only gave the players belief but he gave the country belief that it was our year. That is why it hurts even more than other years because everyone believed we were going all the way.

“Everyone has to process it. He has to process it himself. We’re still in that grieving stage, the emotional stage, and we’ll be in that for the next few weeks. It won’t be until the next camp where you think about what the future holds and what the next target is. We’ll have conversations as captain and manager and with other teammates and staff, to see where we can be better.”

Sports.title: England 2026 World Cup squad: player-by-player ratings
Sports.content:
Goalkeepers

Jordan Pickford Could he have done better with Enzo Fernández’s equaliser for Argentina? Jude Bellingham certainly thought so. But the man who has made more World Cup finals appearances than any other Englishman made some crucial saves, including a brilliant stop from Nicolas González in the semi-final. 7

Dean Henderson Had to wait until the third-place playoff for some action and ended up conceding four goals despite a strong performance. Will hope to challenge Pickford over next two years. 7

Defenders

Djed Spence Emerged as an unlikely cult hero thanks to some wholehearted performances. He will always be remembered for snubbing Thomas Partey’s handshake and his tackle on Giuliano Simeone against Argentina. 8

Marc Guéhi Somehow wasn’t Thomas Tuchel’s first-choice initially, although that was rectified after the Croatia game. England’s most consistent and reliable defender – the way he handled Erling Haaland was a masterclass. 8

John Stones Arrived painfully short of match fitness and it showed in the opening game against Croatia. Much improved when called upon in the quarter- and semi-finals. A huge asset when he plays. 7

Ezri Konsa A few shaky moments during the group stage but recovered well and filled in capably at right-back when needed. At 28, young enough to be there again in four years. 7

View image in fullscreen Dan Burn’s headed block from this Raúl Jiménez bicycle kick cleared the halfway line. Photograph: Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images

Dan Burn Showed his limitations against Argentina. But he will always have those two epic appearances off the bench against Mexico and Norway. No one will forget the clearing headers so powerful they ended up in the opposition’s half. 7

Nico O’Reilly Had his strongest game against Norway in the quarter-final when he was at his marauding best. Will be disappointed not to have scored and to have been on the pitch as a substitute when Argentina instigated their semi-final comeback. 6

Reece James Such a good player when fit, which is sadly far too rare. Missed most of the tournament owing to a hamstring injury and England suffered when he went off against Argentina. 6

Trevoh Chalobah The Chelsea player was a surprise choice to replace Tino Livramento, who pulled out injured at the last minute. Managed only six minutes against France in the end. 6

Jarell Quansah Brought in to solve the right-back conundrum against Panama, he was doing well until the rush of blood against Mexico and subsequent red card. Recalled for the France game and had to be replaced. 5

Midfielders

Jude Bellingham Showed his supreme quality when it mattered and could not be more committed to his country’s cause, even if his rocky relationship with Tuchel had to be carefully managed. 9

Elliot Anderson Didn’t allow himself to be distracted by his £116m move to Manchester City and grew as the tournament progressed. Ran his heart out against Norway and Argentina. 8

View image in fullscreen Morgan Rogers (left) crossed for Anthony Gordon to put England ahead against Argentina. Photograph: Julian Finney/FIFA/Getty Images

Morgan Rogers Made the most of his limited minutes in unfamiliar roles. Showed what a good player he is by playing as one of the two central midfielders against Norway before setting up Anthony Gordon from the right wing against Argentina. 8

Declan Rice Clearly affected by the hamstring and back problems that marred the second half of his season with Arsenal, even if his effort – as ever – could not be faulted. Needs a long rest to recharge his batteries but may not get one. 6

Eberechi Eze Could not have the impact he would have wished for in four substitute appearances before starting against France. Did a decent job in central midfield against Panama but was largely on the periphery when given a chance on the left in the quarter-final. 6

Jordan Henderson Spent 12 minutes on the pitch, in a historic appearance against Panama when he became the first England men’s player to appear at seven major international tournaments. But managed to get booked against Mexico as a substitute and break an arm celebrating the win. 5

Forwards

Bukayo Saka Three goals and three assists despite playing through the pain of an achilles injury was a courageous effort from Arsenal’s talisman. It was a huge surprise not to see him come off the bench against Argentina and he showed what England were missing against France. 8

Anthony Gordon A quiet start having been preferred to Rashford before responding magnificently to being dropped. Three assists and a goal against Argentina showed why Barcelona were so keen to sign him. 8

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s two goals against the Democratic Republic of the Congo saved England from an early exit. Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA

Harry Kane Sadly his tournament will be remembered for a largely anonymous display against Argentina rather than rescuing England against the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Will he ever have a better chance to win the World Cup? 8

Marcus Rashford Made a good start to his third World Cup by coming off the bench to score against Croatia, and started against Panama. But wasn’t seen again until England were chasing the game against Argentina in injury time. 6

Ivan Toney Sat on the bench until Lautaro Martínez’s goal in added time of the semi-final. Could not make an impact in the three minutes he was given but did well against France. 6

Ollie Watkins Largely a frustrated spectator despite his heroics in the Euro 2024 semi-final and arriving here in a rich vein of form. A half on the left flank against France and a brief appearance against Panama were scant reward. 6

Noni Madueke Some promising moments but lacked end product in his four starts and had slipped down the pecking order by the semi-final. Needs to be much more clinical at this level. 5

Did not play: James Trafford and Kobbie Mainoo

Sports.title: Fifa gives fraud ‘an open door’ with betting, says Council of Europe chief
Sports.content:
Fifa has been accused of providing an “open door to fraud” and allowing political influence to cast doubt on the integrity of the World Cup in a stinging rebuke by the Council of Europe’s secretary general.

In an open letter published to coincide with Sunday’s final, Alain Berset also called for a new integrity framework to be built before the 2030 tournament, which is mainly being staged in Europe, and warned that Fifa was embroiled in a crisis involving money and power.

Berset referenced the scandal surrounding Fifa’s decision to shelve the suspension of the USA striker Folarin Balogun and made apparent allusions to comments made by the Paraguayan senator Celeste Amarilla about Kylian Mbappé and by the former Spanish prime minister Mariano Rajoy about the France team.

“The Fifa World Cup 2026 has raised question after question,” Berset wrote. “A sanction suspended under pressure, within days, with no reasons given. The authority of referees called into question. Racist abuse of players, some of it from elected officials. Betting on every pass, every card, every corner. The celebration will end tonight. The questions will not.”

It is a significant intervention given Fifa and the Council of Europe signed a memorandum of understanding in 2018, which remains valid. The agreement was struck to strengthen their work together on a number of topics, including “human rights, integrity and good governance in sport”. Open criticism of one partner by another is extremely rare.

Berset took aim at Fifa’s deal with ADI Predictstreet, which became the World Cup’s official prediction market partner in April. “Betting has moved from the result of a match to moments a single player can produce without changing the score,” he said. “A bet is won by making others lose. It is an open door to fraud. And this World Cup has opened the door wider.”

In further reference to the lifting of Balogun’s ban by Fifa, which occurred after a phone call to its president, Gianni Infantino, by his US counterpart, Donald Trump, Berset said: “When the rules bend under pressure, every result is open to doubt.”

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino with Donald Trump at the World Cup final reception at Trump Tower on Friday 17 July in New York. Photograph: Ira L Black/Fifa/Getty Images

Infantino has said the decision to revoke Balogun’s ban was taken independently by Fifa’s disciplinary committee “based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts”.

Berset, who is Swiss, proposed a “working dialogue that starts tonight” to begin the “urgent work of strengthening the integrity of sport” before future World Cups. He referenced work by the Council of Europe – which is the continent’s intergovernmental human rights organisation – in creating a binding treaty to keep fans safe three months after the Heysel Stadium disaster in 1985, as well as further legislation set up to tackle doping in athletics and match-fixing.

The letter comes a week and a half after 72 members of the European parliament wrote to the 27 EU-based football associations asking for an investigation into Infantino’s involvement in the Balogun case. It pointed to alleged breaches of political neutrality and suggested Fifa had contravened its own code of ethics.

It does not appear likely that Uefa, European football’s governing body, will formally take the matter further. In June, 50 members of the European parliament wrote to Infantino and the Fifa council requesting an investigation into the awarding of the Fifa peace prize to Trump.

Fifa was contacted for comment.

This past week it was revealed that more that 200 of Fifa’s member associations have formally backed Infantino’s attempt to be re-elected for a fourth term in March.

Sports.title: Trump's cringe World Cup cameo was a fitting finale to a tournament blighted by excess, greed and FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's twisted dreams
Sports.content:
Night was closing in over New Jersey. The smog had cleared, the storms had passed, the fireworks had stopped crackling and the spotlight had shifted a few meters away from a vast presentation crew headlined by Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino.

Only then – at nearly 7pm local time, at long, long last - could Spain captain Rodri thrust the World Cup trophy toward the setting sun. It had been nearly six weeks since Mexico and South Africa lit the fuse on this World Cup. It had been nearly four hours since this final kicked off and more than five hours since the festivities began.

In that time, Spain took 120 minutes to beat Argentina but Infantino needed even longer to crowbar in all the manifestations of his twisted dreams.

How smug the FIFA president looked as he ignored the boos and stood beside Trump to crown the new world champions. How cringeworthy it was to watch them hand over the trophy together. And how unfortunate that – as gold glitter fell from the sky – Trump and Infantino refused to exit stage left and let the real heroes of this story have their moment.

But who expected any different on a day when sports was – time and again – barged into the shade by politics and music and the circus of showbusiness?

Only FIFA and its Teflon president know why Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal and Co needed to share soccer's greatest stage with Justin Bieber, Madonna, Shakira, Coldplay, the Muppets and a clown.

Spain celebrate their World Cup triumph while President Donald Trump stands nearby

The FIFA president and the US president handed over the World Cup trophy together

Madonna, flanked by Ronaldinho (L) and Ronaldo (R), performed during the halftime show

Shakira sung Dai Dai with Burna Boy during halftime of Spain's win over Argentina

But whatever the motivation – and some guesses are better than others – this will be remembered as a final but also a first. A first World Cup final to feature a halftime show. A first World Cup final where fans could pay $1million to watch from a pitchside sofa. A first World Cup final when, apparently, soccer wasn't enough.

It was, in many ways, a fitting apex to a tournament when the sport nearly drowned under a tidal wave of greed.

For much of this summer, the performances of superstars such as Messi and Jude Bellingham ensured this World Cup has been a triumph in spite of FIFA. There will be some who sat through these 120 minutes and concluded that Spain and Argentina needed an added dose of drama and sparkle.

But, unfortunately for Infantino, his halftime show, his closing ceremony and the rest of his add-ons fell flat, too. History suggests that won't be enough for him to change tack.

Not even the haze which has hung over New York in recent days could blur the grimmer aspects of this World Cup. When the child mascots were sponsored by Quaker Oats. When the prize was delivered on to the field in a Louis Vuitton 'Trophy Trunk.' When some fans were barred from entering the country and many others were priced out of going to games. When organizers are selling everything from commemorative rings to a patch of MetLife grass for $450.

On Sunday, adverts for the halftime show were plastered across the walls of the men's toilets. Perhaps the urinals will be the next souvenir to hit the market. That might be all an average fan could afford. This was, after all, among the priciest sporting events in history with some tickets – on FIFA's own resale platform – going for up to $2.3m in recent days.

Perhaps those with the deepest pockets want more for their money than 120 minutes of soccer. And at the end of the first half, the players had barely reached the tunnel when Bruce Buffer appeared on the jumbotrons and began a five-minute countdown to 'what we've all been waiting for.' That scripted line rather summed up FIFA's warped priorities this summer.

Ferran Torres scored the winning goal for Spain as they overcame Argentina in extra time

Justin Bieber sang a World Cup-themed version of his song Everything Hallelujah on Sunday

Trump and Infantino watched the game together from a luxury suite at MetLife Stadium

For those who missed it, here is a brief run-through of 27 forgettable minutes: Madonna opened the show, 'driven' around the bowels of the stadium by Brazilian legends Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

The 67-year-old made it to the edge of the field but no further before K-Pop band BTS took over. Before long, Ted Lasso was introducing Justin Bieber. His a capella performance was followed by Shakira and Burna Boy's rendition of 'Dai Dai.'

The final act of the 11-minute show belonged to a local choir, PS22 Chorus, who performed with Coldplay while the Muppets had a cameo, too. Production wise, it wasn't a patch on the Super Bowl.

So what did the crowd make of it? Well, England legend Wayne Rooney – watching from the BBC studio in the stands – called it 'crap' and supporters of both Spain and Argentina made their feelings clear, too. As soon as the music stopped, they broke into song and attempted to turn this into a soccer game once more.

Perhaps it should come as no surprise that FIFA chose this summer to turn the World Cup final into a spectacle resembling the Super Bowl. Over here, the lines separating sports, music and celebrity culture are more blurred than perhaps anywhere else. But there was still a heavy dose of irony in their decision.

Because back in 1994, the last time the USA hosted the World Cup, organizers attempted to put on a halftime show. Whitney Houston was supposed to perform on the field. Alas, FIFA torpedoed that plan and their idea to sell final tickets for $1,000.

It turns out US soccer chiefs were on to something. That day at the Rose Bowl, organizers also devised – what they claim was - sports' first ever hospitality package. It wasn't much – fans received a parking pass, a program and some hors d'oeuvres. But three decades on, this circus, these $1m sofas, were a garish illustration of what can happen when you open Pandora's Suite.

Trump and Infantino opted for a box rather than a couch and it is fortunate this was the first and only game the US president attended. Because by midmorning, the perimeter of MetLife Stadium had descended into chaos. As the sun burned overhead, lines snaked around parking lots and tempers began to boil over.

Influencer IShowSpeed was among those to perform at the closing ceremony on Sunday

Tom Cruise delivered a speech before the game that was largely drowned out by supporters

Agents from the Department of Homeland Security, state police, and Transportation Security Administration were on hand to help the secret service check everyone and everything coming inside. Among the items that had to be 'surrendered' at the gates? Bicycles, balloons and, in a real blow to any influencers posing as soccer fans, selfie sticks.

It is a well-polished routine by now – since returning to the Oval Office, the president has barely missed a major sporting event on these shores. But the exhaustive security operation still led to long delays. All to keep one man safe. All for Trump to miss the closing ceremony. How will he ever forgive himself?

There was around an hour and a half until kickoff when some of Spain's squad decided to take in their surroundings. Moments after they wandered off the field, a small army went to work. They covered the pitch with a giant flag depicting many of New York's most iconic monuments; they erected a small golden stage in the center circle. They were orchestrated by a maniac in fluorescent green who gesticulated with all the aggression of a North Korean army general.

How to describe the next 15 minutes? There were plenty of pyrotechnics. There were also performances by the influencer IShowSpeed, who danced and mimed his way around the field, and Post Malone, who closed the show after walking through a corridor of fire.

Trump and Infantino greet new World Cup winner and rising superstar Lamine Yamal

Infantino and Trump also fawned over Lionel Messi as they handed him a runners-up medal

Off went the flag and on came the corner flags to be stuck back into the ground. That was a timely reminder that a soccer match would soon break out. Alas, the end of the closing ceremony did not mean an end to the noise. And so resumed the adverts, the music, the invitations for fans to turn up the volume. No doubt they would have obliged if they had been given some silence to fill.

Instead? As kickoff approached, we heard from Coldplay's Chris Martin, who addressed the crowd in broken Spanish, from Nicole Scherzinger and Robbie Williams, whose performance was interrupted by a four-jet flyover, and from Tom Cruise, whose speech was – mercifully – drowned out by the Argentina supporters.

By then, Trump had announced his arrival. A fleet of helicopters including Marine One fluttered over MetLife Stadium and before long, the president was sitting on halfway with only bulletproof grass obstructing his view of this final.

After extra time, he was joined on the field by Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum and other dignitaries. Trump handed over winners' medals to Spain as, a few meters away, tears filled Messi's eyes. This was not the ending that the Argentina captain wanted. In truth, this is not what anyone envisaged at a World Cup final. Except for Infantino.

Sports.title: Donald Trump ignores FIFA president's call to leave the stage as he joins Spain's World Cup final trophy lift in awkward moment
Sports.content:
US President Donald Trump took center stage at MetLife Stadium on Sunday as he awkwardly invaded Spain's iconic trophy lift at the end of the FIFA World Cup final.

The European outfit clinched their second World Cup title after beating Lionel Messi's Argentina 1-0 in extra time, following a late strike from forward Ferran Torres.

Shortly after the full-time whistle, the US President made his way down to the field, where he was loudly booed by the crowd before making his way onto the stage alongside FIFA chief Gianni Infantino.

Trump and Infantino handed out various awards to match officials and players, before officially welcoming Spain's players up to the stage to lift the World Cup trophy.

The US President presented the prestigious title to Spain captain Rodri, who took great pleasure in raising it aloft in East Rutherford.

Much like when he presented the Club World Cup title last summer, Trump stood awkwardly alongside the Spain squad as they lifted the trophy and celebrated wildly.

Donald Trump took center stage as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday afternoon

The President, along with FIFA chief Gianni Infantino, presented the trophy to Spain's Rodri

It appeared as though Infantino attempted to usher Trump away - but the President remained

It seemed as though, when Spain were about to perform the trophy lift, Infantino had attempted to usher Trump away from the players - though the President remained.

He stood to the side of the squad as the confetti cannons went off at MetLife Stadium, clapping and grinning while Infantino laughed off Trump's awkward cameo.

There were an estimated 1.5-1.8 billion viewers tuning in to watch the summer tournament's showpiece finale, where Trump and Infantino took center stage once again.

Loud boos had come from the stands when Infantino and Trump made their way onto the pitch, as fans made their feelings on the duo undoubtedly clear.

Prior to the official trophy lift, Trump also handed out silver medals to Argentina's players - including Lionel Messi - after their heartbreaking defeat in New Jersey.

Fans noted that one Argentina star - Tottenham defender Cristian Romero - completely ignored the President as he collected his medal from Infantino.

In a video which swiftly went viral on social media, the Argentinian could be seen receiving his silverware from the FIFA chief before waltzing past Trump on stage.

Meanwhile, Trump also presented a trio of awards to Spain's stars; including the Young Player of the Tournament, the Golden Glove and the Golden Ball - which were claimed by Pau Cubarsi, Unai Simon and Rodri respectively.

Trump and Infantino stood on stage as golden confetti rained down around them in New Jersey

The US President welcomed Spain's stars onto the stage before presenting the prestigious title

The President also handed out silver medals to Lionel Messi and Argentina after their loss

Trump pictured presenting Lamine Yamal with his medal after the 1-0 win at MetLife Stadium

Argentina defender Cristian Romero appeared to ignore Trump as he walked on stage

There was a degree of irony in regards to Trump presenting Spain with the World Cup trophy, after previously launching a stinging attack on the country at a UN summit earlier in July for not contributing enough money to NATO.

'Spain is a terrible partner in NATO. They don’t participate. They don’t pay. I don’t want anything to do with Spain. Cut off all trade with Spain, please, including visits,' he said. 'Don’t even talk to them. They’re hopeless, bad people.'

Then, on his way back to the United States on Air Force One, Trump said Spain had tried to improve their standings with him.

'I did have issues, and ​I still do. But Spain, they came back all the way today. Spain was very generous today,' he said.

'They honoured a request for lots of payments, and if they didn't, we wouldn't have even ⁠talked to them.'

Earlier in the day, Trump and his wife Melania were seen taking in the action inside a packed MetLife Stadium suite - alongside FIFA President Infantino, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Trump also shook hands with Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez as Infantino stood beside them.

Spain's Queen Letizia and King Felipe VI also greeted the president. Javier Milei, the president of Argentina, is watching the game from home due to 'superstition,' The New York Times reported.

Trump cozied up to FIFA President Gianni Infantino in the private suite on Sunday afternoon in New Jersey

Inside the private suite, Infantino posed for pictures with the president's son, Eric Trump, his wife, Lara, and their children

President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania joined the massive crowd at MetLife Stadium on Sunday afternoon for the 2026 World Cup final match

The commander-in-chief also waved at the crowd from behind the glass.

Inside the private suite, Infantino posed for pictures with the president's son, Eric Trump, his wife, Lara, and their children. Barron Trump also showed up for the big game.

Ahead of the match, Trump told Fox News' Jenny Taft on the FIFA Red Carpet that 'it's hard to bet against Messi,' speaking of Argentina's 39-year-old star.

However, in the end, it wasn't to be for the veteran soccer star after he and Argentina came up short in their battle against European outfit Spain in East Rutherford.

The match was decided by a ferocious, close-range strike from Spanish star Ferran Torres in the 106th minute, after a 0-0 stalemate at the end of regulation time.

However, there were ugly scenes once the full-time whistle blew - with a number of frustrated Argentina stars taking out their anger on Spain's players after their loss.

After the whistle, Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes was sent off for punching Eric Garcia and pushing Gavi to the ground.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina also punched Rodri in the torso as he was running by, while Thiago Almada was involved, too.

Lionel Messi's bid for back-to-back World Cup titles ended in failure after their loss to Spain

Several stars clashed after Spain's 1-0 win over Argentina - but the South Americans started it

Argentina's Leandro Paredes was sent off after the whistle for getting violent with Spain

Micah Richards said of their behaviour on the BBC: 'It's embarrassing. They were on the cusp every single time.

'Seeing that sort of stuff after the game was played, it's not good, it's embarrassing to be honest. Paredes is better than that. We all know what it's like to lose a game but this is not good enough.'

Argentina only had two shots in the entire match, and the first of those only came in the 117th minute.

By contrast, they committed 24 fouls - though Spain didn't have clean hands themselves, as they gave away 21.

Elsewhere on the day, World Cup fans branded FIFA's controversial first-ever World Cup halftime show starring Madonna and Justin Bieber a 'disaster' on Sunday.

The futuristic segment began with Madonna, 67, singing her 2000 hit Music, accompanied by giddy Brazilian World Cup legends Ronaldo Nazario and Ronaldinho.

The toned music legend was dressed head-to-toe in Saint Laurent, wowing in a pink satin teddy jacket and corset, mini shorts and lace-up boots, paired with stockings as she embraced the soccer icons, before they drove her out into the stadium.

The unlikely trio then posed up on the grass and smiled at the crowds.

Madonna and Justin Bieber's performances during the World Cup halftime show divided fans

Shakira showed off her toned frame as she performed her hit Dai Dai with Burna Boy

Justin Bieber made a starkly different impact on the crowd as he stepped out with only a guitar to sing a World Cup-themed version of his song Everything Hallelujah - leaving fans baffled

Bieber, 32, made a starkly different impact on the crowd as he stepped out with nothing but a guitar to sing a World Cup themed version of his song, Everything Hallelujah.

The singer was bizarrely subbed onto the pitch by Jason Sudeikis, playing his manager alter-ego Ted Lasso.

The star looked relaxed as he casually walked onto the pitch before belting out his hit track, adding the final line, 'it's the World Cup, Hallelujah' - with fans left baffled by his song choice.

Shakira returned to the World Cup stage as she flaunted her toned abs in a pink and yellow sequined bodysuit to perform her hit Dai Dai, with Burna Boy, while K-pop sensations BTS regaled the crowd with Dynamite.

As well as a halftime show, the World Cup final also included a closing ceremony that featured performances and appearances from Post Malone, Tom Cruise, Nicole Scherzinger, influencer IShowSpeed, Oscar winner Jennifer Hudson, Robbie Williams and Italian singer Laura Pausini.

Sports.title: Argentina set unwanted - and barely believable - record after underwhelming World Cup final defeat
Sports.content:
Argentina set unwanted - and barely believable - record after underwhelming World Cup final defeat

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Argentina suffered a historic embarrassment on football’s biggest stage as they turned in a shockingly toothless display in the World Cup final against Spain.

Expectations were sky-high before kick-off at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, with fans anticipating an explosive performance from the reigning champions.

However, instead, the crowd in East Rutherford was subjected to a staggering lack of attacking ambition from Lionel Scaloni's side, as they fell to a 1-0 defeat on the day.

The underwhelming display saw the holders write their names into the history books for all the wrong reasons by setting an unwanted all-time tournament record.

The defending champions became the first team in history to fail to record a single shot of any kind during the initial 90 minutes of a World Cup final.

Lionel Messi and Julian Alvarez were left utterly isolated upfront, starved of service as the midfield struggled to string passes together or breach the Spanish press.

Argentina failed to record a single shot in 90 minutes during Sunday's World Cup final

Lionel Messi and Co. were defeated 1-0 by Spain after an underwhelming clash in New Jersey

The incredible statistic painted a clear picture of Spain's tactical superiority, with the European champions dominating proceedings at a sunny MetLife Stadium.

They did eventually end their attacking struggles during extra time when Messi powered an effort at goal, only to see it blocked by Spain star Mikel Merino.

Argentina eventually ended the game with two total shots, while Spain had 20.

However, after the game, the final descended into chaos as fights broke out among the two sets of players.

Some of Argentina's players lost their heads as Spain's substitutes and staff ran on to the pitch to celebrate their 1-0 win against the South Americans.

Ferran Torres scored a 106th-minute winner after Enzo Fernandez had been sent off in the 93rd minute for a desperately poor Argentina side.

After the whistle, Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes was sent off for punching Eric Garcia and pushing Gavi to the ground.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina also punched Rodri in the torso as he was running by, while Thiago Almada was involved, too.

Several stars clashed after Spain's 1-0 win as Argentina - but the South Americans started it

Argentina's Leandro Paredes was sent off after the whistle for getting violent with Spain

Micah Richards said of their behaviour on the BBC : 'It's embarrassing. They were on the cusp every single time.

'Seeing that sort of stuff after the game was played, it's not good, it's embarrassing to be honest. Paredes is better than that. We all know what it's like to lose a game but this is not good enough.'

Joe Hart added: 'Disgusting behaviour. There was one man on that pitch with class and that was Lionel Messi.'

Wayne Rooney said: 'It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this from Argentina before. It's just sad, very poor from them.

'If you lose a game of football, be graceful. It's a reaction to them being outplayed. Enzo Fernandez has got what he deserves.'

Sports.title: Distraught Lionel Messi bursts into tears as his World Cup career ends in heartbreak after brutal loss to Spain
Sports.content:
A heartbroken Lionel Messi burst into tears on the pitch after collecting his runners-up medal in what will almost certainly be his final ever World Cup appearance.

The Argentina captain - who spent most of his career playing in Barcelona - was ineffectual against Spain in the New Jersey showdown as his team failed to find the net in 120 minutes.

The tournament in America was almost certainly Messi's final international bow, and his emotional full-time reaction went some way to confirming that.

When the final whistle blew, he dropped to the ground and held his hands to his face, inconsolable by his teammates and opponents alike.

After gathering himself to collect his runners-up medal from Donald Trump, the emotions of the moment became too much for the sport's greatest-of-all-time as he burst into tears just before Spain lifted the trophy.

Messi's career will continue with Inter Miami but he is unlikely to play at the highest level again for his country, given he will be 43 when the next World Cup takes place.

Lionel Messi let the tears flow just moments after collecting his World Cup runners-up medal

At the end of what was likely his last World Cup game, Messi appeared inconsolable

In a heartbreaking scene, he sat alone on the turf at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium

Messi was appearing in his third World Cup final, four years after he lifted the trophy for his country in Qatar.

His first time in the biggest game of them all came in 2014 in Brazil, when he and his countrymen were beaten in extra-time by Germany.

It was the same result for the heartbroken Messi on Sunday, as Spain's Ferran Torres scored the only goal of the game deep into the additional 30-minute period.

In the game itself, Messi struggled to make an impact against the country he knows so well, barely getting a kick against the likes of Lamine Yamal and Co.

As an estimated 1.7 billion people watched on from around the world, waiting for Messi to produce the magic we so often see from him, he struggled to find the pace of the game and could not help his team to victory.

Messi sits on the grass at MetLife and watches Spain's players celebrate their triumph

It is unlikely football fans will ever see the great man grace the World Cup stage ever again

Eric Garcia hugs Messi on the pitch at the end of a hard-fought 1-0 Spain win in New Jersey

After collecting his losers' medal from Trump, he stood in front of the Argentina fans inside the stadium, letting the emotion pour out of him.

On X, one fan wrote of the moment: 'You aren't a football fan if you don't feel sad for Messi.'

A second added: 'Thanks for everything you put into this game. You'll always be the best.'

A third, meanwhile, said: 'Damn, the greatest of all time. The best to ever do it.'

Sports.title: Ian Wright hits out at 'ridiculous and poor' World Cup final pitch at the MetLife Stadium - and that was BEFORE extravagant half-time show featuring Justin Bieber and Shakira
Sports.content:
Ian Wright hits out at 'ridiculous and poor' World Cup final pitch at the MetLife Stadium - and that was BEFORE extravagant half-time show featuring Justin Bieber and Shakira

How much is David Beckham set to pocket from his World Cup brand deals? Take on our quiz in our newsletter HERE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Ian Wright has hit out at the state of the World Cup final pitch, dubbing it 'ridiculous, bobbly and poor'.

The MetLife Stadium has been criticised throughout this summer's tournament and once again appeared dry and patchy as Spain took on Argentina tonight.

A number of instances saw stars, including the great Lionel Messi, struggle to control the ball as it bobbled along the uneven surface.

And speaking during ITV's half-time coverage of the clash, Wright didn't hold any punches while assessing the venue for the biggest game in the footballing calendar.

He said: 'For a World Cup final this pitch is ridiculous, it's poor, it (the game) shouldn't be on it.

'I think Spain are playing and showing how good they are because even on a bobbly, dry pitch like this, they're doing really good stuff.

Ian Wright has hit out at the state of the World Cup final pitch, dubbing it 'ridiculous, bobbly and poor'

The turf in New Jersey has come in for criticism throughout the tournament

'I think Argentina will stay in it but, for me, Spain are passing it all over the place. It's only a matter of time before they take one of these chances.'

The 80,000-capacity MetLife sits on the outskirts of New York, which was hit by severe thunderstorms causing flooding in the hours ahead of kick-off in the sweltering east coast sunshine.

Yet the pitch had been deemed subpar by players and managers long before it was hit by rainfall.

The turf predominantly consists of natural grass, but it has been installed over an artificial surface which can make it 'dry out' quickly when temperatures soar.

Brazil's Vinicius Jr was one of the stars who expressed his annoyance earlier in the tournament, telling reporters after his country's 1-1 draw with Morocco: 'Because of the weather and the heat, the grass dries out quickly and the game ends up being very slow.

'We can't build up a rhythm. That makes things difficult because we want to move the ball from one side to the other and this disrupts our game.'

French coach Didier Deschamps later criticised the venue, saying: 'The pitch in New York was really tough - it took a lot out of the players' muscles.'

Wright's comments came moments before the broadcaster's coverage cut to the highly-anticipated half-time show, which was facilitated by a controversial interval of 30 minutes.

A star-studded half-time show featured performances from Shakira (pictured) and Justin Bieber

Madonna kickstarted the performance with her hit 'Music', walking out onto the field with 2002 World Cup winners and Brazilian legends Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Bieber was then introduced by Ted Lasso for a short, slow acoustic performance while a montage of the tournament was playing on the big screens around the 80,000-seater stadium.

Shakira later returned and injected some energy into the show before the performance came to an end and the preparation for the second half quickly restarted.

Yet ITV's panel of pundits were left less than impressed - nor was Wayne Rooney on the BBC.

Keane said: 'A bit of anti-climax but I think the people in the stadium probably enjoyed it more than us. It was nice to see Shakira.'

Wright added: '(Justin) Bieber should have done something a bit more upbeat to liven us up a bit.'

While Rooney reflected bluntly: 'My favourite bit of the half time show was when it finished… I like all of them artists but I thought it was crap.'

A host of stars flooded to New Jersey for the climax of this summer's tournament.

Before kick-off, Top Gun and Mission Impossible superstar Tom Cruise took to the pitch to give a motivational pre-match speech. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump was pictured sat in his luxury suite next to FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

Celebrity couple Timothee Chalament and Kylie Jenner were also snapped in the stands, as were Mick Jagger, Pharrell Williams, Victoria Beckham and Will Ferrell.

Despite the substandard quality of the surface, Spain ultimately ran out victorious on the east coast thanks to a late goal from Ferran Torres.

Nico Williams nodded a header down to the Barcelona man with the scores level in the 106th minute, and he fired an effort into the roof of the net sparking jubilant scenes both in the US and back in Madrid.

The South Americans applied pressure of their own in search of a goal late on and Tottenham Hotspur defender Marcos Senesi almost levelled from close range.

But, in the end, it wasn't to be for Messi on what could his final appearance on football's biggest stage as Lamine Yamal and his Spanish team-mates held on for a historic victory.

Joe Hart said on the BBC: 'They were never rattled or under pressure. They haven't nibbled once. They played beautiful football the entire time.

'Yamal, at 19 years old, his confidence, the ways that he's doing this. Everyone will be trying to get on his back and hate on him, but he's got a Euros and World Cup. He kept so cool, kept his head, and had those standout moments.'

The match was, however, at times overshadowed by the antics of the Argentinians.

After taunting England's stars in Atlanta on Wednesday, Argentina's behaviour against Spain was dubbed 'embarrassing' by pundits after the final whistle tonight.

Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez saw red in the 90+3-minute for a late challenge on Pau Cabarsi before chaotic scenes ensured when Spain's win was confirmed.

As the Spanish bench descended onto the pitch to celebrate, Argentinian substitute Leandro Paredes took issue with Barcelona midfielder Gavi.

The pair became embroiled in a row, causing Scaloni to intervene, before ex-Juventus midfielder Paredes appeared to direct two punches at Gavi as he fell to the turf.

And, speaking on the BBC, ex-Man United striker Wayne Rooney was scathing in his criticism of Argentina's behaviour, not only on Sunday, but throughout the entire tournament.

He said: 'It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this from Argentina before. It's just sad, very poor from them. If you lose a game of football, be graceful. It's a reaction to them being outplayed. Enzo Fernandez has got what he deserves it's well.'

Sports.title: Spain fans direct sarcastic chants of 'Infantino' at FIFA President after Nico Williams goal controversially disallowed - amid 'rigged' World Cup accusations
Sports.content:
Spain fans directed sarcastic chants at Gianni Infantino during the World Cup final after Nico Williams saw a goal chalked off for a 'soft' foul on Nicolas Otamendi.

With the score poised at 0-0 in the first half of extra-time, the Spanish winger thought he'd won it when he slotted a side-footed effort under Argentina goalkeeper Emi Martinez.

But as Williams wheeled away to celebrate, Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic - taking charge of his first World Cup final - blew his whistle to signal a foul.

He deemed that Mikel Merino had trampled on the foot of Otamendi moments before Williams found the back of the net, causing the ex-Man City defender to collapse dramatically to the floor.

It was a decision which was reviewed but ultimately upheld by VAR, sparking fury in the stands at the 80,000-capacity MetLife Stadium.

The thousands of Spaniards who flocked to New Jersey were heard chanting 'Infantino', not for the first time during the match, amid accusations that the World Cup has been 'rigged' in the favour of Lionel Messi and Co.

Nico Williams was left bemused after seeing a goal in extra-time of the World Cup final disallowed

It came after Mike Merino was deemed to have trampled on the toes of Nicolas Otamendi

Infantino sat in the a suite at the MetLife Stadium with Donald Trump - before the pair presented the two teams with their medals after the match

Commentating on the game for the BBC, Alan Shearer said there was 'not enough' contact to warrant a foul.

'Was it just the way Mikel Merico went sliding in?', he questioned. 'That is not a foul for me.

'The only thing I can see is there is a slight touch of the toes on Nicolas Otamendi's toe, but not enough for me to give it as a free-kick.

'Otamendi makes a meal of it and that's what has won them the free-kick.'

The notion of a rigged World Cup is one which has plagued much of this summer, with fans questioning whether referees have been biased towards Messi in what is almost certainly his final major tournament.

The South Americans struggled on their route to the World Cup final, only narrowly scraping past Cape Verde, Egypt and Switzerland in their earlier knockout games.

The manner of those victories - in which Egypt had a goal controversially disallowed and the Swiss saw striker Breel Embolo sent off - resulted in huge backlash surrounding the officials.

Ex-Man City defender Manuel Akanji fumed after Switzerland were defeated by the Argentinians: 'Every little thing was called against us' and 'I've never experienced such a one-sided game,' before his manager Murat Yakin called the refereeing 'incomprehensible'.

It came after Egypt winger Motafa Ziko argued: 'This tournament has been fixed', and his manager Hossam Hassan added: 'This match was rigged, and the whole world saw it.'

FIFA's chief refereeing officer Pierluigi Collina responded, stating that 'nobody can question the integrity' of the refereeing and 'unfounded allegations have no place in our sport'.

Ferran Torres won the final for Spain with a powerful finish in the 106th-minute

It sparked jubilant scenes as Spanish fans back in Madrid celebrated wildly together

Argentina's so-called luck, however, ultimately ran out on Sunday night as Spain rallied after the disallowed goal to find a winner.

It came through Ferran Torres in the 106th minute. After a ball was swung in from the right, Nico Williams nodded a header down from the far post which the Barcelona striker latched on to and fired into the roof of the net to spark jubilant scenes.

The South Americans applied pressure of their own in search of a goal late on and Tottenham Hotspur defender Marcos Senesi almost levelled from close range.

But, in the end, it wasn't to be for Messi on what could be his final appearance on football's biggest stage as Lamine Yamal and his Spanish team-mates held on for a historic victory.

Joe Hart said on the BBC: 'They were never rattled or under pressure. They haven't nibbled once. They played beautiful football the entire time.

'Yamal, at 19 years old, his confidence, the ways that he's doing this. Everyone will be trying to get on his back and hate on him, but he's got a Euros and World Cup. He kept so cool, kept his head, and had those standout moments.'

The match was, however, at times overshadowed by the antics of the Argentinians.

After taunting England's stars in Atlanta on Wednesday, Argentina's behaviour against Spain was dubbed 'embarrassing' by pundits after the final whistle in New Jersey.

Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez saw red in the 90+3-minute for a late challenge on Pau Cabarsi before chaotic scenes were sparked on the pitch when Spain's win was confirmed.

As the Spanish bench descended onto the pitch to celebrate, Argentinian substitute Leandro Paredes took issue with Barcelona midfielder Gavi.

The pair became embroiled in a row, causing Scaloni to intervene, before Paredes appeared to direct two punches at Gavi as he fell to the turf.

And, speaking on the BBC, ex-Man United striker Wayne Rooney was scathing in his criticism of Argentina's behaviour not only on Sunday, but throughout the tournament.

He said: 'It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this from Argentina before. It's just sad, very poor from them. If you lose a game of football, be graceful. It's a reaction to them being outplayed. Enzo Fernandez has got what he deserves it's well.'
