JAMnews reserves the right to delete comments it considers to be offensive, inflammatory, threatening or otherwise unacceptable.

Should Abkhazia’s MPs be required to speak Abkhaz?

World.title: Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from Council of Europe: sovereignty strategy and possible consequences
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from the Council of Europe

On 13 July, speaking at the opening ceremony of the 4th Global Media Forum in Shusha, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said the country was considering a complete withdrawal from the Council of Europe (CoE). His remarks came after the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) decided in January 2024 not to ratify the credentials of the Azerbaijani delegation, effectively suspending its voting rights.

Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe voluntarily in 2001. According to the government’s official position, it sought membership to make use of international mechanisms and secure support for resolving the Karabakh conflict. Relations between Baku and the organisation, however, gradually deteriorated. After Azerbaijan restored full control over its internationally recognised territory in 2023, the authorities described PACE’s decisions as unfair and politically motivated. Aliyev’s latest statement reflects a broader reassessment of sovereignty in Azerbaijan’s foreign policy and its approach to international organisations.

This article draws on official statements, independent analysis and international sources to examine Azerbaijan’s position, the criticism it has faced, and the potential consequences of leaving the Council of Europe.

Official position and arguments

Speaking at the 4th Global Media Forum in Shusha, President Ilham Aliyev said Azerbaijan was seriously considering leaving the Council of Europe altogether.

“I openly say that Azerbaijan is considering the possibility of completely withdrawing from the organisation. This is not about suspending or freezing our membership. We are definitely considering leaving this institution.”

Aliyev also argued that if Azerbaijan were to leave the Council of Europe, ordinary citizens would not notice any significant changes and the situation could even improve. State officials and pro-government media framed the issue as one of protecting national sovereignty and accused international institutions of treating Azerbaijan unfairly.

According to the government’s official position, Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe in 2001 in the hope of securing international support for resolving the Karabakh conflict. Officials argue that those expectations were never fulfilled. They also describe PACE’s January 2024 decision not to ratify the credentials of the Azerbaijani delegation and suspend its voting rights as punishment for Azerbaijan’s restoration of its territorial integrity in 2023.

“We did not take part in the vote on the election of judges and have been subjected to discrimination for the past two years,” Aliyev said.

The Council of Europe’s leadership, including Secretary General Alain Berset, has contacted Aliyev and urged Azerbaijan not to leave the organisation, while calling for a way to resolve the dispute.

Baku maintains that the next step should come from the Council of Europe. According to the government, PACE should first restore the Azerbaijani delegation’s voting rights, after which the delegation could return to its work in the Assembly. Officials argue that leaving the organisation would have little impact on the country’s domestic situation because Azerbaijan already has its own institutional mechanisms in place and regards sovereignty as a top priority. Analysts close to the government have echoed this position, saying Azerbaijan should reject what they describe as bias by international organisations and put national interests first.

Critical assessments and the international perspective

In reports and video coverage published on 13 July, Meydan TV argues that Aliyev’s statement signals preparations for Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from both PACE and the jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). The outlet published its coverage under the headline: “Aliyev is preparing to withdraw Azerbaijan from PACE and the ECtHR – who will lose out?” It focuses primarily on the risk that Azerbaijani citizens could lose their right to file individual applications with the ECtHR.

According to Meydan TV, such a move would weaken human rights protections, particularly against the backdrop of cases involving the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia and Meydan TV, as well as the broader state of media freedom. In contrast to the government’s position, the outlet argues that withdrawing from the Council of Europe and ending the ECtHR’s jurisdiction would have significant consequences for ordinary citizens. It notes that the ECtHR dealt with 2,180 cases involving Azerbaijan in 2025 alone, arguing that this reflects the large number of people who turned to the international court after failing to obtain justice in the country’s domestic courts.

RFE/RL places the issue in a broader context. It notes that PACE imposed sanctions on Azerbaijan amid a wave of arrests that began in 2023, a growing number of political prisoners and continued concerns over media freedom. The outlet also points to Azerbaijan’s refusal to invite PACE observers to monitor the presidential election held in February 2024.

RFE/RL also recalls that, as part of the process of joining the Council of Europe between 1996 and 2002, Azerbaijan introduced a number of reforms, including abolishing the death penalty, reforming its penitentiary system and acceding to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The outlet further compares Aliyev’s claim that “little will change, and things may even improve” after withdrawal with Russia’s departure from the Council of Europe in 2022. It argues that Russia’s experience suggests such a move can deprive citizens of access to international human rights protection mechanisms. According to RFE/RL, any Azerbaijani withdrawal from the Council of Europe would primarily affect people seeking justice for human rights violations.

From an international perspective, the possible consequences of Azerbaijan’s full withdrawal from the Council of Europe include greater international isolation and reputational damage, although the Azerbaijani authorities reject this assessment. At the same time, the Council of Europe’s leadership has publicly expressed its desire for Azerbaijan to remain a member of the organisation.

Alternative platforms and a long-term strategy

Azerbaijan’s foreign policy has traditionally been based on a multi-vector approach that seeks to balance relations with different international partners. This strategy allows the country to engage selectively with international organisations in line with its national interests. According to the government’s official position, regional and international bodies such as the Organization of Turkic States, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation offer forms of cooperation that place greater emphasis on sovereignty and equal partnership. Officials argue that these organisations provide opportunities to expand cooperation in areas including the economy, energy, culture and security.

At the same time, Azerbaijan continues to deepen its energy partnership with European countries. Projects such as the Southern Gas Corridor and natural gas exports operate independently of the country’s membership in the Council of Europe. As a result, Baku argues that a stronger focus on sovereignty can coexist with pragmatic economic and energy cooperation with Europe.

In the longer term, this diversification is intended to give Azerbaijan greater flexibility in its foreign policy and allow it to maintain balanced relations with different partners. Critics warn that leaving the Council of Europe could weaken international human rights safeguards available to Azerbaijani citizens. The government, however, argues that alternative international platforms can offset any gaps in economic and political cooperation. Overall, officials present this strategy as part of a broader effort to pursue an independent foreign policy based on Azerbaijan’s national interests.

Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from the Council of Europe

World.title: Russian MFA spokeswoman: ‘West cannot stomach Georgia’s independence’
World.content:
Maria Zakharova on Georgia and OSCE

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze‘s assessment of Western institutions required no further confirmation from Moscow, adding that the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly had long pursued a course of “aggression, aggressive rhetoric and destructive actions”.

Zakharova’s remarks came in response to a question at a news conference on whether the Russian Foreign Ministry shared Kobakhidze’s assessment. Kobakhidze had earlier accused the OSCE and European institutions of involvement in attempts to bring about a violent change of government in Georgia.

Maria Zakharova: “The Georgian prime minister’s remarks require no confirmation from us. We are talking about the leader of a sovereign state who knows and loves his country and represents its people.

Modern Georgia is a clear example of brazen, and at times unprecedented, external interference in the affairs of a state that possesses all the attributes of sovereignty

Tbilisi’s determination to pursue an independent and nationally oriented policy — meaning one focused on its own people, who are themselves multi-ethnic — is perceived by the ‘collective West’ as a direct challenge. To put it in plain Russian, it sticks in their throat.

This irritates Western representatives so much that they are prepared to use every lever at their disposal to remove the current government simply because it serves the interests of its own people, thinks about them, understands them and their history, and builds the country’s future on that basis, rather than serving those who have nothing to do with the Georgian people or their history.

The Georgian prime minister’s remarks apparently relate to the adoption of the Hague Declaration at the annual session of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly. The declaration includes a number of resolutions, including one concerning Georgia’s ‘undemocratic’ elections.

Such destructive activity by the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly comes as no surprise to us. The assembly long ago chose the path of aggression. A number of states use the OSCE platform to launch unrestrained criticism not only of Russia but also of other countries, including through the use of the ‘Moscow Mechanism’ — an outdated, pseudo-human-rights and non-consensual instrument.

Everything they allege against Georgia, including the accusations you have asked about, is false.”

OSCE resolution

On 8 July, the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly adopted a critical resolution on Georgia calling on the country’s authorities to release political prisoners, repeal legislation restricting civil liberties and uphold democratic standards.

The resolution, entitled Protecting Electoral Integrity and Fundamental Freedoms in Georgia, forms part of the Hague Declaration, the final document adopted at the assembly’s 33rd annual session, held in the Netherlands from 4 to 8 July.

Representatives of Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party attended the session but walked out in protest at the adoption of the resolution.

World.title: Armenia begins ratifying TRIPP agreement with US: foreign minister outlines key details
World.content:
Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

Armenia has begun the process of ratifying the framework agreement on strategic cooperation with the United States under the TRIPP project.

The agreement concerns the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit route linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhichevan. The project forms part of the Armenian government’s Crossroads of Peace initiative, which aims to reopen regional transport links.

The government has approved the agreement and submitted it to the Constitutional Court. The court must now determine whether it complies with Armenia’s constitution.

“If the Constitutional Court finds that the obligations set out in this international agreement are compatible with Armenia’s constitution, we will submit it to the National Assembly in accordance with the established procedure and bring it before parliament for discussion,” Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said, outlining the next steps. Parliament must ratify the agreement before it can take effect.

Mirzoyan said Armenia must also finalise two more documents before it can complete the TRIPP project. They include a shareholders’ agreement and the charter of the TRIPP Development Company.

The foreign minister also commented on reports about the TRIPP+ fund. Britain’s The Guardian reported on the fund a day earlier, prompting questions in Armenia about the new structure. Mirzoyan said it was an American investment fund and would have only “an indirect connection” with the company that Armenia plans to establish.

Armenia and the United States initialled the framework agreement on strategic cooperation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity project on 26 May 2026. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took part in the initialling ceremony in Yerevan. They signed the agreement shortly afterwards through a remote procedure. Rubio signed it in Washington on 1 June, while Mirzoyan signed it in Yerevan on 4 June. “To dispel any possible questions, I would like to note that international practice and Armenian legislation both provide for the signing of such non-simultaneous, remote agreements, and this is a widely accepted practice,” Ararat Mirzoyan said during today’s government meeting. On 8 August 2025, the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed a joint declaration at a summit in Washington, marking the launch of the regional connectivity project. The declaration mentioned the Trump Route project for the first time. Before that, Armenia and Azerbaijan had failed to reach agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan had demanded a route it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia said it was ready to reopen all transport links. At the same time, it firmly rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied the loss of sovereign rights over its territory. The parties reached a compromise only in Washington. They agreed that Armenia would retain sovereign control over the route, while the United States would join the project as a business partner.

“Armenia and the US will help strengthen peace in the South Caucasus”

According to Armenia’s foreign minister, the TRIPP project will help bring peace, stability and prosperity to the South Caucasus. He said it would achieve this by promoting:

transport connectivity;

infrastructure development; and

regional and global trade.

Under the framework agreement, Armenia and the United States will establish the TRIPP Development Company. The company will have the authority to create special purpose entities and bring in additional partners to implement individual projects in Armenia.

“The entire process, from the establishment of the development company to its future operations, will fully respect Armenia’s sovereignty, jurisdiction and territorial integrity,” Ararat Mirzoyan said.

He recalled that the development company would receive land use and development rights for the relevant areas. The parties have set the initial term at 49 years. The United States will hold a 74% stake in the company, while Armenia will own the remaining 26%. If the partnership continues for another 50 years, Armenia’s share will automatically increase to 49% after the first 49-year term.

“If the term is extended, Armenia will not need to take any additional steps to obtain its 49% stake,” the minister said.

Armenia will retain control over border, customs and migration procedures

The foreign minister again stressed that, in line with Armenia’s domestic legislation and international agreements, the Armenian authorities will continue to oversee:

security and the protection of rights;

border control and border security;

customs and migration procedures;

the collection of taxes and customs duties for the state budget;

state information systems; and

public administrative functions.

He said these guarantees should address public concerns about Armenia retaining its sovereign rights over the territory.

What is the link between the TRIPP Development Company and TRIPP+?

Britain’s The Guardian reported that the US State Department had appointed Konstantin Sokolov to lead the TRIPP+ trade fund. Sokolov is a US investor who was born in the Soviet Union and now lives in Chicago.

Armenian media quickly picked up the report. However, questions remained about the nature of the fund and its relationship with the company that Armenia plans to establish to implement the Trump Route project.

Journalists raised the issue during the government meeting. Ararat Mirzoyan replied that the agreement between Yerevan and Washington provides for the creation of the TRIPP Development Company.

“Its founders will be the Armenian government and the TRIPP Development Company-USA, which will be established in the United States,” Mirzoyan said.

As for TRIPP+, he said it is an American company established under the TRIPP Development Company-USA. Its role will be to attract investment for the project.

“From a legal perspective, TRIPP+ has only an indirect relationship with the TRIPP Development Company that will be established in Armenia,” the minister said..

Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

World.title: 'Animal on road': AI-assisted cameras and smart signs to warn drivers
World.content:
An artificial intelligence-powered alert system is being trialled on a stretch of the Monaro Highway between Canberra and the Snowy Mountains in a bid to stop wildlife from becoming roadkill.

The Protective Animal Warning System (PAWS) uses thermal and optical roadside cameras to detect animals close to the roadside, and an AI computer vision-aided model identifies common species such as kangaroos, deer and wombats.

When an animal is detected, a smart road sign then flashes up the words "Animal on road slow down", to alert approaching motorists in real time.

"This new technology enables us to give motorists early warning that there would be a target species on the road ahead of them," New South Wales Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said.

" It gives them time to slow down and be ready for the animal, so that the animal can hopefully get off the road in time. "

Loading...

Roadkill hot spot

It's the first time the technology has been used in New South Wales, with the trial being conducted on a 300 metre section of the Monaro Highway at Michelago, between Canberra and Cooma.

"This is an area that has been assessed as having one of the highest rates of animal wildlife strikes on the network in New South Wales," Ms Aitchinson said.

Wildcare Queanbeyan president Elena Guarracino described the area is "an incredible hot spot" for kangaroos in particular.

The trial area covers 300 metres of the Monaro Highway at Michelago. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

"There are a couple of dams on one side of the Monaro Highway, and they're continually crossing there and it's just a very … horrible area," she said.

"I've counted up to 30 dead kangaroos at that spot. Along that road towards Williamsdale every 10 metres you'll see a dead kangaroo.

"That's partly fuelled by the ski traffic, but also there's a lot of traffic just generally that commutes to Canberra along that road.

" What we see from the road is just a fraction of what's been hit and moved away from the road until it succumbs to its injuries. "

Wildcare Queanbeyan president Elena Guarracino is hopeful the new technology will help reduce animal-vehicle collisions. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

An estimated 10 million animals are killed on Australian roads each year at a huge cost to motorists, insurers and native animals — as well as to wildlife volunteers.

"When those animals are struck, the wildlife group has to send people out to rescue that injured animal or potentially euthanise it," Ms Guarracino said.

"And then there's the impact of the joey that's in the pouch which, when it's rescued, can take up to two years to rehabilitate before it can be old enough to be released.

"That costs at least $1,200 and enormous volunteer hours — that's if everything goes well and vets aren't involved."

Wildcare Queanbeyan's Elena Guarracino and Christian McDonald are regularly called to the Monaro Highway to attend to injured wildlife. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

'Smart' version of traditional sign

Ms Guarracino said research had shown the traditional yellow and black wildlife warning signs along roads and highways "don't work".

"They might initially warn the motorists that there is wildlife in that area, but drivers get habituated to those signs," she said.

The digital sign being used as part of the trial, on the other hand, will only display words when activated to alert drivers.

"What this is about is targeting the message so that it's exactly correct for what is happening on the network," Ms Aitchinson said.

" So it just means that drivers will get more of a warning that will be more appropriate to actually whether there's animals there or not. "

The smart signs will activate when there is wildlife activity nearby. (Supplied: Transport for NSW)

The development of PAWS and the subsequent trial is a result of recommendations from the 2024 Wildlife Symposium in Sydney, exploring how emerging technology could be used to reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions.

The AI model behind PAWS has been developed by Transport for NSW's technology and biodiversity teams, combined with animal data from the Symbio Wildlife Park near Wollongong.

Specialist cameras filmed how different species moved and behaved in a controlled setting to build an image library, which was then cross-referenced with time-of-day and weather data to sharpen the system's accuracy in different types of conditions.

The $10,000 per kilometre solution to roadkill These fence posts are connected only by a sensor but advocates say they could reduce roadkill incidents by 90 per cent.

"This is an investment of around half a million dollars in just developing the technology," Ms Aitchison said.

"And the benefit of it being done and developed in-house with Transport for New South Wales is that we can ensure that we have the technology, we can use it."

Passengers urged to help lookout for wildlife

The trial at Michelago is due to begin next month, and Transport for NSW will track whether there is a reduction in wildlife strikes in the test area.

Ms Guarracino is hopeful that if the technology proves successful it will not only be rolled out to other hot spots, but also expanded to bring real-time alerts into cars as they drive past.

"It'd be great if the cameras could be integrated into guideposts and give a warning to a driver [via Bluetooth] through their warning devices in their cars," she said.

Wildcare Queanbeyan volunteers Christian McDonald and Elena Guarracino say the trial area on the Monaro Highway is a wildlife hot spot. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

In the meantime, she continues to urge drivers and passengers to keep their eyes peeled for animal activity, especially during dusk and dawn.

"I drive very carefully and scan the sides of the road the whole time, even in the daytime," she said.

"And instead of having passengers watching their phone, they need to be scanning the road and helping the driver and going, 'Oh, kangaroo on the left, slow down'."

World.title: Uranium export deal sparks talk of opportunities for Broken Hill
World.content:
The outback mining city of Broken Hill is well known for its silver, lead and zinc.

It hosts one of the world's largest ore bodies, after all.

The city is not known for its uranium, but a recent agreement to supply India for its nuclear energy industry has some questioning whether there could be hidden opportunity in the city.

The Minerals Council of Australia says the prospectivity for uranium around Broken Hill is strong.

But with a ban on uranium mining in New South Wales, and no identified ore bodies in the state, extraction could be a pipe dream.

The start of another mining boom?

When Jim Hickey first moved to Broken Hill in the 1970s, the mining city had a population of about 28,000.

Now, Cr Hickey is the deputy mayor and he has seen the city shrink to about 17,500 people.

Broken Hill has a rich mining history. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

The Broken Hill City Council is expecting an increase in population with the looming commencement of major mining and renewable projects, but Cr Hickey sees uranium as a chance to bring about another mining boom for the city.

"If the [uranium] ban was lifted … mining companies would come in and stake some claims," Cr Hickey said.

"They would know now exactly what the exploration has shown and where it would be.

" This would be another string to our bow and keep Broken Hill well and surely alive and increase our population back to a good-sized city again. "

With the export deal with India freshly signed, Cr Hickey said he believed pressure would start mounting on the NSW government to repeal the prohibition on mining uranium.

A bill to do just that has passed NSW parliament's upper house, but that is as far as it is likely to go given longstanding opposition by the Labor party.

NSW Resources Minister Courtney Houssos told the Legislative Council in February that Labor's position would not change.

She also said that while exploration for uranium was allowed, "there has been very little interest in uranium exploration in this state, and no licences have been granted".

Jim Hickey would like to see a ban on uranium mining lifted in NSW. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

Cr Hickey is urging the government to reconsider, particularly in light of the economic opportunities.

"We pay a lot of royalties now and we'd be increasing our royalties to the government … [and] they need every cent they can get.

"I think it'd be very profitable to them."

Broken Hill Labor Party branch president and local councillor Blake Edgecumbe said he did not doubt there would be an economic boom should a ban be lifted, but believed it would need to be weighed on balance with environmental concerns.

"I'm sure there'd be a lot of discussions happening, state and federally," Cr Edgecumbe said.

"I know certain political parties and certain people of certain persuasions would be pushing for the affirmative, but I think it's important that we look at environmental impacts as well as economics."

Economic opportunity

The Minerals Council of Australia would like to see NSW, Western Australia and Queensland collectively repeal prohibitions on uranium mining.

CEO Tania Constable said even if all three of Australia's operating uranium mines were to expand, it would still not be enough to meet India's ambitious uranium targets.

"India is going to require around about 23,000 tonnes of uranium each year to get their 100 gigawatts of nuclear energy," Ms Constable said.

"That would almost double what we're currently producing, and they're going to still need so much more.

"If we get mines going in Western Australia, if we see more opportunities in South Australia or the Northern Territory, and indeed if prohibitions are lifted in NSW, there is real opportunity for our industry."

Tania Constable would like to see bans on uranium mining in NSW, WA and Queensland lifted. (ABC News: Phil Hemingway)

There is a growing demand for uranium globally as countries chase net-zero emissions targets, and Australia is a significant resource.

It is the world's fourth-largest uranium producer but holds almost a third of the world's total resources.

"There's plenty of opportunity to move the needs of the nuclear energy industry across the world, for India, for the United States, for France, for other countries that are looking to decarbonise their economies," Ms Constable said.

She also supports exploring uranium opportunities around Broken Hill.

"It's unlikely to be the deposit itself, but [Broken Hill] does have prospectivity given the location that it is in."

Not the frontline for uranium

Emeritus Professor and Hancock Prospecting executive director Ian Plimer said he expected any battle to repeal a uranium ban would take place outside of NSW.

"[It would be] in Western Australia and Queensland, both of which have got identified uranium deposits," Professor Plimer said.

While he agreed there was prospectivity around the outback city, he said it would not draw focus for governments and mining companies.

Uranium is often referred to as "yellow cake" because of its colour. (Reuters: Mariana Bazo)

"My geological reasoning would be that you would go west, you would actually deal with the material that has leached off a great pile of Broken Hill rocks and ended up in the Frome Basin.

"That's where you would have the traces of uranium that are found in Broken Hill, concentrated in salt lakes."

But where Broken Hill could reap some rewards is through an expansion of the Honeymoon Uranium Mine, 80 kilometres away in South Australia, which is supported by a workforce in Broken Hill.

"[The community would benefit] in terms of infrastructure, in terms of employment," he said.

World.title: Has AI changed your life in unexpected ways? The ABC wants to hear from you
World.content:
Most of us never chose to live in an AI world. Yet over the past few years, artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of everyday life, changing how we think, learn and communicate.

Across the Asia Pacific, countries are taking very different approaches. For example, Singapore is expanding AI into education and public services, while India is trialling AI in governance and local administration.

'The future is happening without us' We asked readers if they had thoughts or concerns about the rise of AI. This is what you told us.

We want to understand what these changes look like from your perspective. So if you have a view, experience or concern, we want to hear from you via the form below.

We're especially interested in views that don't usually make headlines: the unofficial, unexpected or creative ways AI is being adopted in everyday life, particularly in key institutions where trust, expertise and accountability matter most.

Do you think it has potential to improve education, the legal system or governance? Or are you concerned the risks are unknown or too high? Has it changed dynamics at home? Or who family members turn to first for advice or information?

Your responses will help inform our reporting on how Australia compares to countries going through similar changes.

Please be assured any personal information you provide will be treated as strictly confidential and the ABC will not publish any personal details that may identify you without getting your permission.

Loading...

World.title: L7 bassist Jennifer Finch dies days after brain cancer diagnosis
World.content:
Jennifer Finch, the longtime bassist for influential grunge rock group L7, has died.

Finch, who had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer in 2011, was diagnosed with an aggressive form of brain cancer last week. She was 59.

L7, who last toured Australia as part of the 2024 Good Things festival, are closely linked with the grunge and riot grrrl movements, creating space in the late 80s and 1990s for women in male-dominated punk and rock scenes.

Finch's bandmates shared the news of her death on Saturday on Instagram, calling her a "beloved bandmate, friend, and fellow troublemaker".

"She had a long courageous fight with brain cancer and was loved by many wonderful friends, musical peers and fans worldwide," wrote L7's Donita Sparks, Suzi Gardner and Demetra "Dee" Plakas.

Loading Instagram content

Finch was due to join L7 on the feminist rock band's The Last Hurrah farewell tour later this year. However, she pulled out last week after revealing her brain cancer diagnosis, giving the band her blessing to forge ahead.

A GoFundMe campaign to help pay for her treatment, launched by friends and family, swiftly surpassed its goal and raised nearly US$400,000. Despite initial radiation treatment, "unforeseen complications" led to Finch enduring "multiple surgeries and a string of difficult setbacks".

Loading Instagram content

Born August 5, 1966, and raised by her adoptive parents in Los Angeles, Finch had a passion for photography, often documenting the city's burgeoning punk and alt-rock scenes, snapping influential groups like The Cramps and Bad Religion.

In the early 80s, Finch played bass in Sugar Babydoll, led by future Hole frontwoman Courtney Love, and The Pandoras.

Finch joined L7 in 1986, a year after Donita Sparks and Suzi Gardner formed the band. They released their self-titled debut in 1988 via influential independent record label Epitaph.

After adding Dee Plakas on drums, the group's 1990 album Smell The Magic made them one of the few non-Seattle bands signed to Sub Pop and earliest all-female groups in the grunge explosion. Finch even dated Nirvana drummer Dave Grohl for a time.

L7 blazed a trail for women in grunge – they just wanted to rock "We've all got terrible flaws as musicians," frontwoman Donita Sparks says. "But when we come together, it sounds great

Their 1992 album Bricks Are Heavy is considered one of the era's most significant, featuring L7's biggest crossover hit Pretend We're Dead, a searing political commentary on the marginalisation of women in society inserted into a hooky anthem.

Fiercely rejecting traditional beauty standards and fearlessly advocating for women's rights, L7 co-founded Rock for Choice in 1991, a concert series raising funds and awareness for reproductive rights.

Four women playing loud, aggressive tunes confronting sexism and political disillusion was considered a feminist statement in and of itself. But L7 did not actively try to be a feminist band.

"We don't write in any contrived way," Donita Sparks told Double J in 2019. "We write from very personal experiences and they just morph into something else.

"We're not writing feminist lyrics, we're writing L7 lyrics, and I think they speak to everybody."

Why L7 want you to tap into your inner teenager Donita Sparks on feminism in grunge, wild mosh pits and why she feels like a superhero

In 1996, two years after their fourth album Hungry for Stink, Finch left the band and played in other groups, namely OtherStarPeople and The Shocker, and launched her own label, Little Pusher Records.

Following an acrimonious split in 2001, L7 reunited in 2014 and Finch rejoined, playing on their 2019 reunion album Scatter The Rats.

The band have toured regularly since, playing headline shows and festivals throughout the US, UK and Australia, where, in 2023, they performed Bricks Are Heavy in full on tour.

Among those in the music industry mourning Finch's death are Courtney Love, Kathryn Valentine of the Go-Go's, Lunachicks and Garbage.

World.title: Premier says 'witch' billboard dehumanises women, drives violence
World.content:
The Victorian premier says a controversial billboard seen around Melbourne labelling her a "witch" sets a dangerous tone for how women are spoken about.

The truck carrying the billboard was removed from the streets last week after being issued a defect notice, but was seen again in the city over the weekend.

Premier Jacinta Allan said it sent a clear message about a lack of respect for women, which she said had an impact on rates of gendered violence.

"Violence against women starts with disrespect for women," she said.

" We have to drive cultural change. Governments can't do this alone, it requires society. "

The mobile billboard has been widely condemned as sexist. (Supplied)

Speaking to 774 ABC Melbourne, Ms Allan said the recent spate of gendered violence made her angry and showed there was a need for change.

"It makes me furious. It's devastating," she said.

"We are continuing to see too much of this ... we need to continue to drive cultural change alongside the huge system reform."

Two girls and two women, aged between 13 and 39, were allegedly murdered within a four-day period earlier this month, sparking calls for more research and better funding for domestic violence prevention.

Two of those deaths were in Victoria.

Ms Allan said the use of words such as "witch" had long been used to "attack and bring down" women.

"It has been used for centuries to dehumanise women, to other women," she said.

" And when you see that portrayal on our streets, it's sending a really clear message about the corrosive nature of a lack of respect for women that has to change. "

Jacinta Allan told the ABC that a billboard using a "ditch the witch" slogan was driving a lack of respect for women. (ABC News)

She argued it also sent a dangerous message to young boys and girls.

"The message it sends to a young boy, a young boy who would also, I think, be disturbed by that image, but for some, it can trigger something else," she said.

"That is why it is dangerous, it is corrosive, and why it should be at every turn condemned and not just seen as part of the rough and tumble [of politics]."

The controversial billboard was condemned across the political divide when it first appeared in Melbourne.

At the time, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the campaign was sexist and "totally unacceptable".

"Young girls will see that, you know, depiction of a premier as a witch, just like the denigration that Julia Gillard suffered from as prime minister, and it is just not on," he said.

Former prime minister Julia Gillard, who was also targeted with similar slogans during her time in the top job, also slammed the campaign.

"I am saddened to see that improvement cast aside and this tired old trope resurrected," she said in June.

The state opposition leader and other MPs also denounced the slogans, while One Nation's Pauline Hanson told Ms Allan to "suck it up, sweetheart".

The truck's anti-premier ads have been interspersed with visually explicit ads for Melbourne brothel Gotham City. (Supplied)

Melbourne brothel Gotham City had previously confirmed it was involved with funding the campaign, along with many other businesses.

The truck briefly disappeared from the city's streets after the driver was issued a defect notice.

Police said the defect notice was issued after an investigation into whether the billboards fell "outside the standards of regulation".

"Police have been advised the truck was presented to VicRoads for inspection and the vehicle was deemed roadworthy," a police spokesperson said.

"As such, police will not be taking any further action in respect to the vehicle."

World.title: Reese accepts Brondello's apology over 'protected species' comment
World.content:
Angel Reese has accepted Australian coach Sandy Brondello's apology for an inappropriate comment about the Atlanta Dream star.

The WNBA suspended Brondello for one game after she was overheard calling Reese a "protected species" during the Dream's 111-92 win over Brondello's Toronto Tempo at the weekend.

"First, I appreciate Sandy's apology, but I also appreciate the love and support that I've had for the last 48 hours," Reese said before the Dream played the Chicago Sky on Monday (AEST).

"It has been very overwhelming with a lot of love and also other things. But I am grateful that the league did take action."

Brondello's comment about Reese was picked up by the broadcast after Toronto player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury and was called for a foul following contact with Reese.

Brondello apologised on social media and Reese posted "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" after the game, tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

The "protected species" phrase is used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player. However, in the US, the phrase suggests that someone isn't human and could be seen as derogatory toward Black people.

"There is no place for discrimination or hate in this league from anyone — from fans to coaches to players," Reese said.

"I'm just grateful that we are able to move on from the situation and just play winning basketball. The WNBA is supposed to be positive and we are going in a great light right now, so I just want to continue that and move forward."

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Argentina lose heads in defeat, Trump crashes Spain's party
World.content:
Argentina's players lash out in defeat, Ferran Torres becomes a Spanish icon forever, and Donald Trump attempts to crash the winners' party.

Here are today's quick hits.

1. Ferran Torres. Remember the name

The surest way to ensure your name lives forever in the annals of football history is to score the winner in a World Cup final. With a brilliantly struck half-volley in the 106th minute of the 2026 final, Spain's Ferran Torres joined that illustrious group.

Spain had dominated the game. It had ridden the many, many challenges of an Argentina side hell-bent on destroying the match's flow, but had still been taken deep into extra time without a breakthrough.

Ferran Torres celebrates scoring the winning goal in a World Cup final. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

Lamine Yamal nearly scored from a free-kick in regulation. Nico Williams thought he had scored, before the referee's whistle intervened. Mikel Merino should have scored moments later, but his free header blazed wide.

But in the end, it was all just in service of Torres's magic moment. Williams did brilliantly to keep a cross alive with a clever header back into a dangerous spot. Without the requirement of a settling touch, Torres lifted the killer blow above Argentina's keeper, Emi Martinez.

An injury time winner settled Spain's first World Cup title, Andres Iniesta the provider in 2010. He now has company in Spanish folklore. Ferran Torres, a legend forever.

2. Disgraceful Argentinian head-loss in defeat

There are ways to win, and there are ways to lose. Argentina had already tread the line of the former this World Cup, but blew any notion of sportsmanship out of the water in the final defeat.

As Spain's players ran onto the field in celebration at the final whistle, Argentina's Nahuel Molina threw a punch to the chest of Spanish midfielder Rodri.

Rodri turned, reacting with surprise and anger, and from there, a scrap broke out.

Leandro Paredes lashed out Gavi after full-time. (Getty Images: Marvin Ibo Guengoer)

Argentina's Leandro Paredes, who had already been yellow carded in the game for pushing a player over in an earlier stink, completely lost his head.

Paredes went after Spain's Gavi, grabbing him by the neck and throwing him to the ground.

Paredes was shown a red card after the match had finished for his outburst, while Argentina's manager Lionel Scaloni had to run onto the field to break up the melee.

A disappointing exit for Argentina on an overall disappointing day.

3. Wild challenge and red card cost Argentina

Paredes was not the first Argentinian to see red, and indeed the game's first dismissal had far more bearing on the result.

Enzo Fernández was shown a second yellow and then a red just before the end of regulation time, forcing Argentina to try to hold on with 10 men through the 30 minutes to come.

Pau Cubarsi goes flying after Enzo Fernandez's tackle.

Fernandez's first booking was seemingly for dissent, as he vociferously disagreed with a refereeing decision, but his second was an outrageously dumb and reckless challenge.

With a 50-50 there to be won, Spain's Pau Cubarsi got to the ball a split second before Fernandez, but the Argentine made no effort at all to avoid the contact he was about to create. He leapt into the challenge, sending Cubarsi flying head over heels through the air.

Fernández again tried to argue the point with the referee, but there was no chance at all of a reprieve. A moment of recklessness had taken Argentina's precarious position and made it somehow even worse.

4. Messi can't rescue a dismal performance

Lionel Messi could not hold back the tears at the full-time whistle, or indeed after he had received his runners-up medal. If this is to be his final World Cup bow, as must surely be the case, it was a desperate way to say goodbye.

Argentina was pitiful for almost the entirety of this final. It did not manage a single shot until the 116th minute of the game — not just a shot on target, a single shot at all. Not one!

Lionel Messi slumped to the turf after Argentina's defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

It had clearly come with a plan to try to frustrate Spain, disrupt its rhythm with fouls and time-wasting, and hope Messi could create some magic the other way.

It succeeded on the first two fronts, but even Messi, playing a lone hand against a disciplined and tactically supreme Spain side, could not find a way to threaten.

Spain, to its credit, remained patient with the ball and alert to any danger in defence. It continued to play its football, metronomic at times and very easy on the eye at others, and eventually got the result it deserved.

As did Argentina.

5. Trump crashes the Spanish party

It had long since been telegraphed that Donald Trump's first game day appearance at this World Cup would be at the final, and that he would join his mate Gianni Infantino on the pitch to present the medals and trophy after the game.

And yet it remained a curious sight as he stood in the middle of the Spanish celebrations, aimlessly wandering around and gesturing towards players, refusing to get out of the way so they could enjoy the fulfilment of their lifelong dream.

Donald Trump inserted himself in Spain's World Cup celebrations. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

This too was no surprise, as Trump did the same thing last year when Chelsea won the Club World Cup. That time, the players were surprised as Trump stood in the middle of the trophy celebration, grinning widely.

This time, Spain captain Rodri made a point of trying to usher him out of the way. Infantino chased him across the stage, trying in vain to get him out of the way. He remained on the periphery, but crucially still within camera shot, when Rodri lifted the World Cup.

Perhaps a perfect way to sum up this tournament. Brilliant at its heart, when the football was the focus, but rather unseemly in the background and on the fringes.

World.title: US launches more strikes on Iran, says another service member killed
World.content:
The US military has begun a new round of air strikes targeting Iran after announcing the death of another American service member, and Iran fired missiles towards Jordan that risked widening the conflict into neighbouring Israel.

Step by step, the US and Iran have inched closer to all-out war as last month's interim deal meant to permanently end the fighting has crumbled and shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has largely stalled.

Both sides have targeted civilian infrastructure relied on by millions of people.

The US military said the service member was killed in northern Iraq on Saturday, local time, during the "controlled detonation" of a downed Iranian drone.

Earlier, the military said its strikes targeted Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard to retaliate for Friday's killing of troops in Jordan.

One service member was missing after that attack, and the military's new statement said "unidentified remains" were found Sunday and were being examined.

Since the war began, 17 US service members have been killed.

The renewed exchanges of fire, now in their second week, have seen the US target bridges and electrical facilities in Iran.

The US military's Central Command announced a new round of strikes early Monday, now into their ninth straight night.

"The strikes will continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz," Central Command said in a statement.

As the strikes began, a ship caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz near the coastline of Oman, the British military reported, saying it was unclear what had started the blaze.

The US military has been encouraging ships to use a route near Oman to transit the strait and Iran has responded with attacks targeting those vessels, insisting it must have control over the crucial waterway.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations says it received reports a vessel was ablaze near the coast of Oman. (Supplied: UKMTO)

Tehran has retaliated to American attacks by hitting US-allied countries throughout the Middle East.

Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait again activated air defences for incoming Iranian drones and missiles.

Early Monday, the US Embassy in Bahrain issued a warning saying "Iran may seek to target unspecified locations in central Manama", the capital, without elaborating.

Israel warned that missiles launched towards neighbouring Jordan could cause fire to spill over into Israeli territory for the first time in weeks.

Iran says nuclear site under construction hit

Footage released Sunday by the US military appeared to show strikes carried out by fighter jets and by Tomahawk cruise missiles launched from the sea.

One target site appeared to be in a valley of a mountainous region. The Guard often has missile bases and other military equipment tucked into mountain ranges.

Iran's atomic energy agency said US strikes targeted the construction site of a planned nuclear power plant in the south-west, state television reported.

Satellite images from Planet Labs PBC of the Darkhovin nuclear plant site showed earth clearing but little construction as of July 9. Iran did not previously announce it as being targeted.

The International Atomic Energy Agency said the site, in the "very early stages of construction", contained no nuclear material when the UN watchdog last visited.

Jordan and nearly every Gulf Arab state targeted

Jordan's military said it shot down several Iranian missiles. The country hosts major US bases and relies on US air-defence systems. The missiles did not cause casualties or damage, according to Jordan's military.

Jordan later summoned Iran's chargé d'affaires to protest, state-run television reported.

Israel's military said Iranian missiles launched towards the Jordanian port city of Aqaba just across the border could spill over, warning Israelis to expect the first air-raid sirens in weeks.

Eilat, the Israeli city that neighbours Aqaba, cited security officials as saying two interceptors were launched from its outskirts to prevent the fall of debris.

"We are prepared to immediately resume combat," the Israeli military chief of staff, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir, said.

During the latest fighting, Iran has focused attacks on US-allied Arab states rather than Israel, which launched the war with the US on February 28.

Kuwait said one of its power and water desalination plants was attacked for the second time in two days, causing fires.

Its Ministry of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy said the power grid remains stable. In Kuwait, about 90 per cent of drinking water comes from desalination.

The secretary-general of the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, Jasem Mohamed al-Budaiwi, has accused Iran of war crimes for strikes on infrastructure and civilian facilities.

International humanitarian law generally protects civilian infrastructure such as bridges and power plants from attack, but such sites can lose protections if used for military purposes. In such cases, attacks must be proportionate and minimise civilian harm.

Hormuz remains key to the conflict

US President Donald Trump has threatened to target Iran's power stations and bridges to try to compel Tehran to loosen its hold on the Strait of Hormuz, which saw one-fifth of global oil supplies transit before the war.

Recent attacks suggest the US military is carrying out that plan.

The US in the past week reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports to halt its shipments of crude oil. The military on Saturday said it had redirected six ships and disabled one since then.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has stalled in the last week. (Reuters)

A maritime organisation overseen by the US Navy said Sunday that the threat to mariners was severe after previous Iranian attacks, "with deliberate hostile action considered highly likely".

It said traffic remained low, with eight transits on Saturday and three on Friday. The daily average before the war was almost 140.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in a statement Saturday, warned of "unforgettable lessons" if the US keeps attacking the Islamic Republic.

An Iranian negotiator said Tehran was suspending its commitments to the interim deal and accused the US of violating it.

The halfway point has passed in the 60 days the deal set out to negotiate the permanent end of the war and other issues, including Iran's nuclear program.

Iranian authorities on Sunday said at least 50 people have been killed and 517 wounded in the latest US strikes. Iran has provided no overall information on its material losses.

AP

World.title: ‘It’s not going to be perfect’: The Sydney town centre overhauls no one can agree on
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘It’s not going to be perfect’: The Sydney town centre overhauls no one can agree on David Barwell July 20, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney’s suburban town centres have emerged as the latest battleground in the city’s housing debate, with councils advancing plans for significantly taller buildings in established shopping precincts, exposing tensions between the need for more homes and concerns about preserving neighbourhood character. New masterplans for Bondi Junction, Brookvale and Gladesville would collectively deliver more than 6400 new homes alongside upgraded public spaces, revitalised retail strips and expanded community facilities. A new masterplan for Bondi Junction will face a crucial vote this week. Waverley Council But while councils argue the projects are essential to address Sydney’s housing shortage and renew ageing commercial centres, many residents fear excessive building heights, worsening traffic congestion and mounting pressure on local infrastructure. The most advanced proposal is in Gladesville, where Hunters Hill Council this month voted to forward a new town centre masterplan to the NSW Government. The proposal includes towers up to 19 storeys, 522 homes and the redevelopment of the ageing Gladesville Shopping Centre.



Deputy mayor Julia Prieston described the project as an opportunity to revive a precinct that had languished through decades of failed development attempts, calling Gladesville “a case study in Sydney’s planning paralysis”. A council report found lower building heights would not generate sufficient economic value to fund new community facilities, particularly given rising construction costs and softer apartment market conditions. A new masterplan for Gladesville would allow buildings up to 19 storeys high in the town centre. Hunters Hill Council Despite that, community opposition remains strong. Gladesville Residents for Responsible Development member Nina Ardle noted the consultation attracted 596 objections compared with just 45 submissions in support, highlighting community concern over the scale of the redevelopment. Conversely, Melissa Neighbour, a member of Sydney YIMBY, said the ageing shopping precinct on the busy Victoria Road corridor was precisely where housing should be concentrated.



“If we can’t say yes to homes here, then we seriously need to ask ourselves where are we prepared to say yes to?” she said. A similar debate is unfolding in Bondi Junction, where Waverley Council is expected to face a packed public gallery on Tuesday as councillors consider advancing a masterplan that would pave the way for about 3000 homes, improved transport links and a revitalised Oxford Street Mall. Increased housing density and public amenities form part of the Bondi Junction masterplan. Waverley Council The council argues that concentrating growth in Bondi Junction would reduce pressure for higher-density across surrounding suburbs while retaining local oversight of major developments. The proposal attracted 830 public submissions, many lodged using an AI-assisted platform organised by a community group raising concerns about building heights, wind impacts and traffic. Councillor Steven Lewis criticised the proposal, saying rows of high-rise towers had “East Berlin written all over it” and likened the vision to “Alexanderplatz by the sea”.



Supporters, meanwhile, backed plans to revitalise Oxford Street Mall, while landowners Scentre Group and Meriton supported increased height limits. A new masterplan for Brookvale has been developed by Northern Beaches Council. Northern Beaches Council Northern Beaches Council will also meet on Tuesday to consider a planning overhaul for Brookvale for up to 2900 homes over the next 15 years. Related Article City life The Sydney suburbs bracing for population boom as reforms reshape housing map The proposal significantly increases density from an earlier draft of 1350 homes. While that plan received majority community support, residents raised concerns about traffic and further pressure on limited public transport.



Hunters Hill mayor Zac Miles said councils faced difficult choices balancing housing growth with community expectations, but stressed locally led planning delivers better outcomes than allowing developers to pursue state planning pathways that can result in even taller developments with fewer public benefits. “It’s not going to be perfect for everyone.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up here.

World.title: Older Sydney town: the suburbs where the over 65s outnumber those under 20
World.content:
NationalNSWAgeing Older Sydney town: the suburbs where the over 65s outnumber those under 20 Matt Wade July 20, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The share of Sydney suburbs where over-65s outnumber those aged under 20 has trebled during the past two decades as the city’s population ages and the high cost of housing locks young families out of many neighbourhoods. The population of those aged over 65 outstripped those aged up to 19 in 54 Sydney neighbourhoods in 2024, new analysis of Bureau of Statistics population data shows. That compares with only 18 neighbourhoods in 2001. Potts Point-Woolloomooloo in the inner city had the highest population balance in favour of seniors, with 1889 more people aged over-65 than under 20. It was one of several inner-city neighbourhoods where seniors outnumber those up to 19 years; others included Double Bay-Darling point (114 more people aged over 65), Darlinghurst (636 more) and Surry Hills (481 more). Affluent neighbourhoods north of the harbour also had a large population balance in favour of seniors, including Neutral Bay-Kirribilli (1127 more aged over 65 years than aged 0-19), North Sydney-Lavender Bay (508 more) and Avalon-Palm Beach (505 more).



Parts of the Central Coast also had a high share of seniors, especially Umina-Booker Bay-Patonga (1693 more aged over 65 years than under 20) and Erina-Green Point (1203 more). Among the reasons for this outnumbering is the ageing of the population. In the mid-1970s, about one in 12 Australians was aged over 65, but that has now climbed to one in six. The share of over-65s nationally is forecast to reach one in four by the 2060s. Terry Rawnsley, a KPMG urban economist who analysed the latest local area population figures, said the high cost of housing has also played a role, especially in well-located Sydney suburbs. “It also comes down to housing affordability,” he said. “Families with young children just can’t get their foot in the property door in many suburbs.” Fewer births have also been a factor. Sydney’s fertility rate – the number of expected births per woman – has fallen by nearly 20 per cent in the past decade to a historic low of 1.44.



The age profile of some neighbourhoods has shifted rapidly over the past two decades. In the Cronulla-Kurnell-Bundeena area, for instance, under-20s outnumbered over-65s by 1179 in 2001. But by 2024 that had reversed and seniors outnumbered those aged 0–19 years by 863. In Mosman North in 20221 there were 480 more under-20s than over-65s; by 2024 there were 458 more aged over 65 than under 20. The cost of housing has been a factor in the growing number of Sydney suburbs where seniors outnumber those aged 0-19. Oscar Colman It has been a different story in a swath of suburbs stretching from Sydney’s north-west to south-west where the over-65s are far outnumbered. The population balance in favour of under-20s was greatest in the north-western suburb of Schofields East (9848 more under-20s than over-65s) and neighbouring Marsden Park-Shanes Park (8343 more). Next was Oran Park in the city’s south-west (7280 more).



These are relatively newly developed areas where many young families have moved during the past decade, in part boosting the cohort of children and teens. Rawnsley says the character of many suburbs will shift as the share of older residents increases. School enrolments will fall, parks will be used differently, there will be fewer childcare centres yet there will be greater demand for aged care. “Even the local high street in some places will start to look different because the spending patterns of older people differ from other age groups,” he said. “The whole vibe in some suburbs will change.” Areas with older age profiles also tend to have more women than men, reflecting females’ longer life expectancy. Rawnsley’s analysis showed that in 2001 there were more people aged over 65 than those aged between 0 and 19 in 5 per cent of Sydney neighbourhoods, but that had risen to 15 per cent by 2024.



The proportion of Sydney suburbs where seniors outnumber under-20s increased gradually between 2001 and 2019 but has accelerated noticeably over the past five years. “That share has ramped up with the ageing population,” Rawnsley said. The analysis drew on Australian Bureau of Statistics data for localities called “Statistical Area Level 2” (SA2) which are similar to urban suburbs.

World.title: Derryn Hinch state funeral live updates: Legendary journalist farewelled at The Timber Yard
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our rolling coverage of the state funeral of Derryn Hinch.

The event will be live-streamed on this blog, and 9Now and broadcast on Nine.

Loading

For decades, Hinch was one of the biggest names in media in this country, a newspaper man who became a radio man and then a television man. He published books, he fought for the rights of survivors of sexual abuse, he outed paedophiles and went to jail for doing so. He lunched long and hard, he had a liver transplant, he married and divorced a string of beautiful women. He even became a senator.

Little wonder he was known, both affectionately and derisively, as The Human Headline.

The stage at Derryn Hinch’s state funeral. Eddie Jim

In his last months, he was unsentimental about the death he knew was imminent – he had been in serious ill health following a series of falls – but he’d love the fact he is being remembered in such a public way. He’d no doubt love the fact he’s generated one last tranche of headlines as he’s leaving the building forever, too.

World.title: Brunswick East home discounted after auction to eventually sell for $1.69m
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Brunswick East home discounted after auction to eventually sell for $1.69m Shona Hendley July 20, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A freestanding house in Brunswick East sold for $1.69 million on Saturday after passing in at auction without a genuine bid, with the vendor lowering their reserve in negotiations. The three-bedroom weatherboard home at 17 Lanark Street sits minutes from inner-north landmarks Merri Creek, CERES Environment Park and the Brunswick Velodrome, and features its own lush front and rear gardens, and classic hardwood-floored interiors. It had a price guide of $1,575,000 to $1.65 million, with a reserve of $1.7 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



The property was one of 587 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 59 per cent from 391 reported results throughout the week, while 48 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Related Article Auctions First home buyers battle for stylish $1.2m Northcote townhouse The preliminary clearance rate is likely to be revised lower as more results are collected, leaving the result weaker than the 60 per cent threshold that indicates a balanced market, and suggesting prices are still falling. Jellis Craig Brunswick agent Anthony Monteleone said he went to auction with two registered bidders for the Brunswick East home, but both declined to bid on the day. A $1.6 million vendor bid opened the auction, followed by another at $1.65 million, after which it passed in.



“For the age of the home, it was in really, really good condition,” Monteleone said. “Well-maintained, structurally very sound… I actually expected it to sell under the hammer.” He said the property sold to a young couple who had inspected but not registered any intent to bid. He thought the fact it hadn’t sold at auction, but ended up selling comfortably within a day, was a reflection of the state of the market. “Things are just taking a bit longer, and buyers are just a little bit more hesitant at the moment to pull the trigger,” he said.



Monteleone said the vendors had bought land in Brunswick East and were in the process of building their next home. Elsewhere, a young family paid $100,000 over reserve, spending $980,000 at auction for a four-bedroom home in Fawkner. The brick-veneer family home at 2 Seacombe Street was listed with a guide of $850,000 to $890,000 and a reserve of $880,000. Selling agent Louis Saba from Harcourts Coburg said the bidding opened at $800,000, and the three active bidders, young couples and young families, went “head-to-head.”



Related Article Auctions ‘Like going back in time’: Moonee Ponds mansion sells for $1.92m “They were all looking to upsize,” said Saba. Bidding rose in $20,000 increments before slowing to $10,000 and $1,000 once it reached $900,000. “A young couple who were the underbidder just missed out by $2,000,” Saba said. Although they were disappointed, he said they were “ready to go and buy something soon.” The new owners wanted to move closer to family who already live in Fawkner and were drawn to the property’s tidiness, said Saba.



“The fact that it had four bedrooms and a second living area, plus the fresh coat of paint, was really appealing,” he said. The seller was an investor wanting to “get out of the Melbourne market.” “He isn’t happy with how things are changing and decided it was best to get out,” said Saba. “He is pretty happy with the result.” Meanwhile, in Altona, a two-bedroom villa sold under the hammer for $602,000.



Related Article Auctions Downsizers win keys to stylish $1,385,000 inner-north home The home at 3/15 David Street had a price guide of $550,000 to $600,000 and a reserve of $600,000. Selling agent, Prue McKay from Nelson Alexander, Flemington, said the market had been “unpredictable”. “I honestly didn’t know how today would go, but I was happy in the end,” she said. The villa, which is located at the rear of a block of three, was in a “good position”. “It is close to the Altona shops and not far from the beach either,” she said. “It is ready to move in and has good potential, too. People really love these solid brick homes.”



Two active bidders took part in the auction; both were first-home buyers “supported by mum and dad.” Bidding opened at $550,000 and rose in $10,000 increments before dropping to $1,000 and $500 for “the last stretch”. The sellers had been renting the property out. In Broadmeadows, a two-bedroom townhouse sold at auction for $470,000, $20,000 above its reserve.



The home at 4/15 Colin Court had a price guide of $410,000 to $451,000. The reserve was $450,000. The selling agent, Omer Koksal from Ray White in Glenroy, said there were four registered bidders, three of whom were active. “Two first-home buyers and one investor took part in the auction, with the other investor never getting an opportunity,” he said. Bidding opened at $400,000 and rose in $10,000 increments up to $450,000, then fell to $5,000 increments. “The successful bidder had been actively looking to buy a property for the last nine months,” said Koksal.



Related Article Victoria residential property ‘I love it’: The Melbourne suburbs people never leave The court location and the green space offered by the property’s entertaining deck, along with mature screening trees, were two of the major drawcards for the buyers. “It was well kept,” said Koksal. Although this property sold at auction, Koksal said that only four of his office’s 12 scheduled Saturday auctions sold. “It’s a really tough market,” he said. “Properties under $600,000 are selling out; anything over that isn’t.”



PRD’s chief economist, Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo, said this week’s auction clearance rate was “quite a jump compared with last week’s 52 per cent”. “It indicates that buyers are becoming more active in the market and probably want to capitalise on the slightly reduced house prices before the upcoming RBA decision in August,” she said. Mardiasmo said the results also show that “people are coming to terms” with the changes to property tax, which took effect on June 25. “People are making decisions about what is best for them based on this,” she said.

World.title: Early pressure a plus for Eagles while Freo star emerges unscathed
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Early pressure a plus for Eagles while Freo star emerges unscathed Paddy Sweeney July 20, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the Western Watercooler, where we digest the talking points from the weekend’s games – and the highlights, frustrations and silver linings WA footy fans can cling to as the season progresses. The minor premiership is almost within the Dockers keeping. Fremantle withstood an undermanned Port Adelaide and their 16th win of the season, coupled with Sydney’s loss to Adelaide, extended the Dockers advantage to three games on top of the table. Hayden Young made it through the match against Port Adelaide unscathed. Getty Images A spirited West Coast took it up to the two-time defending premiers Brisbane.



And while they led at half-time, the Eagles were eventually outclassed, but didn’t lose any admirers. Fremantle Dockers What went right? Their third term blitz. It was shift, powerful and match defining - as they’ve done on countless occasions this year. Five goals in 10 minutes were enough to turn a 12-point half-time deficit into a 19-point lead at the final change.



And it came on the back of the improved centre clearance work which was below par in the opening half. What went wrong? First-half centre clearance work. Port Adelaide entered the match minus their best four players. Zac Butters, Connor Rozee, Jason Horne-Francis and Mitch Georgiades were all absent through injury or suspension. But in the opening two quarters, it was the Dockers who were on the back foot, Justin Longmuir saying his players didn’t “get their hands dirty.”



Port monstered Fremantle in the centre clearances, winning the stat 12-2, which resulted in 5.3 (33) as the Dockers didn’t generate a score from the source. The fitness of veteran Jaegar O’Meara will be closely monitored after he was unable to play out the game with an ankle concern. Silver lining: Hayden Young got through his return unscathed. The 25-year-old was back after missing the previous week with a groin injury, managing 20 disposals and a goal from 67 per cent game time.



Continuity and confidence in his body are the two things he will be chasing with finals edging closer. He’s a star when fully fit and has the potential to supercharge the Dockers post-season finals run if he gets a clean run at it. West Coast Eagles What went right? Applying pressure early. The Eagles stunned Brisbane, jumping out to a 21-point lead in the first term.



They booted five of the first six goals as a result of their centre clearance work. West Coast won the centre clearances and draw level at stoppages, no mean feat against a midfield possessing an abundance of stars. They matched their grunt work with intent, hunt and pressure while also out-tackling the Lions. Brisbane eventually wrestled back control and played at their tempo of choice on the back of a one-sided mark stat (115-67). But the exposure the young Eagles will get from facing a side challenging for a three-peat will be invaluable.



What went wrong? Injury and suspension. The Eagles lost forward Jack Hutchinson to a hamstring injury in the opening minutes and it only got worse. Star Harley Reid lost his footing while on the interchange bench and spent the majority of the opening quarter getting treatment. West Coast star Harley Reid spent time on the bench early after an ankle injury. Getty Images He clearly wasn’t fully fit, and although playing out the game to finish as one of the Eagles best, there’s some doubt over his availability for Friday’s Western Derby.



Right now, co-captain Liam Baker won’t face Fremantle, with the 28-year-old offered a one-match ban for rough conduct on Cam Rayner. Silver lining: Rhett Bazzo. The Eagles defence has been severely stretched in the absence of Reuben Ginbey and Harry Edwards. But it brought about an opportunity for Bazzo, managing 37 games in five seasons on the list. The 22 year-old was locked in an engrossing battle with Logan Morris, who despite being a year younger, is considered one of the competition’s best young key forwards - playing 61 games and winning two premierships. Bazzo ended the night restricting Morris to one goal, while effecting a game-high 11 spoils and taking four intercept marks.

World.title: ‘The right fit’: How first Devils coach Ken Hinkley won the job
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘The right fit’: How first Devils coach Ken Hinkley won the job Peter Ryan Updated July 20, 2026 — 11:12am ,first published 10:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Tasmania Devils’ inaugural AFL coach, Ken Hinkley, has been formally unveiled by the AFL’s 19th team on Monday after swooping in ahead of the early favourites to nab the job. The announcement is the culmination of a 12-month search for the right candidate to unify the island state and build the start-up team ahead of their entry into the league in 2028. In a statement on Monday morning, club chair Grant O’Brien said the Devils had appointed Hinkley because he was the right fit. New Tasmania coach Ken Hinkley. AFL Photos “We didn’t set out to find the candidate with the single best win-loss record in this process, we set out to find the right coach for exactly what Tasmania needs right now,” O’Brien said.



“Ken’s ability to build relationships with young players, and to build an environment that people want to be part of is exceptional, it is the number one reason we believe he is the right fit for this club. “We are building a list, a program and a club from the ground up, largely with young and developing talent. “That demands a head coach who is, first and foremost, a brilliant teacher and a builder of people, and that is exactly what Ken is.” Hinkley said while the journey will have ups and downs, the opportunity to build the club and oversee the Devils’ entry into the AFL was special. “It’s a huge privilege to be given the opportunity to build something from the very beginning,” Hinkley said.



Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 Why Hinkley’s arrival in the Apple Isle will awaken Tasmania’s enemies “The responsibility to lead Tasmania’s entry into the AFL is something very special, it excites me. “There will be many ups and downs, and challenges that lie ahead, including the build of our football department, but I have unique and directly relevant experience to take these on alongside the broader football club. “Tasmania is a proud football state, and I can’t wait to get to know the players, staff, partners and community who have, and will continue to be part of this from day one.” Former Collingwood champion and coach Nathan Buckley was initially fancied for the position, with the Swans’ premiership coach John Longmire also a candidate.



However, Hinkley swept into Hobart on Sunday morning to present to the Devils board and by Sunday evening had beaten both Buckley and Longmire to the position. The 59-year-old Hinkley coached the Power for 13 years and while he did not lead them to a flag they played in four preliminary finals on his watch. The Tasmania job was one of three live coaching processes, with Carlton narrowing down the field to replace Michael Voss and Essendon searching for Brad Scott’s replacement. Hinkley had publicly ruled himself out of the Essendon hunt after James Hird announced his interest in the role. More to come Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
