World.title: It may offend the book’s rusted-on fans, but this series should be approached with an open mind
World.content:
Philippa Northeast’s oddball audition wowed the creators of a new take on Miles Franklin’s beloved novel, My Brilliant Career. But will fans accept the changes?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Philippa Northeast is having a moment. The 31-year-old is currently on stage with Shaun Micallef and Daniel Henshall in the MTC’s Uncle Vanya, and next month she’s in the running for an acting Logie for her turn as a depressed young mum in the ABC drama The Family Next Door. But it’s the Netflix adaptation of My Brilliant Career, in which she plays Sybylla Melvyn, the hot-headed heroine and narrator of Miles Franklin’s much-loved novel, that is certain to put her on the radar globally. “I’m glad it’s this story,” she says of her looming breakthrough moment, “because I think any anxiety I had in terms of levelling up is quite squashed by the fact that is entirely what Sybylla stands for and wants. So, weirdly, I can throw myself into the protection of that.” Sybylla is a dirt-poor farm girl in 1890s Australia, damned by her father’s alcoholism and incompetence to endless drudgery. But she dreams of and aspires to a creative life. She wants a brilliant career – of letters, of music, on the stage, it hardly matters. Just something other than an existence defined by when the sun comes up and when the cows need milking. Philippa Northeast as Sybylla in My Brilliant Career. Ian Routledge/Netflix Playing her in Gillian Armstrong’s 1979 film launched the career of one Judy Davis, who was 23 at the time and had never acted on screen before. Northeast, though, already has some serious runs on the board, with notable turns as a junkie in The Newsreader and as the highly capable daughter who would surely take over the farm in Territory, if only she weren’t a bloody girl. “I’m not in any capacity an overnight sensation,” says Northeast, who was born in Richmond, in inner-city Melbourne, and grew up in Warrandyte on the north-eastern fringe, where she attended a Steiner school that allowed her free rein to explore whatever creative instincts she might harbour. “I feel like I’ve been sort of knocking at the door and putting my head down and tail up for over a decade. I really identify with the determination and the boldness and the bravery to continue following a creative life in the face of constant rejection,” she says. “I relate to Sybylla’s endurance.”



Northeast’s first onscreen appearance was in the sketch comedy series Skithouse in 2003. But it was on Home and Away, where she did a 341-episode, five-year stretch as Evelyn MacGuire from 2013, that she cut her acting teeth. Still, My Brilliant Career – a big-budget, somewhat freewheeling adaptation in which she’s on screen for almost every minute of its six episodes – represents a huge step up in terms of visibility. And she’s relishing the opportunities that come with it. “As a younger actor, I was just jumping up and down and happy to do whatever – not whatever, but a wide array of things so that I could prove myself,” she says. “Now I’m starting to have a little more creative choice and become maybe a bit more publicly known. The really exciting part to me – and I know it can ebb and flow and be fleeting – is that I’m getting an opportunity to have an intentional career and start to make a few choices about the stories I would like to put out into the world.” Northeast’s Instagram account is testament to her rising profile: fashion shoots, magazine covers, red-carpet premieres on the arm of her actor boyfriend Sam Reid (who is having his own turn in the spotlight as star of The Vampire Lestat). Northeast, right, with Bella Heathcote and Jane Harber in The Family Next Door. ABC TV But if she is very definitely stepping into the spotlight with this role, so too – finally – is Miles Franklin. For decades, she was best known as the author of the book Armstrong adapted in 1979, with Davis as Sybylla and Sam Neill as Harry Beecham, the man she might be destined to marry if love alone were to determine her course. The book – like the literary award she established in her name – cemented her place in Australian literary history. But to some extent, Franklin herself remained in the background.



Recently, though, she has been celebrated on stage in no fewer than three productions, with a straight adaptation of My Brilliant Career in 2020, the acclaimed musical version in 2024, and this year’s musical biopic, Stella. There have been two books, too – Kerrie Davies’ biography Miles Franklin Undercover last year and, just last month, The Very Secretive And Passionate Stella Miles Franklin, a biographical novel by French author Alexandra Lapierre. Miles Franklin in 1901, the year My Brilliant Career was published. Alamy Stock Photo And now, of course, we have a lavish series made for the world’s biggest streamer. It’s a remarkable legacy for a book that was, as Northeast puts it, “bold, brilliant, brave for its time and unique, but also still written by a teenager, that is chunky and clunky and sort of naive”. My Brilliant Career was written when Franklin was just 19 and published in 1901, when she was 21. Despite her protestations to the contrary, it was widely assumed to be autobiographical. And even with an enthusiastic (if somewhat patronising) endorsement by Henry Lawson in the foreword, it had only middling sales. In 1910, a deeply frustrated Franklin withdrew it from publication. To that point it had, according to the National Museum of Australia, “only earned her £24”.



The book didn’t reappear in print until 1966, 12 years after the author’s death at the age of 74. Franklin had a reasonable career, mostly in Britain and the US, churning out another 18 books. Though she was never wealthy, she left £9000 as seed funding for the Miles Franklin Award, which now pays out $60,000 annually to the winner and $5000 to each of its other five short-listed novelists. Reading the novel now, 125 years after it was published, what strikes you most is how it bristles with an energy and attitude that makes it seem alive, fresh and utterly relevant. Which is not to say everything stands the test of time; the casual racism in particular is quite awful. The 2024 stage musical of My Brilliant Career, which was revived earlier this year. MTC Liz Doran, who wrote the series, had never read the book until she was approached by the production company Jungle about five years ago. But she did know the story. “The Gillian Armstrong film had this huge influence on me as a young person,” she says. “It was a huge inspiration for me, one of the things that made me think, ‘oh, maybe I could actually be a writer’.” When she did finally read the book, she says, “I was actually really surprised at all the other things that are in it. We know what Sybylla’s story is – it’s so strong – but I was really interested in the other characters. And then you look at that book through a contemporary eye …”



What she saw was all the stuff that would have been present in Sybylla’s (and Franklin’s) world, but wasn’t – perhaps couldn’t be – acknowledged. And Doran felt that was where the opportunity, the thrill and the challenge of this version lay. “Whenever I’m looking at an adaptation, I’m always thinking – especially for a period thing, and especially for this book – who is in this world who didn’t get put into the book. Because we’ve got six episodes, we can explore those other characters. Aunt Helen (Genevieve O’Reilly) gets a little storyline, and Uncle Julius (Alexander English) gets a storyline. And then, of course, we’ve invented the First Nations characters who also get a storyline. And we put all of those characters under an umbrella of career-versus-love, which is the main through line of My Brilliant Career. That was the big-picture approach.” Judy Davis as Sybylla in Gillian Armstrong’s 1979 film. NFSA Come at this adaptation with an open mind and you’re likely to enjoy how the story, and the world, has been opened up. Julius — Uncle Jay Jay – for instance, is gay. He arrives at the Caddagat homestead with his Sydney friend Everard Grey, who is actually his lover. Grey’s clumsy proposal to Sybylla is nothing more than an attempt to cover his real romance. It’s ingenious and plausible but likely to offend some of the book’s rusted-on fans. “I don’t think we worried about that,” says producer Chloe Rickard when I ask if she was concerned about alienating the book’s solid fan base. “The reason I say that is because this is Sybylla’s story, right, it’s about a young woman who chooses herself against all odds. And I think inspecting the world around her with a contemporary critical gaze about who was there and what their lives would have been like, and what were their dreams and hopes and ambitions … just because Franklin didn’t write about them back then because of the times doesn’t mean we shouldn’t explore the vast, colourful nature of our country at that time. “It doesn’t feel like we’ve imposed anything fake onto the story,” she says. “I think we’ve just used our imagination around the central premise.” In this version, Aunt Augusta moves from the fringes to become a central character, an independently wealthy suffragette (played with typical verve by Kate Mulvany) who nurtures Sybylla’s creative passions, while never quite believing any path other than marriage is available to her. The time shifts slightly, too: we’re in 1900 now, on the cusp of Federation, rather than 1897.

World.title: Port guide: Papeete, French Polynesia
World.content:
InspirationCruises Port guide: Papeete, French Polynesia Brian Johnston July 20, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This modest port may be drab and unexciting, but it’s the gateway to one of the world’s most stunning, must-visit cruise regions. Who goes there Papeete is visited by the larger ships of companies such as Norwegian Cruise Line, Princess Cruises and Royal Caribbean during extended South Pacific journeys. It’s also the departure and arrival port for French Polynesia cruises operated by luxury lines such as Ponant, Silversea and Windstar. Mixed freight-passenger company Aranui and Paul Gauguin (now owned by Ponant) are locally based. Sail on in Papeete – the gateway to one of the world’s most stunning, must-visit cruise regions. iStock



On a French Polynesia cruise, you might well arrive in the dark following a short hop from Moorea. During the sail away, however, the steep green mountains that rise behind Papeete and the lagoon that fronts it redeem the town. That said, you’ll be getting far more spectacular approaches and departures at every other island. 



Going ashore Papeete’s town centre is full of markets and shops. French Polynesia is ravishing, but its gateway capital unfortunately anything but – and hot and humid too. Only the coconut palms and bougainvillea soften its edges. Still, the waterfront is pleasant, and the town full of markets and shops. If you’re after Polynesian black pearls, this is your opportunity. Those with more time should explore beyond town. Don’t miss The Museum of Tahiti and the Islands, 15 kilometres from Papeete, is the best museum in French Polynesia and has sumptuous views across the strait towards Moorea from extensive gardens. It has exhibits on geology, flora, fauna and handicrafts, and you can learn more about customs such as tattooing and tapa-weaving. It also does a good job of explaining Polynesia’s pre-European history and the impact of colonialisation.



Related Article Tahiti There’s more to this paradise than just overwater bungalows Get active Tu Marama Promenade links several squares and parks along the waterfront. You’ll pass Paofai Gardens, which has outdoor exercise equipment. Otherwise, you can jet ski or sail in the harbour. Tahiti’s rugged interior is splendid, but you’ll need a full day for four-wheel-drive tours that might include rappelling down the side of waterfalls or crawling through lava tubes. Best bites Papeete residents are fond of food trucks or roulottes and, given the high cost of dining, so are visitors. You’ll find several outside the cruise terminal, and more along the waterfront. They might serve anything from coffee and firi firi (the local doughnut) to full meals. They generally offer Polynesian, French or Chinese cuisine. Two dishes to try are pua’a roti (glazed roast pork) and poisson cru (raw fish marinated in lime juice and coconut milk). Most roulottes are cash only.



Further afield The most popular excursion takes cruise passengers on a drive around the road that circumnavigates most of the island. You’ll stop in places such as Matavai Bay for the view, Point Venus associated with Captain James Cook, and the Water Gardens of Vaipahi. Alternatively, a four-wheel-drive excursion will take you into the lush Papenoo Valley, which has archaeological sites and waterfalls.

World.title: ‘It’s not going to be perfect’: The Sydney town centre overhauls no one can agree on
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘It’s not going to be perfect’: The Sydney town centre overhauls no one can agree on David Barwell July 20, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney’s suburban town centres have emerged as the latest battleground in the city’s housing debate, with councils advancing plans for significantly taller buildings in established shopping precincts, exposing tensions between the need for more homes and concerns about preserving neighbourhood character. New masterplans for Bondi Junction, Brookvale and Gladesville would collectively deliver more than 6400 new homes alongside upgraded public spaces, revitalised retail strips and expanded community facilities. A new masterplan for Bondi Junction will face a crucial vote this week. Waverley Council But while councils argue the projects are essential to address Sydney’s housing shortage and renew ageing commercial centres, many residents fear excessive building heights, worsening traffic congestion and mounting pressure on local infrastructure. The most advanced proposal is in Gladesville, where Hunters Hill Council this month voted to forward a new town centre masterplan to the NSW Government. The proposal includes towers up to 19 storeys, 522 homes and the redevelopment of the ageing Gladesville Shopping Centre.



Deputy mayor Julia Prieston described the project as an opportunity to revive a precinct that had languished through decades of failed development attempts, calling Gladesville “a case study in Sydney’s planning paralysis”. A council report found lower building heights would not generate sufficient economic value to fund new community facilities, particularly given rising construction costs and softer apartment market conditions. A new masterplan for Gladesville would allow buildings up to 19 storeys high in the town centre. Hunters Hill Council Despite that, community opposition remains strong. Gladesville Residents for Responsible Development member Nina Ardle noted the consultation attracted 596 objections compared with just 45 submissions in support, highlighting community concern over the scale of the redevelopment. Conversely, Melissa Neighbour, a member of Sydney YIMBY, said the ageing shopping precinct on the busy Victoria Road corridor was precisely where housing should be concentrated.



“If we can’t say yes to homes here, then we seriously need to ask ourselves where are we prepared to say yes to?” she said. A similar debate is unfolding in Bondi Junction, where Waverley Council is expected to face a packed public gallery on Tuesday as councillors consider advancing a masterplan that would pave the way for about 3000 homes, improved transport links and a revitalised Oxford Street Mall. Increased housing density and public amenities form part of the Bondi Junction masterplan. Waverley Council The council argues that concentrating growth in Bondi Junction would reduce pressure for higher-density across surrounding suburbs while retaining local oversight of major developments. The proposal attracted 830 public submissions, many lodged using an AI-assisted platform organised by a community group raising concerns about building heights, wind impacts and traffic. Councillor Steven Lewis criticised the proposal, saying rows of high-rise towers had “East Berlin written all over it” and likened the vision to “Alexanderplatz by the sea”.



Supporters, meanwhile, backed plans to revitalise Oxford Street Mall, while landowners Scentre Group and Meriton supported increased height limits. A new masterplan for Brookvale has been developed by Northern Beaches Council. Northern Beaches Council Northern Beaches Council will also meet on Tuesday to consider a planning overhaul for Brookvale for up to 2900 homes over the next 15 years. Related Article City life The Sydney suburbs bracing for population boom as reforms reshape housing map The proposal significantly increases density from an earlier draft of 1350 homes. While that plan received majority community support, residents raised concerns about traffic and further pressure on limited public transport.



Hunters Hill mayor Zac Miles said councils faced difficult choices balancing housing growth with community expectations, but stressed locally led planning delivers better outcomes than allowing developers to pursue state planning pathways that can result in even taller developments with fewer public benefits. “It’s not going to be perfect for everyone.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. World.title: Older Sydney town: the suburbs where the over 65s outnumber those under 20
World.content:
NationalNSWAgeing Older Sydney town: the suburbs where the over 65s outnumber those under 20 Matt Wade July 20, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The share of Sydney suburbs where over-65s outnumber those aged under 20 has trebled during the past two decades as the city’s population ages and the high cost of housing locks young families out of many neighbourhoods. The population of those aged over 65 outstripped those aged up to 19 in 54 Sydney neighbourhoods in 2024, new analysis of Bureau of Statistics population data shows. That compares with only 18 neighbourhoods in 2001. Potts Point-Woolloomooloo in the inner city had the highest population balance in favour of seniors, with 1889 more people aged over-65 than under 20. It was one of several inner-city neighbourhoods where seniors outnumber those up to 19 years; others included Double Bay-Darling point (114 more people aged over 65), Darlinghurst (636 more) and Surry Hills (481 more). Affluent neighbourhoods north of the harbour also had a large population balance in favour of seniors, including Neutral Bay-Kirribilli (1127 more aged over 65 years than aged 0-19), North Sydney-Lavender Bay (508 more) and Avalon-Palm Beach (505 more).



Parts of the Central Coast also had a high share of seniors, especially Umina-Booker Bay-Patonga (1693 more aged over 65 years than under 20) and Erina-Green Point (1203 more). Among the reasons for this outnumbering is the ageing of the population. In the mid-1970s, about one in 12 Australians was aged over 65, but that has now climbed to one in six. The share of over-65s nationally is forecast to reach one in four by the 2060s. Terry Rawnsley, a KPMG urban economist who analysed the latest local area population figures, said the high cost of housing has also played a role, especially in well-located Sydney suburbs. “It also comes down to housing affordability,” he said. “Families with young children just can’t get their foot in the property door in many suburbs.” Fewer births have also been a factor. Sydney’s fertility rate – the number of expected births per woman – has fallen by nearly 20 per cent in the past decade to a historic low of 1.44.



The age profile of some neighbourhoods has shifted rapidly over the past two decades. In the Cronulla-Kurnell-Bundeena area, for instance, under-20s outnumbered over-65s by 1179 in 2001. But by 2024 that had reversed and seniors outnumbered those aged 0–19 years by 863. In Mosman North in 20221 there were 480 more under-20s than over-65s; by 2024 there were 458 more aged over 65 than under 20. The cost of housing has been a factor in the growing number of Sydney suburbs where seniors outnumber those aged 0-19. Oscar Colman It has been a different story in a swath of suburbs stretching from Sydney’s north-west to south-west where the over-65s are far outnumbered. The population balance in favour of under-20s was greatest in the north-western suburb of Schofields East (9848 more under-20s than over-65s) and neighbouring Marsden Park-Shanes Park (8343 more). Next was Oran Park in the city’s south-west (7280 more).



These are relatively newly developed areas where many young families have moved during the past decade, in part boosting the cohort of children and teens. Rawnsley says the character of many suburbs will shift as the share of older residents increases. School enrolments will fall, parks will be used differently, there will be fewer childcare centres yet there will be greater demand for aged care. “Even the local high street in some places will start to look different because the spending patterns of older people differ from other age groups,” he said. “The whole vibe in some suburbs will change.” Areas with older age profiles also tend to have more women than men, reflecting females’ longer life expectancy. Rawnsley’s analysis showed that in 2001 there were more people aged over 65 than those aged between 0 and 19 in 5 per cent of Sydney neighbourhoods, but that had risen to 15 per cent by 2024.



The proportion of Sydney suburbs where seniors outnumber under-20s increased gradually between 2001 and 2019 but has accelerated noticeably over the past five years. “That share has ramped up with the ageing population,” Rawnsley said. The analysis drew on Australian Bureau of Statistics data for localities called “Statistical Area Level 2” (SA2) which are similar to urban suburbs.

World.title: Derryn Hinch state funeral live updates: Legendary journalist farewelled at The Timber Yard
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our rolling coverage of the state funeral of Derryn Hinch.

The event will be live-streamed on this blog, and 9Now and broadcast on Nine.

Loading

For decades, Hinch was one of the biggest names in media in this country, a newspaper man who became a radio man and then a television man. He published books, he fought for the rights of survivors of sexual abuse, he outed paedophiles and went to jail for doing so. He lunched long and hard, he had a liver transplant, he married and divorced a string of beautiful women. He even became a senator.

Little wonder he was known, both affectionately and derisively, as The Human Headline.

The stage at Derryn Hinch’s state funeral. Eddie Jim

In his last months, he was unsentimental about the death he knew was imminent – he had been in serious ill health following a series of falls – but he’d love the fact he is being remembered in such a public way. He’d no doubt love the fact he’s generated one last tranche of headlines as he’s leaving the building forever, too.

World.title: Brunswick East home discounted after auction to eventually sell for $1.69m
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Brunswick East home discounted after auction to eventually sell for $1.69m Shona Hendley July 20, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A freestanding house in Brunswick East sold for $1.69 million on Saturday after passing in at auction without a genuine bid, with the vendor lowering their reserve in negotiations. The three-bedroom weatherboard home at 17 Lanark Street sits minutes from inner-north landmarks Merri Creek, CERES Environment Park and the Brunswick Velodrome, and features its own lush front and rear gardens, and classic hardwood-floored interiors. It had a price guide of $1,575,000 to $1.65 million, with a reserve of $1.7 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



The property was one of 587 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 59 per cent from 391 reported results throughout the week, while 48 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Related Article Auctions First home buyers battle for stylish $1.2m Northcote townhouse The preliminary clearance rate is likely to be revised lower as more results are collected, leaving the result weaker than the 60 per cent threshold that indicates a balanced market, and suggesting prices are still falling. Jellis Craig Brunswick agent Anthony Monteleone said he went to auction with two registered bidders for the Brunswick East home, but both declined to bid on the day. A $1.6 million vendor bid opened the auction, followed by another at $1.65 million, after which it passed in.



“For the age of the home, it was in really, really good condition,” Monteleone said. “Well-maintained, structurally very sound… I actually expected it to sell under the hammer.” He said the property sold to a young couple who had inspected but not registered any intent to bid. He thought the fact it hadn’t sold at auction, but ended up selling comfortably within a day, was a reflection of the state of the market. “Things are just taking a bit longer, and buyers are just a little bit more hesitant at the moment to pull the trigger,” he said.



Monteleone said the vendors had bought land in Brunswick East and were in the process of building their next home. Elsewhere, a young family paid $100,000 over reserve, spending $980,000 at auction for a four-bedroom home in Fawkner. The brick-veneer family home at 2 Seacombe Street was listed with a guide of $850,000 to $890,000 and a reserve of $880,000. Selling agent Louis Saba from Harcourts Coburg said the bidding opened at $800,000, and the three active bidders, young couples and young families, went “head-to-head.”



Related Article Auctions ‘Like going back in time’: Moonee Ponds mansion sells for $1.92m “They were all looking to upsize,” said Saba. Bidding rose in $20,000 increments before slowing to $10,000 and $1,000 once it reached $900,000. “A young couple who were the underbidder just missed out by $2,000,” Saba said. Although they were disappointed, he said they were “ready to go and buy something soon.” The new owners wanted to move closer to family who already live in Fawkner and were drawn to the property’s tidiness, said Saba.



“The fact that it had four bedrooms and a second living area, plus the fresh coat of paint, was really appealing,” he said. The seller was an investor wanting to “get out of the Melbourne market.” “He isn’t happy with how things are changing and decided it was best to get out,” said Saba. “He is pretty happy with the result.” Meanwhile, in Altona, a two-bedroom villa sold under the hammer for $602,000.



Related Article Auctions Downsizers win keys to stylish $1,385,000 inner-north home The home at 3/15 David Street had a price guide of $550,000 to $600,000 and a reserve of $600,000. Selling agent, Prue McKay from Nelson Alexander, Flemington, said the market had been “unpredictable”. “I honestly didn’t know how today would go, but I was happy in the end,” she said. The villa, which is located at the rear of a block of three, was in a “good position”. “It is close to the Altona shops and not far from the beach either,” she said. “It is ready to move in and has good potential, too. People really love these solid brick homes.”



Two active bidders took part in the auction; both were first-home buyers “supported by mum and dad.” Bidding opened at $550,000 and rose in $10,000 increments before dropping to $1,000 and $500 for “the last stretch”. The sellers had been renting the property out. In Broadmeadows, a two-bedroom townhouse sold at auction for $470,000, $20,000 above its reserve.



The home at 4/15 Colin Court had a price guide of $410,000 to $451,000. The reserve was $450,000. The selling agent, Omer Koksal from Ray White in Glenroy, said there were four registered bidders, three of whom were active. “Two first-home buyers and one investor took part in the auction, with the other investor never getting an opportunity,” he said. Bidding opened at $400,000 and rose in $10,000 increments up to $450,000, then fell to $5,000 increments. “The successful bidder had been actively looking to buy a property for the last nine months,” said Koksal.



Related Article Victoria residential property ‘I love it’: The Melbourne suburbs people never leave The court location and the green space offered by the property’s entertaining deck, along with mature screening trees, were two of the major drawcards for the buyers. “It was well kept,” said Koksal. Although this property sold at auction, Koksal said that only four of his office’s 12 scheduled Saturday auctions sold. “It’s a really tough market,” he said. “Properties under $600,000 are selling out; anything over that isn’t.”



PRD’s chief economist, Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo, said this week’s auction clearance rate was “quite a jump compared with last week’s 52 per cent”. “It indicates that buyers are becoming more active in the market and probably want to capitalise on the slightly reduced house prices before the upcoming RBA decision in August,” she said. Mardiasmo said the results also show that “people are coming to terms” with the changes to property tax, which took effect on June 25. “People are making decisions about what is best for them based on this,” she said.

World.title: Early pressure a plus for Eagles while Freo star emerges unscathed
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Early pressure a plus for Eagles while Freo star emerges unscathed Paddy Sweeney July 20, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the Western Watercooler, where we digest the talking points from the weekend’s games – and the highlights, frustrations and silver linings WA footy fans can cling to as the season progresses. The minor premiership is almost within the Dockers keeping. Fremantle withstood an undermanned Port Adelaide and their 16th win of the season, coupled with Sydney’s loss to Adelaide, extended the Dockers advantage to three games on top of the table. Hayden Young made it through the match against Port Adelaide unscathed. Getty Images A spirited West Coast took it up to the two-time defending premiers Brisbane.



And while they led at half-time, the Eagles were eventually outclassed, but didn’t lose any admirers. Fremantle Dockers What went right? Their third term blitz. It was shift, powerful and match defining - as they’ve done on countless occasions this year. Five goals in 10 minutes were enough to turn a 12-point half-time deficit into a 19-point lead at the final change.



And it came on the back of the improved centre clearance work which was below par in the opening half. What went wrong? First-half centre clearance work. Port Adelaide entered the match minus their best four players. Zac Butters, Connor Rozee, Jason Horne-Francis and Mitch Georgiades were all absent through injury or suspension. But in the opening two quarters, it was the Dockers who were on the back foot, Justin Longmuir saying his players didn’t “get their hands dirty.”



Port monstered Fremantle in the centre clearances, winning the stat 12-2, which resulted in 5.3 (33) as the Dockers didn’t generate a score from the source. The fitness of veteran Jaegar O’Meara will be closely monitored after he was unable to play out the game with an ankle concern. Silver lining: Hayden Young got through his return unscathed. The 25-year-old was back after missing the previous week with a groin injury, managing 20 disposals and a goal from 67 per cent game time.



Continuity and confidence in his body are the two things he will be chasing with finals edging closer. He’s a star when fully fit and has the potential to supercharge the Dockers post-season finals run if he gets a clean run at it. West Coast Eagles What went right? Applying pressure early. The Eagles stunned Brisbane, jumping out to a 21-point lead in the first term.



They booted five of the first six goals as a result of their centre clearance work. West Coast won the centre clearances and draw level at stoppages, no mean feat against a midfield possessing an abundance of stars. They matched their grunt work with intent, hunt and pressure while also out-tackling the Lions. Brisbane eventually wrestled back control and played at their tempo of choice on the back of a one-sided mark stat (115-67). But the exposure the young Eagles will get from facing a side challenging for a three-peat will be invaluable.



What went wrong? Injury and suspension. The Eagles lost forward Jack Hutchinson to a hamstring injury in the opening minutes and it only got worse. Star Harley Reid lost his footing while on the interchange bench and spent the majority of the opening quarter getting treatment. West Coast star Harley Reid spent time on the bench early after an ankle injury. Getty Images He clearly wasn’t fully fit, and although playing out the game to finish as one of the Eagles best, there’s some doubt over his availability for Friday’s Western Derby.



Right now, co-captain Liam Baker won’t face Fremantle, with the 28-year-old offered a one-match ban for rough conduct on Cam Rayner. Silver lining: Rhett Bazzo. The Eagles defence has been severely stretched in the absence of Reuben Ginbey and Harry Edwards. But it brought about an opportunity for Bazzo, managing 37 games in five seasons on the list. The 22 year-old was locked in an engrossing battle with Logan Morris, who despite being a year younger, is considered one of the competition’s best young key forwards - playing 61 games and winning two premierships. Bazzo ended the night restricting Morris to one goal, while effecting a game-high 11 spoils and taking four intercept marks.

World.title: ‘The right fit’: How first Devils coach Ken Hinkley won the job
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘The right fit’: How first Devils coach Ken Hinkley won the job Peter Ryan Updated July 20, 2026 — 11:12am ,first published 10:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Tasmania Devils’ inaugural AFL coach, Ken Hinkley, has been formally unveiled by the AFL’s 19th team on Monday after swooping in ahead of the early favourites to nab the job. The announcement is the culmination of a 12-month search for the right candidate to unify the island state and build the start-up team ahead of their entry into the league in 2028. In a statement on Monday morning, club chair Grant O’Brien said the Devils had appointed Hinkley because he was the right fit. New Tasmania coach Ken Hinkley. AFL Photos “We didn’t set out to find the candidate with the single best win-loss record in this process, we set out to find the right coach for exactly what Tasmania needs right now,” O’Brien said.



“Ken’s ability to build relationships with young players, and to build an environment that people want to be part of is exceptional, it is the number one reason we believe he is the right fit for this club. “We are building a list, a program and a club from the ground up, largely with young and developing talent. “That demands a head coach who is, first and foremost, a brilliant teacher and a builder of people, and that is exactly what Ken is.” Hinkley said while the journey will have ups and downs, the opportunity to build the club and oversee the Devils’ entry into the AFL was special. “It’s a huge privilege to be given the opportunity to build something from the very beginning,” Hinkley said.



Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 Why Hinkley’s arrival in the Apple Isle will awaken Tasmania’s enemies “The responsibility to lead Tasmania’s entry into the AFL is something very special, it excites me. “There will be many ups and downs, and challenges that lie ahead, including the build of our football department, but I have unique and directly relevant experience to take these on alongside the broader football club. “Tasmania is a proud football state, and I can’t wait to get to know the players, staff, partners and community who have, and will continue to be part of this from day one.” Former Collingwood champion and coach Nathan Buckley was initially fancied for the position, with the Swans’ premiership coach John Longmire also a candidate.



However, Hinkley swept into Hobart on Sunday morning to present to the Devils board and by Sunday evening had beaten both Buckley and Longmire to the position. The 59-year-old Hinkley coached the Power for 13 years and while he did not lead them to a flag they played in four preliminary finals on his watch. The Tasmania job was one of three live coaching processes, with Carlton narrowing down the field to replace Michael Voss and Essendon searching for Brad Scott’s replacement. Hinkley had publicly ruled himself out of the Essendon hunt after James Hird announced his interest in the role. More to come Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Authorities had 'concerns' with LynnMall terrorist five years before attack
World.content:
The Coroners Court has heard details about the LynnMall terrorist's first interaction with New Zealand authorities.

Ahamed Samsudeen stabbed six people in a West Auckland supermarket in 2021, before being shot dead by police.

Phases two and three of a coronial inquest into his death are underway in Auckland, looking at Samsudeen's path to violent extremism as well as the time leading up to the attack, and his attitudes towards women.

The court heard on Monday from Detective Superintendent Sean Hansen, who was part of the police's National Security Group at the time. He provided details of the first interaction Samsudeen had with police.

Authorities were alerted to Samsudeen after finding an account on social media in March 2016 under the name Aathill Al-Ceyloni Al-Moori.

The account had posted photographs and videos of graphic violence against Muslims on its public page, along with comments supporting violent extremism and ISIL (Islamic State, or ISIS) terrorist attacks overseas.

That prompted a visit from police to assess Samsudeen's level of risk, as well as give him a verbal warning.

"The first visit, it was assessed that we had some concerns about him and his responses didn't give us a sense that he was likely to stop having those views," Hansen said

"He presented somewhat of a threat."

But a second visit in May that year, Hansen said, appeared more successful.

"He gave the staff that dealt with him at the time a sense that he had acknowledged that what he was doing was wrong, and that he was pulling away from that, and gave them some confidence that we didn't need to undertake any further follow-up with him," he said.

"It was a judgement call by the staff at the time."

Ahamed Samsudeen visiting the New Lynn Woolworths about a month prior to the attack. Supplied

That success was short-lived however, with police learning in October that Samsudeen had reopened his Facebook account and posted more material.

He was finally arrested in 2017 at Auckland Airport, with the Security Intelligence Service (SIS) believing he was travelling to Syria to join ISIL fighters there.

While in prison, Hansen said Samsudeen was obstructive towards staff.

"When we went to visit him in prison, he refused to come out of his cell," Hansen said. "He called obscenities, he really refused to engage with us at all."

As a result, police started pulling back from attempts to physically see Samsudeen, to see if there were other ways they could work with or around him.

Police were still trying to engage with Samsudeen when he was released from prison in 2018 and bailed to a mosque, Hansen said.

"We had some, probably call them transactional visits in terms of getting a passport. We assisted Corrections at times in terms of finding him accommodation.

"Really, what our efforts throughout this period - and they continued through - was to do as much as we could to put him in an environment where he would then cooperate and engage with us so we could start some disengagement work."

But Samsudeen was back in prison by August 2018, where he would stay until his release seven weeks before the attack.

Hansen said shortly before his release, Samsudeen stopped engaging with police altogether.

Hansen was asked by the chair of the mosque, who cannot be named, why the community had been kept in the dark rather than consulted in confidence when Samsudeen first came onto their radar.

"I think to be fair, it was with the benefit of hindsight, that we can now say he was quite clearly radicalised," he said.

"Our view at the time was that he wasn't, hence the reason we stopped any proactive work with him, and the SIS was left to manage that lead as an intelligence case."

The mosque chair asked Hansen if there were people of interest who posed a similar risk as Samsudeen currently out in the community.

"What I can say is New Zealand is not free from violent extremism, we're not free from violent extremists. That's why we have the SIS, and we have other agencies, is to manage that particular risk and threat that faces our communities."

He was asked by the lawyer representing police, Alysha McClintock, if the mosque Samsudeen stayed at in the time before the attack in 2021 had been told about his level of risk.

"As I understand from the staff, the degree of risk that he posed was conveyed, and why he had been in prison had been conveyed."

Hansen said the best outcome for the country was a preventive one, but did not know if prevention should sit with any one agency.

"We are firmly of the view the best long-term outcome for New Zealand in terms of violent extremism and terrorism is a preventive one.

"I've seen the carnage in Australia and the UK in particular with the impact of imprisoning people for long periods of time - it presents them with some very difficult issues when they come out of prison."

World.title: Greens promises to cut power bills and make solar more affordable with $980m 'KiwiPower' plan
World.content:
The Green Party has pledged to set up a publicly-owned entity to boost investment in renewable energy and ensure affordable power and energy security.

Co-leaders Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson unveiled the party's energy policy at the Dunedin Gasworks Museum on Monday, the site of the country's first and last place to manufacture coal gas.

They promised to make power bills more affordable by making it easier for renters and homeowners to generate their own power, and set up and fund the new entity called KiwiPower using $980 million from the party's "super-rich tax" over four years.

KiwiPower would start with $100m a year for operating costs and $142m a year for new investment.

The policy also includes zero-interest clean energy loans to install solar and batteries for up to 90 percent of homeowners, legalising plug-in solar and investing $80m into renewable energy for Māori housing.

It would also expand government grant programme Warmer Kiwi Homes to offer more upgrades to make more low-income homes warm, dry and energy efficient, costing $969.8m over four years for 50,000 upgrades.

The party promised for solar to be installed on more than half of all public homes within four years at a cost of $460m and to invest $200m for community energy projects, which the party said would be funded by reallocating subsidies for fossil fuel companies.

Swarbrick said the market and successive governments had failed to deliver affordable, secure, renewable power.

"200,000 households are unable to afford to heat their homes while four big power companies control over 85 percent of the market and rake in massive profits," she said.

"A warm, dry home powered by clean energy should be within everyone's reach. That is the country we can build, and this is how we do it."

The plan would lower bills, cut emissions and put power back in the hands of New Zealanders and could be funded by making corporations and the super rich "pay their fair share", Swarbrick said.

"KiwiPower will invest directly in new renewable generation and sort out our dry-year problem sensibly, without a billion-dollar LNG facility, and support new, independent players coming into the market."

Swarbrick said the Greens had chosen to launch the plan at the Dunedin Gasworks Museum because gas belonged in a museum rather than in modern policy.

Davidson said the plan gave back ownership to communities and invested in Māori and public housing.

"Tangata whenua are two to three times more likely to face energy hardship," she said.

"This is about rangatiratanga over energy and it is part of our enduring commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi."

World.title: Government moves to keep cement production in NZ with up to $60m in financial support
World.content:
The government is providing up to $60 million in financial support to Golden Bay Cement to ensure its Northland operations can continue.

The move was announced in a release to the NZX on Monday morning by Golden Bay Cement's owner, Fletcher Building.

Fletcher Building said the support reflects a specific, one-time response to an exceptional set of circumstances.

The release states the government has granted Golden Bay Cement up to $60m, but does not go into detail about the terms of the support or the form it will take.

Fletcher Building said the agreement recognises the strategic importance of domestic cement manufacturing to New Zealand's infrastructure supply chain and national resilience, and addresses the carbon cost disadvantage Golden Bay Cement faces relative to imported cement.

Golden Bay Cement's operations in Northland are the country's only domestic cement manufacturing facility, supplying about 60 percent of the cement used in New Zealand.

The financial support follows an independent assessment, which Fletcher Building said confirmed that without support, rising costs, including carbon costs, would force the plant to close and result in a shift to an import-only model from 2030.

Earlier this month, the Employers and Manufacturers Association issued a pre-election policy wish list calling on the government to consider financial incentives for industries deemed critical to the country's economic future.

Fletcher Building chief executive and managing director Andrew Reding said: "Without government support, increasing costs, including carbon emission costs that our competitors importing cement from overseas do not currently incur at the same level, would likely have required us to close the plant and move to an import-only model from 2030.

"Domestic cement production matters for New Zealand's resilience as much as for its economics."

As part of the announcement, Golden Bay Cement has agreed to invest $150m through to 2040 in continued operations, optimisation, resilience and decarbonisation initiatives at its Northland plant.

The investment will be phased over time and remains subject to Fletcher Building's normal capital governance and approval processes, with the specific programme to be agreed with the government.

In a separate statement, Economic Growth Minister Nicola Willis said the government "did not take this decision lightly" and undertook "rigorous" analysis of the situation, including the risk of setting a new precedent.

"Ultimately, we concluded that this is an exceptional case, which meets the very high bar needed to justify taxpayer support."

She said the country would have been left "massively exposed" to global supply disruptions if the Golden Bay factory shut down, as it was New Zealand's only fully integrated cement manufacturing plant.

"Cement has no practical substitutes. It is needed for the building of homes, hospitals, schools, roads, and other nationally significant infrastructure. Any reductions in its availability could bring essential construction and infrastructure development, and the economic activity they support, to a standstill."

Cabinet ministers considered the case in May and included a "limited envelope of funds" in the Budget's operating allowance as a "tagged contingency". They have since been in negotiations with Fletcher over the size of the grant and the conditions attached.

Willis said Cabinet also considered "alternative forms of regulatory relief" to the costs imposed by the Emissions Trading Scheme, but ultimately decided against that so not to undermine the scheme's integrity.

"In an uncertain world, the government has acted to secure New Zealand's national economic resilience," Willis said.

The ACT party - which has long bemoaned "corporate welfare" - said it supported keeping New Zealand's biggest cement plant operating.

But ACT's climate change spokesperson Simon Court said the need for taxpayer intervention proved the country's climate settings were not working.

"The government has loaded emissions costs onto local production, put it at a disadvantage against imported cement, and then handed Fletcher Building $60 million to keep the plant open.

"This is why ACT is campaigning to reset New Zealand's climate targets, so they work for New Zealand, rather than driving jobs and production offshore."

World.title: Former Victim Support staff need to be part of workplace culture investigation - Chief victims advisor
World.content:
The Chief Victims Advisor says former Victim Support staff need to be spoken to as part of an investigation into its workplace culture, confidence in leadership and workplace complaints processes.

But Victim Support said that won't be happening and only current staff would be involved.

The external review comes after reporting by RNZ over claims of a "toxic" and "bullying" workplace culture, four years after an investigation into similar allegations.

RNZ spoke to several current and former workers who raised concerns about the culture at Victim Support. One person described it as a "very unsafe environment".

The agency's chief executive James McCulloch earlier said the agency "does not accept that these claims reflect Victim Support today".

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

However, on Thursday, McCulloch told staff the leadership team and Board had recently agreed "in consultation with our main funder Ministry of Justice" to undertake another independent external review of the agency's workplace culture.

He said the reviewer would speak one-on-one with a random sample of people across the organisation.

There would also be an opportunity for anyone currently working at Victim Support to request a meeting with the reviewer. Participation would be "voluntary and confidential," he said.

Chief Victims Advisor Ruth Money told RNZ on Friday she was happy to learn a review had been agreed to between Victim Support and the Ministry of Justice.

Chief Victims Advisor Ruth Money. (File photo) NZME / Alex Burton

"The terms of reference will be key to ensure that those who have left during the last 18 months are also included as their feedback will provide relevant information for the independent review

"I wish to acknowledge the bravery and resilience of those who have spoken to RNZ to highlight these important issues and ensure that victims across New Zealand get the best support possible from a team who are well supported themselves."

A former Victim Support staff member told RNZ they knew of at least six former staff who wanted to speak as part of the review.

Another former staff member welcomed the review, but said if it only focused on current employees it "risks missing the very people whose experiences prompted the review in the first place".

"Many former staff left because they believed they could no longer work in the organisation. Their experiences are critical if the review is to provide a genuine assessment of Victim Support's culture," the former staffer said.

"If those voices are absent, the review cannot claim to present a complete or balanced picture."

Victims advocate Claire Buckley said she believed the review should include former staff.

Victims advocate Claire Buckley. (File photo) Supplied

"It needs to focus on the last 12 to 18 months of staff leaving, otherwise... we are wasting taxpayer money on yet another review to confirm what is already known."

She repeated her earlier calls for the tender process to be open to the public for another organisation to put in a bid.

In response to questions about whether former staff would be included a Victim Support spokesperson said the review was focused on the agency's current workplace culture, confidence in people leadership, and how well our processes for raising and resolving concerns are working.

"For that reason, it will involve current staff.

"The detailed terms of reference will be agreed with the Ministry of Justice and are designed to give us a clear picture of the organisation as it is today. It will also build on previous work, including the independent 2024 culture check-in, which captured the views of staff at that time."

The review

In a statement to RNZ on Thursday, Victim Support confirmed it had agreed to commission a review of the organisation's workplace culture, confidence in people leadership and the processes for resolving workplace concerns.

"The review has been discussed with the Ministry of Justice and will build on previous independent work, including the 2024 culture check-in.

"Evidence from the past three years - including independent reviews, audits and staff surveys - has consistently indicated that we have a positive workplace culture.

"Getting robust, independent information is already a normal part of how we assess and strengthen our organisation. Being wellbeing-first means we take concerns raised by our people seriously, including those reported through media. With that, now is an appropriate time to get further independent assurance about what is working well and where improvements may be needed."

Victim Support said an independent reviewer would speak one-to-one with a random sample of people across Victim Support.

"Staff can also request an interview. Participation will be voluntary and confidential. The review is expected to begin in August, with the final report anticipated before the end of the year.

"Victim Support will publicly share a summary of the findings and carefully consider any recommendations. To protect people's privacy, findings will be reported in themes rather than attributed to individuals."

In a statement, McCulloch said the team at Victim Support had made "big strides in recent years".

World.title: Christchurch man arrested after alleged breach of medicinal cannabis licence
World.content:
A Christchurch man with a medicinal cannabis licence has allegedly been using cannabis for personal reasons in breach of his licence.

The 40 year old man was arrested after police searched his central Christchurch home over the weekend and found cannabis and paraphernalia alleged to be for personal use.

Acting Detective Senior Sergeant Brad Grainger said this was outside the licence authority and was offending against the Misuse of Drugs Act.

"The medicinal cannabis licensing system exists to support patients who require cannabis-based products for health reasons, not for someone to allegedly hide behind it for their own personal use and profit.

"We're actively keeping an eye on unlawful sale and supply of drugs in Canterbury and will hold those to account that undermine any systems designed to help vulnerable people."

The man has been charged with possession of cannabis for supply and possession of cannabis.

Police are still assessing information and further charges or arrests have not been ruled out

The case has also been referred to the Medicinal Cannabis Agency, the regulatory authority responsible for New Zealand's medicinal cannabis licensing scheme.

The man due to appear in the Christchurch District Court on 24 July 2026.

World.title: Massive Southland data centre's water consent concerns engineer
World.content:
Data centre water consent concerns engineers Nine To Noon Download MP3 18m

A leading expert on consents for water is warning the country's resource management scheme is not fit to manage the long term impact of hyperscale data centres.

Singapore-based company Datagrid was given 10 resource consents this year for an AI factory in Southland, that included the ability to draw more than 600,000 litres of groundwater every day and to discharge some 5000 litres of treated wastewater.

Expected to open in 2028, the 78,000 square metre AI factory in Makarewa was tracking to become the second single biggest user of electricity behind the aluminium smelter at Tiwai Point, near Bluff.

Chairperson of a climate change research group at Water New Zealand, engineer Evan Vaughters, told Nine to Noon, the sheer scale of water the consents allow the data centre to use meant there could be long term unforeseen consequences and the consents did not provide for the kind of monitoring needed to assess this.

But Datagrid said it would not use any groundwater - preferring rainwater when needed.

Vaughters agreed technologies pointed to the fact the centre would primarily use rainwater harvesting but he said it begged the question, why were the consents needed if that were the case.

The volumes consented for, 600,000 litres a day from a groundwater reserve was high, Vaughters said, and would be about the amount a town the size of Kaikōura would run on.

Data centres used large amounts of water mainly for cooling the systems, Vaughters said, and as a water professional it was something he was very interested in.

Inside Google's data centre in Douglas County, Georgia, in the US. (File photo) UNU-INWEH Google Gallery

He said due to the water being used for cooling the wastewater discharge ended up having quite an increased temperature, so additional energy costs then had to go towards cooling the wastewater prior to its discharge.

"Certainly it wouldn't be a long walk off a short pier to say that there is a much wider resource allocation question here.

"For instance, they've been able to demonstrate they can mitigate the localised effects taking from this particular aquifer but the bigger question is, is this the best use of those finite water resources, and the wider energy picture, is that the best allocation for the grid?"

Globally, Vaughters said regulatory frameworks needed to be thinking about doing better with the climate.

"We build and plan on the environment of the past and [we] need to be thinking about the environment of the future."

Data centres were simply a technology that did not exist when these frameworks were created, he said.

A proposed Amazon data centre site in Auckland's Westgate. Google Maps / Screenshot

"At the moment they're [Datagrid], assuming they don't need to use high amounts of groundwater but what if that changes?

"Once you're consented we move on and focus on what's inside our box."

Vaughters said New Zealand could look to Australia or the state of New York for guidance on data centre approvals.

"Australia for instance has now come out and said you need to incorporate new energy projects alongside these projects, the state of New York has just announced a moratorium on new data centres until they can get new framework in place."

Datagrid's executive chairperson Rémi Galasso declined to be interviewed on Nine to Noon, but said in a statement there was a vast difference between the absolute maximum amount permitted in a resource consent and the "highly efficient ultra green reality" of what Datagrid was building.

"Invercargill's cool temperatures allow it to rely entirely on free air cooling, no groundwater draw."

World.title: Entire Christchurch Comancheros gang chapter convicted in major drug bust
World.content:
Every member of the Christchurch chapter of the Comancheros Motorcycle Club has been convicted of drug-related offences following a seven-month police investigation.

Operation Avon, led by the National Organised Crime Group (NOCG) and Asset Recovery Unit identified a multimillion dollar drug trafficking operation from Invercargill to Auckland.

It led police to seizing approximately 5kgs of Class A drugs, 11 guns, ammunition and more than $250,000 in cash.

Police said they also restrained more than $1.9m in assets, including and Auckland property and 11 vehicles.

A motorbike seized by police as part of the operation. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

A second related investigation, Operation Leith, found a further eight people in the Southern South Island taking part in criminal activity, police said.

Twenty-nine people, aged between 18 and 55 were arrested and charged with a range of drug-related offences. All were now convicted.

The Christchurch chapter of the Comancheros became a priority for police due to its significant involvement in drug distribution and money laundering across New Zealand, police said.

Acting Detective Inspector Phil Sparks said investigators quickly uncovered large-scale offending involving methamphetamine, cocaine and extensive money laundering.

"This operation has significantly disrupted the Comancheros' ability to establish and maintain a foothold in Canterbury and has had a major impact on the drug supply chain across New Zealand."

Some of the guns seized. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

The gang coordinated the movement of drugs and cash between Auckland and Christchurch every few weeks, with drugs distributed throughout the South Island as far south as Invercargill, Sparks said.

More than $1 million worth of drugs at wholesale value was trafficked between the North and South Islands - equivalent to an estimated $15 million street value, he said.

"Crucially, the arrest and conviction of every member of the Christchurch chapter has effectively ended the Comancheros' presence in Christchurch and significantly weakened their influence across the wider South Island."

World.title: Tears and excitement as Spain win Football World Cup
World.content:
"Vamos" was heard from both of those cheering for Argentina and Spain.

But Spain came out on top, winning the Football World Cup final 1-0.

Inside central Auckland's Wynyard Pavilion, the whole crowd was singing, stamping.

Hundreds of people, dressed in red, knew their team were just minutes away from being world champions.

Finally, the ball found the back of the net, and the bar erupted. The loud cheering was accompanied by a person banging on a drum.

People hugged and kissed. A couple even threw their dog in the air. A man went outside to video call a family member, tears streaming down his face. The crowd of Spain supporters sang, danced, exalted.

They had watched for long, long minutes as their team had done everything bar beat Argentina.

Spain fans in Auckland CBD. RNZ / Jeremy Rees

Wearing the Iberian red of the Spanish strip, they had been exuberant, excited, then tense and silent as minutes ticked by.

"This is a team that can do everything except we don't have a Messi," said one red shirt at 80 minutes.

That was true. There were still three quarters of an hour of tension and worry to go as the game ticked down to injury time, then extra time.

It was heart stopping stuff. Endless Spanish attacks had the crowd on their feet. Then seconds later that exhalation, "Oooooh" as the shot was wide or blocked.

"España! España!", they chanted to will their team to victory.

But football is a terrible stark game. All that beauty and passing the ball through the eye of the needle means nothing when the score stands at 0-0.

And then, in minute 106, it came.

And the crowd erupted in relief, in joy, in fury, in pent up energy.

An Argentina fan reacts to Spain's game-winning goal. RNZ / Nick Monro

Up on the North Shore, there were also tears - but for a different reason at the Argentina watch party.

About 200 supporters crammed into a warehouse at Pachamama Latino Store in Glenfield to watch the game.

Proudly sporting blue and white and their Argentina kits, they cheered on their team all throughout the nail-biting game.

Fans earlier said they were confident Argentina had what it took to become back-to-back men's World Cup champions after winning the competition in 2022.

But it was not their day.

Football fans packed out Locker Room in Queenstown. RNZ / Katie Todd

Many in the crowd burst into tears at the result and embraced each other to cope with the loss of not only the title but Lionel Messi, who has indicated this would be his last World Cup match.

In Queenstown, the Locker Room sports bar erupted into scenes of equal elation and devastation as Spain locked in the win.

More than 280 fans from both sides had arrived as early as 6am, equipped with face paint and flags.

Spanish fans told RNZ they could not be more relieved or happy, while Argentinian fans said they felt their team had given it all.

World.title: A quick breakdown of the offside rule
World.content:
Spain has just won the FIFA World Cup 1-0 in a match against Argentina that ran down to the wire.

During extra time, it looked as though Ferran Torres had scored a goal that would have brought Spain's lead to two and sealed a victory.

It was the second goal disallowed for Spain, this time for offside.

So what is the offside rule?

It's an infamous question asked by millions of football newbies every tournament.

If you've jumped on the World Cup bandwagon and found yourself trying to wrap your head around this section of the rule book, we're here to help.

Here's a quick breakdown of the rule.

Why does it exist?

The offside rule aims to prevent players from lingering next to the opponent's net to wait for a pass.

It forces teams to build up play carefully and use complex tactics to score goals.

Without the rule, teams would be incentivised to constantly launch long balls, making the game less dynamic.

So how does it work?

If a player is called for an offside offence, the referee will stop the play and award an indirect free kick to the opposing team.

The free kick is taken from the spot where the offside player had been located when their teammate passed them the ball.

What is a free kick? Read more A free kick is awarded when a player on one team does something wrong, with the referee giving the other team a chance to kick the ball while play has stopped. A penalty is essentially the same thing, except the kick is taken inside the penalty box, which is directly in front of the goal, and opposing players aren't allowed to interfere until after the shot is taken. Goals can be scored from either a free kick or a penalty kick, but they are more easily achieved from penalties.

When is a player offside?

A player is in an offside position if:

they're standing in their opponent's half; and

they're nearer to the goal than both the ball and the last line of defenders at the exact moment the ball is passed to them by a teammate.

However, an offside player is only penalised if they become involved in play.

And there's no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from an opposition player, a goal kick, a throw-in or a corner kick.

World.title: Vingegaard forced out of Tour after fracture in 'devastating' crash
World.content:
Jonas Vingegaard will undergo surgery on a fractured collarbone after his Tour de France ended abruptly with a crash near the end of the 15th stage.

The 2022 and '23 Tour champion was among a few riders who fell close to a kerb some 20 kilometres from the end of the stage. After a few moments, Vingegaard's Tour was over as he limped into an ambulance with his right arm in a sling.

"Jonas sustained a fractured collarbone and multiple abrasions," his Visma–Lease a Bike team said in a statement posted on X. "Due to the severity of the collarbone fracture, surgical intervention has been recommended and will be performed in the coming days. Join us in wishing Jonas a smooth recovery."

Vingegaard had been in second place overall behind defending champion Tadej Pogačar heading into Stage 15, which finished with a big climb.

"It is devastating that Jonas has had to leave the Tour de France," the team's sporting director, Marc Reef, said. "It was quickly clear that Jonas could not continue. He was in a lot of pain."

The 29-year-old Danish rider became one of only eight male riders to have won all three Grand Tours this year.

"I'm really sad to see Jonas crash out," the four-time Tour champion Pogacar said.

" Without him, the Tour will not be the same. "

Vingegaard's teammate Sepp Kuss and Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate Isaac Del Toro also fell but were able to continue.

Pogačar's yellow jersey group slowed down after hearing news of the crash — perhaps unsure whether he would continue or not — but resumed racing normally after a few moments when it became clear Vingegaard was out.

Before crashing, Vingegaard looked poised to attack in the 11-kilometre final climb up Plateau de Solaison in the French Alps.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We had two riders in the breakaway and controlled the peloton," Reef said. "Jonas felt extremely good, and we wanted to go for the victory today. Unfortunately, cycling can be very cruel at times."

Del Toro finished the stage in third place behind Pogačar and stage winner Remco Evenepoel.

Evenepoel climbed to second in the standings, five minutes behind Pogačar, with Del Toro 5:58 back in third place.

Pogačar said after the stage that he and Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday morning by officials conducting unannounced anti-doping tests.

Pogačar said his test was carried out at 5am and that Vingegaard's was at 2am.

World.title: Fox takes out British Open, denies Aussie after 'two perfect shots'
World.content:
Golf has been left saluting tough New Zealander Ryan Fox after the son of an All Black gun delivered the round of his life, growing ever stronger as his rivals crumbled, to lift the Claret Jug as the British Open champion.

Feeling so nervous he was barely able to hold his putter on the final green at Royal Birkdale, the popular Kiwi still managed to play the perfect 18th hole, birdieing the brute with a 12-foot putt to win the title by one shot from American Cameron Young in Monday morning's thrilling finale.

Behind the 39-year-old was a host of tales of near-misses, including Australia's Lucas Herbert, who was still hanging tough in the hunt for the crown at the famous Lancashire links as he teed off at 17, still requiring two birdies to match clubhouse leader Young on nine-under.

But an untidy penultimate hole, where the 30-year-old drove into the bushes, got bunkered with his third shot and ended up with a bogey six, followed by a par at the last, ensured Herbert could only finish on six-under, tied for sixth, four shots behind the winner.

But up ahead, Fox, son of World Cup-winning All Black flyhalf Grant Fox, proved unbreakable in his mentality, looking, as he had all afternoon, like the one golfer out there ready to dare to attack for glory.

Fox, who became only the second New Zealander ever to lift the Jug after Bob Charles 63 years earlier, had endured bad luck during the round, coming up against a bunker lip on 15 and just trickling into a fairway sand trap after a fine drive on 17, but he refused to be daunted.

After missing a 10-footer on 17 to take the lead, he drove off on 18 tied with Young, who had earlier given all the field a severe target to match after a 64, the best round of the entire day.

Australia's Lucas Herbert (pictured) fell short of the British Open title despite a gallant effort. (Getty Images: Kate McShane)

Sam Burns was also in a position to match Young's total if he could hole his birdie putt at the last, but it slid by for the overnight leader to finish third on eight under.

But Fox played a glorious approach on the final hole, the popular Aucklander, who never wastes any time on the course, then quickly knuckling down to sink the winning putt for a 68 and a winning total of 10-under, before pumping his arms in joy.

"With me, it's always been 'see a shot, hit a shot'. As soon as I start thinking about it too much, then some bad stuff creeps in," smiled Fox.

"On the last, I hit two perfect shots. I'm not sure how I hit the putt. My hands were all over the place; I was just trying to get it towards the hole somewhere. It's surreal that it went in. Yeah, 'Champion Golfer of the Year' has a pretty good ring to it."

His wife and two children were in Florida. "I spoke to my kids last night, and they said, 'Bring back a trophy'. I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them!"

Ultimately, as the sea breezes kicked up to make Birkdale a real test on the final day, with Fox being one of only three players in the final 12 groups to shoot under par, all his main rivals were far too error-prone.

That included Herbert, who, like Fox, had earlier in the week recorded a record-equalling all-time low round in a men's major championship, with a landmark eight-under 62. His four bogeys on Sunday eventually sank him.

"I can't be too upset," shrugged the Victorian, who shot a final-round 71 but just missed out on the top-five finish which would have earned him a place in all the majors next season.

"A lot of positives to take. It's my best finish in a major. I genuinely contended. I was up around the lead for the last 45 holes. There's a lot to take away from that. I've learned so much this week."

World No.1 Scottie Scheffler (67) finished tied for fourth on seven under, alongside local hero Tommy Fleetwood (68), while South African Casey Jarvis (66) and Korean Si Woo Kim (72) were alongside Herbert in fourth.

Evergreen Australian Adam Scott, at the age of 46 and in his 101st consecutive major, earned his seventh top-10 finish in an Open, with a final round 66 earning him joint-ninth position on five under.

Like everyone else, though, Herbert was delighted for Fox, who's one of the most popular performers in golf. "His manager and my caddie are really close. Yeah, the Aussies and the Kiwis tend to stick together out there, familiar breed," smiled Herbert.

AAP

World.title: Spain will receive championship rings — but they'll also be for sale
World.content:
Spain was playing for more than the World Cup trophy. They were playing for rings as well.

For the first time, FIFA is awarding rings to commemorate a championship. Title-winning teams receiving rings is a tradition in North American sports that dates back to the late 19th century, but something that isn't commonplace in other parts of the world.

With this final in the US, the move by FIFA seems to be a nod to that tradition. Players on the World Cup-winning team will get gold medals, as usual, and the captain and coach of the winning team will get temporary rings as well shortly after the title match.

Eventually, Spain will get 30 customised rings. The World Cup trophy will be on one side, while the other side will be created "to reflect the identity of the winning team," FIFA said.

Only 2,026 rings — a nod to the year — will be made, and each will be individually numbered, custom-fitted and delivered with its own certificate of authenticity. The 1,996 rings that will not go to the winning team will be on sale to the public.

FIFA has not said how much those rings will cost.

The tradition of championship rings is believed to go back to at least 1893 when the Montreal Hockey Club was awarded the Dominion Hockey Challenge Cup, the precursor to what is now called the Stanley Cup. That team also commissioned simple bands with tiny hockey sticks attached at the top.

Major League Baseball teams began giving out championship rings in the 1920s, while NBA champions have received them basically since that league's inception in the late 1940s and NFL teams have gotten them throughout the entirety of the Super Bowl era that dates to the 1960s.

Some Halls of Fame give rings out to their members, and US Olympians and Paralympians have received rings as part of the perk package that comes with representing their country on the world stage.

Rings are now commonly awarded in all US pro sports — along with a number of college, high school and even youth sports — to commemorate championships.
