World.title: 'Open door to fraud': European body slams FIFA's World Cup integrity
World.content:
Europe's top human rights body has questioned the integrity of the World Cup and urged FIFA to help build a stronger framework for the 2030 edition, which will be played mostly in Spain and Portugal.

"The next crisis has already begun. It has two names: money and power," the head of the 46-nation Council of Europe wrote in an open letter to its formal working partner, FIFA, hours before the final between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Swiss politician Alain Berset cited FIFA suspending a ban for United States forward Folarin Balogun while under pressure from US President Donald Trump and the risk of fraud in the soccer body signing a prediction market as a World Cup sponsor.

"When the rules bend under pressure, every result is open to doubt," Berset wrote about Balogun being freed from a mandatory one-game ban to face Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake. Belgium won 4-1.

"Political influence has also moved onto the field," said Berset, who was twice a president of FIFA's home country, Switzerland.

Folarin Balogun was allowed to play after a red card following pressure from Donald Trump. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

"The sanction suspended mid-tournament came after a head of state called the president of FIFA."

FIFA signed a prediction market sponsor deal in April worth a reported $US150 million ($215 million) with ADI Predictstreet, one week after the Abu Dhabi-backed company was formally created. FIFA also has other commercial deals with the gambling industry for this World Cup.

Prediction betting has been criticised as rewarding insider trading, and Berset noted that in soccer it allowed wagers to be won on "moments a single player can produce without changing the score".

"It is an open door to fraud," he wrote.

"And this World Cup has opened the door wider."

The Council of Europe (CoE) aired its concerns publicly despite having a formal working agreement with FIFA signed by its president, Gianni Infantino, in 2018.

The intergovernmental body that created the European Convention on Human Rights has a stated mission: "To promote democracy, human rights and the rule of law across Europe and beyond."

When signing the FIFA-CoE memorandum of understanding eight years ago, Infantino said: "It is a natural relationship, as we share common values and goals: transparency, accountability, integrity, safety in sport and respect for human rights, for children's rights."

Infantino and Berset met in 2024 on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

FIFA's disciplinary ruling on Balogun was fiercely criticised by European soccer body UEFA, which said the decision "crossed a red line" in soccer's rule of law and transparency. FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining the reasoning of its disciplinary judge from the United Arab Emirates.

"A sanction suspended under pressure, within days, with no reasons given," Berset wrote, before adding other concerns about the first 48-team, 104-game World Cup.

The authority of referees is called into question. Racist abuse of players, some of it from elected officials. Betting on every pass, every card, every corner."

The next men's World Cup will be staged mostly in Europe, with Morocco also co-hosting. Three South American neighbours, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, are currently scheduled to host one game each at the start of the centenary edition in June 2030 to mark the original 1930 World Cup host, Uruguay.

"So here is my proposal to FIFA," Berset wrote.

"A working dialogue that starts tonight, to build the integrity framework of the 2030 World Cup before it is played."

World.title: World Cup final ends in glory for Spain and heartache for champion Messi
World.content:
Spain has beaten Argentina 1-0 to win the 2026 World Cup, with Ferran Torres coming off the bench to score the winner in extra time against 10-man Argentina.

Torres's goal came at the start of the second period of extra time, after a furiously tense final at the New York/New Jersey stadium in Meadowlands ended goalless after 90 minutes.

The win gives Spain its second men's World Cup title, echoing the extra-time goal by Andrés Iniesta in 2010 that led to its first title.

And it is impossible to say the European champion didn't deserve it.

Enzo Fernández was sent off for a second yellow card in stoppage time at the end of normal time, clattering into young player of the tournament Pau Cubarsí with an ugly challenge that sent the 19-year-old star flying.

The 10 men of Argentina could not hang on against the increasingly relentless attack of the Spanish.

Fernández's first yellow card was for dissent just 11 minutes earlier, one of six bookings the Argentines received in the game.

He became the sixth player in history to be sent off in a World Cup final. Argentina account for half of those dismissals, with Pedro Monzón and Gustavo Dezotti both sent off in the 1990 decider.

Spain made all the running in today's game, with Argentina failing to have a single shot in the opening 90 minutes of the contest.

The level of Spain's dominance can be illustrated by the fact it completed 235 passes in the final third of the pitch, while Argentina completed just 47.

By the time the referee blew full time at the end of normal time, Spain had 15 total shots, 10 of them on target.

Emi Martínez was by far the more active of the goalkeepers, making a series of stops to deny Lamine Yamal from a free kick and a glancing header from Nico Williams.

But he could do nothing to stop Torres's strike just 37 seconds into the final 15-minute period of extra time.

That was Spain's 20th attempt on goal in the match and, up until then, Argentina had offered none.

After going behind, the defending champion attempted to bring some pressure, with Lionel Messi fashioning chances from the right as Spain sat back and defended.

But even the Argentine magician could not conjure a late miracle, with Argentina only finishing with two attempts at goal for the game, the first of which came 26 minutes into extra time, a woeful return when the trophy was on the line.

Argentina was far more intent on niggly fouls than playing football, its 25 fouls the most in a World Cup game since their 2022 victory in the final against France.

After full time, Leandro Paredes disgraced himself by starting a scuffle with celebrating Spanish players, the 32-year-old shown a post-match red card.

The scrappy game was not helped by a 27-minute half time break, the longest at a World Cup, to accommodate an underwhelming and poorly received Super Bowl-style show.

US President Donald Trump presented the trophy to the victors, hovering awkwardly at the side of the stage as Spain captain and player of the tournament Rodri lifted the trophy.

Look back at how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Antonelli extends F1 championship lead, heartbroken Russell crashes out in Belgium
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has extended his lead at the top of the F1 championship standings with victory in the Belgian Grand Prix, with George Russell crashing out in the first lap and Oscar Piastri overcoming an early knock to finish fifth.

Piastri suffered minor damage to his car in the incident which saw him collide with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc, who was cleared of wrongdoing by race officials and went on to claim second place.

And Piastri, who won this race last year, recovered well to ensure he finished in the scoring places behind Antonelli, with Max Verstappen third behind Leclerc.

Lewis Hamilton was placed fourth, but his Ferrari team are under investigation for an unsafe release, so there could yet be a change of order.

The incident followed another early controversy when Russell was forced to retire on the first lap after a prang with fellow Briton Hamilton to deal a huge blow to the Mercedes man's title hopes.

Russell, who had started third on the grid was attempting to overtake Hamilton when his rear wheel was tagged by the Ferrari driver, sending him spinning into the gravel and forcing the arrival of the safety car.

Russell drops to third in the drivers' championship and was fuming with the outcome having lost further ground on title leader Antonelli, and was once again left baffled by a mystery engine issue causing a speed deficit.

"I just got totally swallowed up down the straight, I lost three positions down the straight, down into turn five, then the incident was a racing incident," Russell told the host broadcaster.

"Maybe I could have gone a bit wider, maybe he could've braked a bit more.

"The incident shouldn't have happened if I had the speed down the straight.

"Very, very disappointing … felt like I was in a position to fight for the lead after turn one and suddenly no power and it's all gone."

Russell was bitterly disappointed with his early exit from the race. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

The victory was the sixth of the season for teenage driver Antonelli and the first since last month's Monaco Grand Prix, which leaves him 45 points clear of Russell in the championship.

"Let's go!" he screamed to the Mercedes team over the radio.

"Thank you so much, guys, thank you."

Piastri's McLaren team-mate, Lando Norris, started 13th due to a grid penalty but he still finished seventh after a pit-stop delay.

Frenchman Isack Hadjar finished sixth behind Piastri for Red Bull, despite starting at the back of the field because of a penalty.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Brondello suspended by WNBA for inappropriate comment
World.content:
Australian coach Sandy Brondello has been suspended for one game by the WNBA for an inappropriate comment she used during a Toronto Tempo game against the Atlanta Dream.

Brondello, who coaches the Tempo as well the Opals, will miss Tuesday's AEST game against the Las Vegas Aces.

"The WNBA expects all coaches and team personnel to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and respect that are fundamental to our league," the league said in a statement announcing the suspension.

During the 111-92 loss to the Dream on Saturday AEST, the broadcast picked up Brondello addressing officials after Tempo player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury following contact with Angel Reese.

Sabally was called for the foul and Brondello could be heard saying Reese was a "protected species".

The "protected species" phrase is commonly used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player.

In the US, however, the phrase can be considered derogatory towards black people.

Angel Reese took to social media in response to Sandy Brondello's comment. (Getty Images: Mark Blinch)

Brondello posted an apology on social media.

"Angel, I'm sorry," Brondello wrote on X.

"Last night, in the emotion of the moment after Nyara's injury, I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that. My frustration was with the officiating, but my words unfairly put the focus on you."

How Brondello hopes to topple US No country has been able to topple the United States at either the FIBA World Cup or the Olympics since 2006. Here's what Sandy Brondello is doing to try to get Australia's Opals over the hump.

Reese took to social media after the game, posting: "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" and tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

"I also understand that my words carried an impact beyond what I intended, particularly for black women in our league, and I'm deeply sorry for that," Brondello posted.

"I've spent my career competing with, coaching and learning from incredible black women."

Brondello added: "I regret that my words caused hurt to a community I respect so deeply.

"I have a lot of respect for you as both a player and a person, and I sincerely apologise to you, your teammates, and the Dream organisation for my comment."

Just why? ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌ ҉ ͡ ͞ ͞ ͞ ҉● ࿀ ● ࿀ ● ҉⃝ ⃝͢ ͞ ͘ ͞⃝̕ ͢ ̛ ⃝ ̸ ̡ ͢⃝̧ ͡ ͡ ̀ ̧ ̢⃝͜ ҉ ͞ ͞ ⃝͞ ͞ ͡⃝ ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊( ̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ What am I supposed to do with this? It’s un-Googleable. Unpronounceable. It doesn’t even render the same way on various platforms. It looks one way on YouTube Music. Another on Apple Music. And yet another on Bandcamp. Even the artist name ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ is an unpronounceable series of glyphs that would make Prince shake his head. So, from here on out, I’m just going to refer to ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ by his more well-known alias, Four Tet, and the album as Wingdings. My apologies to Kieran Hebden for disregarding his intent, but I’ve got readers to consider. Also, shoutout to subscriber morgannels for bringing this one to my attention in last week’s what are you listening to thread. ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌ ҉ ͡ ͞ ͞ ͞ ҉● ࿀ ● ࿀ ● ҉⃝ ⃝͢ ͞ ͘ ͞⃝̕ ͢ ̛ ⃝ ̸ ̡ ͢⃝̧ ͡ ͡ ̀ ̧ ̢⃝͜ ҉ ͞ ͞ ⃝͞ ͞ ͡⃝ ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊( ̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ by ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ For years, Hebden has kept this alias somewhat of a secret. But now that this collection of wingdings has racked up millions of listens on services like Spotify, it’s get a more formal release with wingdings. Some of the tracks here have been released previously, including track five, which Fred Again dropped during his incredible Boiler Room set as “Feelings,” under one of Hebdens’ other aliases, KH. Wingdings leans heavily towards Four Tet’s dancier outputs. And, despite what the project’s origins as some sort of secret b-side dumping ground might lead you to believe, these are not throwaways. They’re undeniable, infectious, and highly polished. Four Tet’s sense for sound design shines from crushed 8-bit drums to the hypnotic handpan grooves and sharp synth melodies. While the songs are definitely groovy and danceable, they’re not high-octane rave-ups, for the most part. Instead, tracks like number seven build to a more ecstatic and spiritual climax as layers pile up and textures demand you turn your eyes towards the sky. Not unlike last week’s recommendation, Shall We Go On Sinning So That Grace May Increase?, Wingdings is a celebration. No, I might not drop the triphop-esque track one at the club, but it’s perfect for finding your groove while trying to write, or cleaning, or any other activity where you want good vibes and grooves. Track two would feel more at home on a dance floor with its deep four-on-the-floor thump and plucked arpeggios that seem to be constantly climbing off into infinity as house hi-hats tick along. Track three blends metallic gamelan-inspired melodies and ultradeep EDM wubs, while track eight is beautiful comedown ambiance. Four Tet’s Wingdings is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Deezer, and Qobuz.

Tech.title: I hate that I don’t hate this song made with Suno
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I would never go so far as to say there’s no place for AI in music (I’m a fan of Holly Herndon, after all). But I generally find music made with generative AI to be offensively boring, especially the outputs of Suno. So I’m having a bit of a tough time processing the fact that I actually quite enjoy 1010Benja’s “Semiramis’ Dream.”

Benja has been unapologetic about his use of generative AI on his latest EP, Time Has Nothing To Do With What You Choose… The other three tracks can’t quite hold a candle to what you find on 2024’s Ten Total. But the opener “Semiramis’ Dream” is infectious. It explodes out of the speakers with a jungle beat and Benja’s incredible, obviously human voice front and center.

You’d be forgiven for not immediately realizing that the song is the product of Suno. It lacks many of the dead giveaways. Even the most obviously AI part of the song — the choir of backup vocalists — is easily camouflaged amidst the hyperpop-influenced rapid-fire chops. Heavily processed and artificial-sounding vocals are a staple of many modern pop genres and, by leaning into that uncanniness, Benja is able to mask their origins.

But Benja isn’t hiding. He told Hearing Things in an interview:

My friend Patrick Holder did the beat. I recorded the vocals. Then we fed Suno the elements, settled on something, brought it out, edited it on Ableton, and then put it back into Suno. So when you look in Deezer, it marks the song as AI-generated. We’re not hiding it. We don’t feel any shame about it.

Benja’s process certainly separates it from the rest of the Suno slop out there. He wrote the lyrics, sang the vocals, and worked with collaborators to perform the music. Then fed that into Suno, took what the AI spit out, brought it into Abelton, edited it, added more layers, fed that back into Suno… rinse repeat ad naseum. Benja estimates he did this a few hundred times for “Semiramis’ Dream.”

While Benja professes to be agnostic about the tools he uses, he is under no illusion that using generative AI doesn’t come with ethical baggage. He acknowledges the damage it’s doing to the planet, but somewhat nihilistically says we can’t stop greedy corporations or put the AI genie back in the bottle: “The good guy doesn’t win this one,” he says.

The only reason I’m using gen at all is because my visions are currently far beyond my means. People have been asking me, “Did you use gen AI for this EP?” I’m like, [sarcastically] “No, I hired a professional children’s choir.” What are we talking about? I haven’t paid rent last month, and I won’t pay rent this month. I don’t know where the fuck I’m gonna be.

It’s hard not to empathize with Benja. Despite seeming to be on the verge of a breakout and earning a coveted Best New Music from Pitchfork for Ten Total, he’s a struggling artist who has endured periods of homelessness.

Still, it’s also worth acknowledging that there is little on “Semiramis’s Dream” sonically that he couldn’t have achieved without AI. Sure, he couldn’t hire a children’s choir, but it’s not like the AI one found throughout the Time Has Nothing To Do With What You Choose… is particularly convincing. A similar effect could be accomplished with some layered performances and smart vocal processing.

1010Benja hasn’t converted me — I still remain deeply skeptical of AI art. But he has proven that, in the right hands, Suno doesn’t have to be a slop engine.

Tech.title: The FBI reportedly won’t investigate ICE anymore
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to the New York Times, federal agents have been told that the FBI will no longer be investigating confrontations involving ICE agents. The DHS and DOJ denied the change in policy to The Times.

The reported change in guidance follows renewed scrutiny of violence by ICE agents who have killed two people in the last two weeks. The shootings in Maine and Texas were just the latest civilian deaths at the hands of ICE agents, who have attempted to intimidate witnesses following its recent spate of high-profile killings.

The new guidance would end FBI investigations of assaults against DHS agents. The government has aggressively pursued cases against protesters and others who have had even fleeting and unintentional physical contact with agents. But those felony assault cases routinely fall apart, with nearly half of them ending with an acquittal, the charges being thrown out, or withdrawn, according to a Times analysis.

While the FBI investigations are ostensibly to help the government make a case against protesters and others, they often provide evidence against the officers that could be used in future trials against them.

According to The Times:

Under the change, responsibility for investigating cases involving federal immigration officers would likely fall to Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, effectively leaving the agency to investigate itself…Homeland Security Investigations does not have jurisdiction to investigate civil rights violations, so putting the change into practice would make it far less likely that shootings of unarmed people by ICE agents would be investigated to determine if the agents broke federal law.

Tech.title: Orchid is a delightfully retro and approachable hipster synth
Tech.content:
In 2017, I bought an old Magnus chord organ off Craigslist for $10. It’s one of my favorite music gear purchases. Electric chord organs let you play full chords with just a press of a button, making them perfect for aspiring singer-songwriters or fooling around at home. But chord organs largely fell out of favor in the ’80s, as digital keyboards like those from Casio grew in popularity.

The Telepathic Instruments Orchid attempts to recapture some of that simple parlor instrument magic. Just like those vintage electric chord organs, the Orchid allows you to play rich chord progressions without having to master a ton of theory or complex fingering. It’s not an instrument that demands mastery. It’s a way for songwriters to sketch out ideas with minimal fuss, and it expands on the chord organ heritage with distinctly modern twists.

The Orchid was designed in collaboration with Kevin Parker of Tame Impala. Aesthetically, it harkens back to ’60s brown-and-tan organs by the likes of Magnus and Bontempi. The speaker grill even resembles the fan vents on those classic instruments. It’s definitely a spiritual successor, just, you know, a lot more expensive at $649.

But where a Magnus organ is limited in how many one-button chords it can play by the number of physical reeds it can hold, the Orchid is all digital and can theoretically play any chord, in any voicing, from any scale. It also means that the Orchid can sound like more than just the beautiful droney cousin of an accordion.

Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

For a songwriter, this means you can focus on your lyrics and vocal melody. If, like me, you struggle to sing and play an instrument at the same time, this can take a huge mental load off. The variety of sounds also means that not everything needs to sound like a funeral dirge or a sea shanty, which isn’t necessarily the case with an old-school chord organ.

If you have even a passing knowledge of music theory (and it would be generous to call mine even passing), you should have little trouble with Orchid. There’s a one-octave keyboard and a handful of buttons to the left of it that correspond to different chord types, i.e., major, minor, diminished, major 7th, and so on. Press C and major, and you get a C major. Press F# and 9, and you get an F#9. Simple.





The Orchid’s E-Piano sound playing chord stabs over a drum beat.(opens a new window) The Orchid’s E-Piano sound playing chord stabs over a drum beat.

The Orchid can really hold your hand if you want it to (and I usually do). You can lock the Orchid to a particular key, so that it will only play chords in the key of E minor or Bb major. That means almost anything you play will at least sound decent and in tune. If your understanding of chord theory is limited, this can really expand your sonic palette with minimal frustration. I often found myself using the chord engine to find a progression I liked as the backbone of a track I could build on top of when jamming in my studio.

But the Orchid can do more than just blast out chords in a single block. It has strum, harp, and arpeggiator modes, plus 13 different preprogrammed patterns. My favorite performance mode (as they’re called) is “slop,” which introduces tiny random timing imperfections that approximate a human actually playing the chord, rather than a machine. The more you turn it up, the more unevenly the notes are struck.





The Orchid’s drum machine and a simple synth pad make a gorgeous combo.(opens a new window) The Orchid’s drum machine and a simple synth pad make a gorgeous combo.

Vintage chord organs have a uniquely droney sound, not unlike a particularly buzzy accordion, that, even 40 years later, was still inspiring artists like El-P. But the Orchid can produce a much broader palette of sounds.

There are three simple synth engines under the hood: one is a virtual analog (VA) synth, another an FM synth for ’80s-style e-pianos and bells, and lastly, a reed piano, perfect for getting those Wurlitzer sounds, but it can also give you more gentle Rhodes electric piano tones as well. I often found myself firing up distorted and heavily reverbed pads on the VA engine and using the Orchid almost like a fidget toy, noodling on simple chord progressions when I needed to focus. You can always connect Orchid to a computer or another synth and use it as a MIDI controller if you want access to its one-key chords but a broader palette of sounds.

Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

There are 70 presets (excluding bass patches, which we’ll get to in a minute) built into the Orchid, and they cover most of your bases. It’s a good thing, too, since there are very few ways to tweak the sounds directly on Orchid. You can change the filter cutoff or tweak the intensity of effects like reverb or phaser, but that’s basically it. Instead, if you want to design your own patches, you’ll need to spend $99 for the Pistil virtual synth ($50 bundled with the Orchid), which can send custom sounds to Orchid. I’ve found Pistil to be a bit buggy, and the UI often freezes after transferring patches.

Orchid also has a dedicated bass section, separate from the main synth, that you can turn on and off. There are only 12 sounds, but they cover most essentials, from low electric piano octaves to Moog-style synth bass, tuned 808s, and aggressive EDM drones. They can be layered with the main keys to add subtle depth to a chord progression or be played solo.





The Orchid handling both synth arp and bass duties simultaneously. (opens a new window) The Orchid handling both synth arp and bass duties simultaneously.

The accompaniment options are where Orchid can become a bit more complicated than just a simple chord machine. If you don’t lock it to a specific key, and you set the bass to only play along with chords, then you can have the low-end thump locked to your chord progression, and still add melodic flourishes on top without the bass when you’re not pressing any of the chord buttons. Though because of how Orchid handles polyphony — you can’t play multiple keys at once — this can be more frustrating than useful, depending on the patch. If a patch has a long decay time, for instance, chords will cut off abruptly if you try to play a solo note. You’re better off using the built-in audio looper, which lets you record chord progressions, basslines, and melodies separately, for a bit more flexibility.

I am head over heels for the built-in drum machine. It’s extremely limited. You can’t program a custom beat, you can’t tweak the sounds. Yet I think it’s basically perfect, even if it would be nice to have the option for user-uploaded beats from within Pistil. It’s again inspired by vintage gear from the ’70s, namely rhythm machines like the Korg Mini Pops that played preprogrammed beats to accompany home organs. The lo-fi, almost twee sound of these machines is among my favorites in the world of drum machines.





Playing drums, bass, and synth all at the same time on the Orchid. (opens a new window) Playing drums, bass, and synth all at the same time on the Orchid.

The Orchid is fun, sounds good, and is simple to use. But it’s also quite limited. You can’t design your own sounds without paying extra for the Pistil software. The keyboard is small, and you can’t actually play chords on it: You can only play one key at a time, and all the chord voicings come from the chord buttons on the left. That means that if you do know how to play a Dm13 on the piano, for example, you can’t do it on the Orchid’s keyboard. This is a bit of an annoyance, and one of the key differences between it and a vintage chord organ. It varies from model to model, but my personal Magnus organ only has dedicated buttons for Bb, F, C, A, D, and G major chords. Of course, I can always play any chord I want using the Magnus’ regular two-octave keyboard.

Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

There are far more capable synths in the $649 price range. But the Orchid isn’t trying to compete with the Korg Minilogue or the Arturia MiniFreak. If you want to tinker and design your own synth patches from scratch, spend your money elsewhere. The Orchid isn’t for tinkering. It’s more of a songwriting tool than a synth. If you’re a singer / songwriter looking to escape the cliché of acoustic guitars or upright pianos, the Orchid offers an approachable, if pricey, electronic option.

Tech.title: US Marshals arrest the Tate brothers in Miami
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested Saturday in Miami by US Marshals in relation to new rape and sex trafficking charges in England. According to the Associated Press, British authorities are seeking the brothers’ extradition.

The new charges facing Andrew Tate include seven counts of rape, three of sex trafficking, three counts of assault, and “19 charges relating to sexual images of children and extreme ‘pornography,’” according to the New York Times. Tristan Tate faces two new charges of rape, one of sexual assault, and three of sex trafficking. This is in addition to the 21 charges already announced in 2025 by British authorities, plus ongoing investigations in Romania and the US.

The brothers had previously been indicted in Romania on trafficking and rape charges, but a judge threw the indictment out over procedural issues. Many believe the lifting of travel restrictions on the two and the judges’ decision may have been related to a pressure campaign by the Trump administration on the Romanian government. The White House was also accused of intervening on Andrew Tate’s behalf last year when customs officials seized his devices.

The two are self-proclaimed misogynists who have amassed a following online despite being banned from most platforms for hate speech, including YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. The two ran an online school that claimed to teach men how to free themselves from “socially induced incarceration” and how to recruit women into “sexual slavery.” They’ve also led an online school on how to make money in crypto, drop shipping, and “scam-adjacent activities,” according to Vox, with a pyramid scheme-like structure.

The two have repeatedly faced arrest and criminal investigations for their activities dating back to 2015.

Tech.title: The Clapper was a bad smart home gadget — and a viral sensation

Clap on. Clap off. Well, more like, Clap, pause for half a beat but no longer because otherwise it’ll stop hearing you, clap again because you waited too long, clap louder and faster, that didn’t work, clap two more times, and suddenly: on. The Clapper didn’t always work — and even when it did, it might fry your gadgets in the process — but it managed to become a big hit anyway.

On this episode of Version History, we tell the story of The Clapper, from its beginnings as The Great American Turn-On to its debut alongside one of the great advertising campaigns of all time. The Verge’s David Pierce and Victoria Song are joined by Allison Marsh, a writer and professor at The University of South Carolina, to dig into the device’s history and legacy, and to try and figure out once and for all whether this was a good product or just a great commercial.
